Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 15:07:06 GMT

The winning captains: Australia's Isabelle Kelly, her men's counterpart Isaah Yeo and England wheelchair skipper Lewis King

Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?

It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.

The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear,, external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.

But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.

For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.

Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.

England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.

And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.

"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.

"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.

"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."

That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.

The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.

That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.

For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.

While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams., external

Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.

With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.

This video can not be played

England become world champions for third time

Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.

That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.

Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.

France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.

Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.

"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.

"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.

"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.

"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."

A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits, external before a ball was kicked.

The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.

In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".

And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.

And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.

This video can not be played

Highlights: Australia beat New Zealand to win world cup for a fourth time in a row

'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point

Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup

Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup

Tonga fans streamed to stadiums in their numbers to support their team

An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer.

Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased.

That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago.

In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts.

This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby.

This video can not be played

Highlights: Australia beat New Zealand to win Women's Rugby League World Cup

Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure.

Instead of adults paying more than £20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to £9.74 per ticket.

But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game.

The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October.

That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full.

"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.

"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."

Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached.

Australia's women cantered to a record fourth World Cup title against New Zealand

Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.

Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.

This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.

In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.

Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.

Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.

"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."

In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."

And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.

The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.

Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.

Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.

And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 14:56:21 GMT

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:42:58 GMT

Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:37:45 GMT

A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.

Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.

"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.

It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.

Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.

Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.

Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

Man dies after being hit by ambulance

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:26:24 GMT

A man has died after being struck by an ambulance transporting a patient near Sunderland, police have said.

Northumbria Police said the crash occurred on the A19, between the junctions for the A1018 and A690, shortly after 02:00 GMT.

The ambulance was travelling on the northbound carriageway and did not have its blue lights on when it hit the man, who was in his 30s and died at the scene.

Neither the patient nor their partner who were travelling in the ambulance were injured in the collision, while the vehicle's driver, a man in his 40s, was also not hurt and remained at the scene to assist police with their inquiries.

The North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said the patient in the ambulance and their partner were transferred to another ambulance.

Officers from Northumbria Police's roads unit have launched an investigation into the collision.

Sgt Ben Rutherford said: "Our thoughts are firmly with the family and loved ones of the man who has tragically died following this collision.

"We will continue to support them in any way that we can at this incredibly difficult time."

Anyone with CCTV or dashcam footage of the incident itself or the moments leading up to the collision has been urged to contact the force.

Rutherford said anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, "could prove key to our investigation and help provide answers for the man's loved ones".

A NEAS spokesperson said: "Around [02:00] one of our ambulance crews was involved in a road traffic incident with a pedestrian on the A19 northbound, while transporting a patient and their partner to a nearby hospital.

"We dispatched a number of resources to the scene.

"The patient on board and their partner were transferred to another ambulance and taken to hospital for further treatment.

"Sadly, despite the best efforts of our crews attending, the patient injured as the result of the collision passed away at the scene.

"This is a hugely tragic incident for all involved.

"Our thoughts and condolences are with the patient's loved ones.

"We will now, of course, be working closely with the police to support their investigation."

Minister backs legal right to job support for young people

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:06:15 GMT

The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.

Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year.

Man and woman die in police pursuit crash

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:38:28 GMT

Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.

West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.

The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.

The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.

The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

A spokesperson for the IOPC said it had launched an independent investigation at about 02:30 and sent investigators to the crash scene to "begin gathering evidence".

The spokesperson said that inquiries were "at a very early stage".

A police scene and road closure remain in place in Gelderd Road, and drivers are advised to avoid the area and seek alternative routes. A steady stream of cars is being directed by officers to turn around at the cordon.

The area is made up of business units and car dealerships and was very quiet on this cold Sunday morning, with very few people about.

A dark car can be seen a short distance away from a very badly damaged white Volkswagen just outside a used car dealership.

Anyone who saw the vehicles before or during the crash and may have information or footage is urged to contact police.

Tearful McIlroy dedicates record-equalling win to ill dad

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:14:04 GMT

Rory McIlroy celebrated defending his Masters title with dad Gerry watching on at Augusta National

DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard

-15 Hatton (Eng); -10 McIlroy (NI); -8 Chacarra (Spa), Lindell (Fin); -7 Olesen (Den), Reitan (Nor), Laporta (Ita), Lindberg (Swe), Perez (Fra)

Selected others: -4 Wallace (Eng); -3 Rahm (Spa), Schaper (SA); Level Fleetwwod (Eng), Reed (US), Fox (NZ); +1 Rai (Eng)

Full leaderboard

Rory McIlroy wiped away tears as he dedicated his eighth Race to Dubai victory to his ill father, Gerry.

Moments after matching Colin Montgomerie's record of season-long European tour titles on Sunday, the Northern Irishman was asked about the health of his father.

An emotional McIlroy revealed Gerry has been in hospital for two months after "a huge operation" - a double lung transplant - at the end of September.

"He's recovering well, thankfully," McIlroy told the DP World Tour.

"But before I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him. He said to me: 'Go win The Race to Dubai'.

"This one's for him."

It came after a thrilling climax at the traditional season-ending DP World Tour Championship with Tyrrell Hatton securing a commanding victory, while McIlroy pipped Spaniard Eugenio Chacarra to the overall crown.

Hatton's closing six-under-par 66 helped him romp to a five-shot victory on 15 under par but most eyes were on the thrilling battle that went down to the final hole.

It is the fifth successive year that McIlroy has won the award and it has drawn him level with Montgomerie, the Scot who set a mark 21 years ago that few thought would ever be matched.

"Yeah, double digits," smiled McIlroy when asked what would be his final target of Race to Dubai victories.

"I'd love to surpass Monty next year and we'll go from there."

McIlroy's confidence in going along with a target shouted out by the fans surrounding the 18th green at the Earth Course in Dubai on Sunday was refreshing to hear.

But he appears to be playing and talking with a little more freedom in recent years - the sort of freedom that comes as a result of finally completing the career Grand Slam and winning successive Masters titles - and leads to declarations of winning 10, or more.

"Winning eight Order of Merits (Race to Dubai titles) was never in my list of goals growing up," said McIlroy, who closed with a bogey-free 67 to finish on 10 under and must surely now be considered Europe's greatest golfer.

"I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European tour and playing with him at the London Club in 2008, so to pull up alongside him and win eight of these means the world to me."

This video can not be played

Highlights: McIlroy wins the Race to Dubai

Race To Dubai finale - As it happened

After Jon Rahm's victory in Abu Dhabi last week, fellow former LIV Golf member Hatton showed his class with a five-shot success at the Earth Course at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

Hatton showed his combustible side earlier in the week but, despite later admitting to being "weirdly nervous" he appeared serene on Sunday.

In the final group and knowing he couldn't win the overall Race to Dubai title, he was detached enough to block out the scramble as he strolled to his ninth DP World Tour victory - even asking an on-course reporter who was going to win as he walked from the 17th green to 18th tee.

It was that head-to-head battle between Chacarra and McIlroy that dominated the tournament, a battle that, after a long hard season, came right down to the wire.

Both players knew victory would win them the title. There were permutations galore for finishing second, third, or below that.

Chacarra and McIlroy went toe-to-toe in and the overall lead in the rankings chopped and changed down an absorbing back nine as neither man backed down.

At one juncture just one-tenth of a point separated the pair.

But a late surge from Northern Ireland's McIlroy allowed him to finish runner-up behind England's Hatton in the tournament and collect enough points to edge out the gutsy Spaniard.

Chacarra, who earned around $15-20m during three years as a LIV player, is in just his second season on the DP World Tour. He is the only three-time winner of this year's campaign and was desperate to add his name to compatriots Rahm and Seve Ballesteros as the third Spanish order of merit winner.

After four early birdies he looked in fine shape. The pressure began to tell as he posted three bogeys in four holes around the turn. But he responded brilliantly with two more birdies to push McIlroy all the way.

Chacarra, the 26-year-old world number 39, finished in a tie for third to end up second in the overall standings and earn a PGA Tour card for next season.

This video can not be played

'This one's for him' - McIlroy dedicates Race to Dubai win to his dad

As tough as it was this year for McIlroy to win, mainly due to playing on the PGA Tour for the first half of the season, 2027 will be even harder because there will be some big names flooding in after the collapse of LIV Golf.

Rahm and Hatton are just two high-profile LIV players who are suspended from the PGA Tour for a year following their involvement with the breakaway tour. They will both have a full season on the European circuit that will give them a big advantage over McIlroy.

Along with many other big names such as Sergio Garcia, Joaquin Niemann and Tom McKibbin, there's even the possibility of Bryson DeChambeau, the biggest LIV name of all, applying to join the DP World Tour for next season.

The American is eligible thanks to his 2024 US Open triumph, at McIlroy's painful expense, and had to apply by the end of the Sunday of the DP World Tour Championship.

Tyrrell Hatton won his first DP World Tour Championship as Rory McIlroy claimed an eighth Race To Dubai

After this latest addition to McIlroy's glowing CV it's hard to make a case against him being Europe's greatest ever golfer – and as he continues to find new targets to stay motivated one of them is very much to unequivocally nail down that title.

Motivation was a problem in the immediate aftermath of finally ending his long wait to win the Masters in 2025 as he became just the sixth man to win the career Grand Slam.

But a year later he had re-found it as he became just the fourth back-to-back Green Jacket winner with his brilliant defence at Augusta National back in April.

That put him on six major titles, level with England's Sir Nick Faldo and just one behind the great Harry Vardon, whose name adorns the trophy McIlroy has just hoisted for the eighth time.

Still only 37, McIlroy still has plenty of time to overhaul Montgomerie and hold the outright record for the most European number one titles – despite playing on two tours throughout the majority of his career.

Targets have changed – McIlroy is not chasing the world number one spot or winning any old trophy. He's voiced his desire to focus on majors, play more in Europe and around the globe and keep stacking up these order of merit titles.

An Olympic title is perhaps the only honour missing from his trophy cabinet, and he will have the chance to change that in 2028 on a familiar Riviera Country Club Course, which is a regular stop-off on the PGA Tour and where he finished second a this year's Genesis Invitational.

He will be attempting to become the first man to win three Masters in a row next April, before the US Open at Pebble Beach and Open Championship at St Andrews offer great chances at venues McIlroy knows he can thrive on.

McIlroy has won six Ryder Cups as a stalwart for Europe and is just seven points behind all-time leader Sergio Garcia.

But even if the Northern Irishman quit the game right now he's already built a more than compelling argument that he's the greatest player the continent has ever seen.

Watch highlights of Sunday's final round on BBC 2 and BBC iPlayer from 16:15 GMT (UK only)

Schoolboy imposter subjected ex-professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:00:09 GMT

An imposter who made headlines around the world for posing as a school pupil in his 30s has appeared in court and admitted hiding in the home of his former university professor before subjecting him to a "terrifying ordeal".

Brian MacKinnon targeted Prof Brian Whiting, 87, as he lay in bed with his wife, the day after a BBC docudrama on his ruse was broadcast.

My Old School chronicled MacKinnon's return to Bearsden Academy, as Brandon Lee, a 16-year-old who had supposedly just moved to Scotland from Canada.

MacKinnon hatched the plan so he could pursue his dream of becoming a doctor having been thrown out of Glasgow University, when Prof Whiting was dean of the medical school.

MacKinnon - who was formerly a pupil at the East Dunbartonshire school from 1974 to 1980 - returned in 1993 and secured five As in his Higher exams.

As a result he earned a place at the University of Dundee to study medicine.

But in 1995 an anonymous tip-off revealed he had previously spent two years as a medical student at the University of Glasgow and did not complete the course.

MacKinnon was thrown out of the medical school in 1983 following a failed appeal.

When his double life was exposed, Prof Whiting was interviewed by BBC Scotland News.

The archive footage was used in the 2022 docudrama, which starred Alan Cumming as MacKinnon.

Details of the case, which called before the High Court in Glasgow on Thursday, were first reported in the Mail on Sunday.

The court heard MacKinnon, now 63, went to the retired academic's home on 28 September last year - the day after My Old School had been repeated on the BBC.

It is believed MacKinnon sneaked into the property, in the west end of the city, around 16:30 as the rear door and gate were unlocked.

Prof Whiting was in his study and his 83-year-old wife, Marlene, was in the garden.

They went to bed around 23:30, unaware MacKinnon was hiding in their home.

About two hours later they were awoken when their room door suddenly opened.

A figure wearing dark clothes, a grey cap and a mask over the lower part of his face walked up to the side of the bed and told Marlene: "No lights."

Prosecutor Eilidh Robertson told the High Court in Glasgow: "She sat up and MacKinnon demanded that she lie back down or he would really hurt her.

"Both the Whitings were very frightened by this point.

"MacKinnon then pointed at her husband and asked: 'Is that Brian Whiting?'."

MacKinnon then said he had brought "two statements" which he wanted the couple to "release".

Robertson said MacKinnon threatened to kill the couple and hurt their families if they did not comply.

Marlene did not know who the intruder was before he said his name was "Brian MacKinnon".

Robertson added: "MacKinnon then spoke to Brian Whiting directly blaming him and two colleagues for ruining his life and having responsibility for the death of his parents."

MacKinnon then briefly left the room and, on his return, suddenly asked to be let out the house.

Marlene got up and led him downstairs hoping he would go.

She asked how he had initially got in, he boasted: "That was easy."

Marlene got a good look at MacKinnon after he took off his mask.

The advocate depute said: "She unlocked the front door.

"As MacKinnon was leaving, he stated that he had people working for him that would check if the witnesses were complying with his demands.

"If not, they would be dead. He then left the house and turned down a lane."

Marlene immediately called her son.

He went on to show her an online photo of MacKinnon and she identified him as the man who had invaded their home.

The court heard how the two statements left by MacKinnon had been made to look as if they had been completed by Prof Whiting.

Each alleged the retired dean had "succumbed to intolerable pressure to make a misleading statement about Brian Lachlan MacKinnon".

They also said: "Via a BBC Scotland television broadcast, I stated falsely that MacKinnon had not met the required standard as a medical student after he had set out to study medicine at Glasgow in 1980. Nothing could have been further from the truth."

The documents claimed there had been a "conspiracy" to exclude "incandescently bright" students like MacKinnon.

They also included "defamatory" remarks about Glasgow University, BBC Scotland and Alan Cumming.

MacKinnon was not initially traced but DNA recovered at the house helped link him to the crime.

CCTV from a nearby property had also captured him walking near the Whitings property that afternoon.

MacKinnon was eventually arrested as he returned to his home in Milngavie, East Dunbartonshire, hours after the incident.

Police Scotland officers went on to recover a mobile phone and three notepads.

In one, there was handwritten text which stated: "I will regain a place to study medicine at a reputable university".

An envelope was also seized and a "statement" similar to those given to the Whitings was discovered inside.

MacKinnon made no comment when quizzed by detectives.

Last week he was brought into court in a wheelchair and pleaded guilty to a charge of attempted extortion.

Sean Templeton, defending, told the hearing: "It is clear that he has had an extraordinary life, thrust into the public gaze in the 1990s by attending a school when he was over the age of 18."

He added MacKinnon had always wanted to be involved in medicine to "assist the public", but his "ambitions to become a doctor came to an end".

Templeton said after he was exposed, it had "characterised" his life in the many years since, including the docudrama which MacKinnon "did not agree to".

The defence advocate said: "It is something that has dogged him since the 1990s."

MacKinnon had been assessed by a psychiatrist after his initial appearance in court in late September last year, but it was eventually concluded that he was "fit to stand trial".

Templeton told the court MacKinnon was "frail" and suffered from uncontrolled movements in one of his arms.

Lady Anwar continued his remand in custody as sentencing was deferred for reports until a later date.

MacKinnon is currently being held at HMP Barlinnie in Glasgow.

She told him: "You subjected Mr and Mrs Whiting, both in their 80s, to a shocking and terrifying ordeal in their home.

"It is likely you will face a significant custodial sentence."

Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:01:46 GMT

Warning: Contains graphic details of Rebekah Arter's death - and references to coercion and sexual abuse

A former Metropolitan Police detective, investigated for sexually exploiting vulnerable crime victims it was his job to protect, later lied about the death of his wife in a Barbados hotel room, BBC Panorama has learned.

Warren Arter first met his wife Rebekah after she reported domestic abuse to the Met. He then abused her for more than a decade. Her death two years ago has never been properly investigated.

Panorama can reveal failures by Barbados authorities to preserve evidence and interview hotel staff about Arter's suspicious behaviour before and after Rebekah's death, aged 47.

Despite a request from her family for assistance, the Met did not send detectives to the Caribbean island.

The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.

Rebekah's family, speaking publicly for the first time, have told Panorama the Met failed her. The cause of her death is still not known with a coroner in the UK recording an open verdict.

We have also spoken to hotel staff who were called to the room in June 2024 after Arter rang reception to say his wife had collapsed.

Interviews with the staff, police sources - plus Arter's erratic communications following Rebekah's death - reveal:

Arter, 54, took his own life in HMP Wandsworth, days after he had returned from Barbados and been arrested for allegedly abusing another woman.

Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship when Arter investigated her case in 2006. The detective then pursued a relationship with her and moved in not long after.

Three years later, he was placed in charge of a unit in south-east London investigating rape cases.

Arter was later suspended by the Met and investigated over his conduct towards eight alleged victims by its watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) - but was never convicted.

Over the seven years he was suspended, Arter continued to receive his full detective inspector salary, before being dismissed in 2023 for drug offences.

All this time, he subjected Rebekah to sexual and domestic abuse, coercive control, and drugging, which the BBC has seen video evidence of.

Panorama has now spoken to several members of staff who were working at the luxury O2 Beach Club in Barbados on the night of Rebekah's death. All say Arter behaved suspiciously.

Two of them entered Arter's hotel room after he had called to say his wife was unwell. Both say it was immediately clear Rebekah was dead.

Andrew, a security guard, says he had to prevent Arter from going to a nearby street party, before emergency services arrived.

"So I'm asking him, why do you need to go when you have a bigger issue here?"

Andrew says Arter responded: "Oh, I just need to clear my head."

Arter then began crying "crocodile tears" and conducting performative CPR despite Rebekah's lips being blue, according to Andrew, who says Arter's explanation of what happened kept changing.

Initially, Arter told Andrew she had fallen near a chest of drawers - but her body was some distance away, near the kitchen. When police arrived, Andrew says he heard Arter tell them he had found her like that.

There was no sign of Rebekah having a head injury, Andrew says, despite bloodstains on the bed, the wall and the living room area.

Arter recorded a video of the room and sent it to family and friends in the UK.

"It looks like chocolate but it's blood," he can be heard saying.

Andrew says he told Arter to phone family in the UK - and then heard him tell them that she had been unwell.

"He was just trying to find the right story that fits and none of them added up," says Andrew.

The security guard says he told Barbadian police officers what he saw and gave a statement but was never formally interviewed.

Panorama has seen some of Arter's messages and spoken to Rebekah's friends and family who were contacted by him shortly after her death.

They reveal that Arter provided other possible causes of death - that Rebekah had "choked" or that her drink had been spiked.

These accounts are contradicted by Rebekah's daughter-in-law, Lacey, who says he told her they had both been asleep for 18 hours and he had woken up and found her dead.

"He was outright lying. He was forgetting what he was telling people," says Lacey.

Arter was briefly detained by Barbadian police but released a short time later.

One of the police officers who attended the room that night refused to share information with Panorama without payment. He still had a photograph of Rebekah's dead body on his phone.

Police in Barbados did not respond to our request for comment.

Other hotel staff members have told the BBC they were concerned about Arter's treatment of Rebekah during their stay.

Security supervisor Kenneth says Arter appeared "controlling" and "didn't allow Rebekah to do anything on her own". Rebekah also frequently appeared to be "intoxicated", he says.

A third member of staff, who worked on the front desk, says staff suspected Arter was "drugging" Rebekah.

Panorama has seen a video, filmed by Arter on his phone when she was still alive, which shows Rebekah clearly intoxicated. She is wearing the same clothes that she is pictured in after she died.

In the early hours of the morning after her death, during the staff member's night shift, Arter approached the hotel front desk to ask when Rebekah last had a massage in the hotel spa.

She says his question struck her as bizarre and felt like he was trying to get his story straight.

Meanwhile, back in the UK, Rebekah's son, Elliot, and his wife, Lacey, were becoming increasingly concerned after visiting the home she shared with Arter.

Inside, they say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up in the house.

They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.

Four days after Rebekah's death, they went to Bexleyheath Police Station, the same station where Arter once led rape investigations, to report her death to the Met and raise concerns about his possible involvement.

"The front office staff said, 'Oh well it's happened in Barbados, it's a Barbados issue' - and tried to brush it off at first," says Elliot.

"The moment I gave Warren's name, it was like chaos - we had sergeants coming down to the front desk," says Lacey.

"But it really wasn't about Rebekah, it was more about Warren," she says.

That evening, an officer briefed a Gold Commander within the Met, a senior boss who decides how to respond to incidents. The Met did not send detectives to Barbados.

UK police forces can be asked to help investigate a death of a British national overseas - usually at the request of local police where the death occurred.

Under Foreign Office guidance, the case for such involvement is strengthened when families request assistance and there are credible concerns about the circumstances of the death, as there were in Rebekah's case.

The Met told the BBC it made immediate efforts to obtain information in order to assess whether to travel to Barbados but decided it would not be appropriate without an allegation of criminality.

An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados.

This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated.

The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted.

The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation".

He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict.

He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out.

The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope.

Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes.

A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later.

In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death.

"We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out."

Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother.

"My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says.

"For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away."

Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:09:29 GMT

Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.

She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."

Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".

She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital.

"I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.

But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it.

"I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."

The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London.

She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.

Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.

She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:07:29 GMT

You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life.

In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar.

"We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London.

"He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."

Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea.

"OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute.

"But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."

Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire and moved to Wales – taking her pets with them.

One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges".

"Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk."

"We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."

Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too.

Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.

Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property.

"It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says.

Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.

The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past.

"I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.

So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year.

"Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."

Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint.

"To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.

Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."

But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant.

Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.

"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses.

"Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."

The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham.

"It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."

The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.

Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop.

"I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says.

"It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."

Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades.

"I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says.

"Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."

That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in.

"I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."

The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.

The single Too Cute To Be Lonely is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party.

"Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.

Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love.

"Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself. "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."

Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie.

"I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals.

"We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us.

"I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."

Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World.

"It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting.

"But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished.

"So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."

That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her.

And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.

Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head.

"If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says.

"Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:06:55 GMT

When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy

BBC News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:06:51 GMT

Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.
