Sitting in her wheelchair, Melinke Visser watches her younger siblings play hide-and-seek.

“I can’t play with you,” she tells them, much to their dismay.

They don’t understand how gravely ill she is – her Diffuse Midline Glioma (DMG) making even simple tasks such as eating and drinking a daily challenge.

The parents of the sports-loving 11-year-old, diagnosed with a rare form of terminal brain cancer last year, say all they want is to give her every chance to live.

Marizaan and Jacob Visser are fundraising in the hope their daughter can receive CAR T Cell Therapy, which is not publicly or widely available in New Zealand.

While the Vissers say they “couldn’t fault” Melinke’s ongoing care at Auckland’s Starship Hospital, they’re hopeful the cutting-edge treatment currently unavailable in New Zealand could help her.

The therapy involves removing a patient’s immune cells, genetically reprogramming them to recognise cancer, and reinfusing them back into the body as a “living drug” designed to hunt down malignant cells.

An initial response from doctors in the United States has been hopeful, but it has been a constant struggle to find options and get overseas doctors in places like China to respond.

“We’ll do everything we possibly can for Melinke. We don’t want to look back and think there was something else we could have tried,” Marizaan says.

If the family is unable to reach their $525,000 fundraising goal, or if circumstances change and the funds are no longer required for Melinke’s treatment, donated money will go to a cancer organisation to help support other families affected by childhood cancer.

The family moved to New Zealand from South Africa in 2023. It was in 2024 that they realised something was not right.

Marizaan noticed behavioural changes in her daughter and Melinke was initially diagnosed with ADHD.

“She started to get severe outbursts. There was a lot of fighting and shouting, and everyone suggested getting her tested for ADHD. We took her to the paediatrician. She confirmed, yes, she’s got a severe or a high grade of ADHD.”

Melinke would also get constant headaches and be prone to vomiting.

Then, one day in March 2025, the family’s lives were turned upside down. Melinke was on the couch when Jacob noticed her face droop to the side.

“I thought she had a stroke. That’s what it looked like,” Jacob said.

Melinke was rushed to urgent care and then taken to Starship Hospital in Auckland, where scans confirmed the dangerous and aggressive tumour on her brainstem.

“Because of where the tumour is situated, sitting on the brainstem, it’s really difficult to operate. It’s a part of the brain that literally controls everything.”

A VP shunt to relieve swelling on the brain and months of chemotherapy followed. And for a while, Melinke’s condition improved.

“Last year, around October and November, we thought she was doing great. She had started walking again, running around. But by April this year, things started going backwards. Now she’s basically in a wheelchair every day, unable to walk,” Jacob says.

Melinke is no longer well enough to go to school and receives 24/7 care from Marizaan, who works from home.

While every day remains a “constant struggle” – especially without support from relatives still living in South Africa – the family is slowly starting to adapt to their “new normal”.

Their local church, school and community have been “amazing”, helping out by bringing meals to the house and providing moral support.

Melinke was always a “sporty kid” who loved netball, athletics, gymnastics, football and just running around. Her parents say it’s devastating to see that passion ripped away from her.

“Now, wherever you go, you need to make the choice of whether you are going to take her with you, or if she is going to stay at home,” Marizaan says.

It’s hard to accept they’ll never hear their daughter is in remission, the Vissers say, but they will continue to fight for Melinke, rather than giving up hope.

Malaghan Institute of Medical Research Professor Robert Weinkove told the Herald earlier this year that New Zealand did not have any publicly funded CAR T-cell treatments.

“It is becoming more and more of a stark difference, with more patients increasingly aware of these options and then seeking to travel overseas to obtain it.”

At present, the Malaghan Institute has treated just over 60 patients in New Zealand using CAR T cells manufactured locally through trials in Wellington, Auckland and Christchurch.

“But those are clinical trials, and they don’t really meet the need,” Weinkove said.

People can support Melinke’s fight by donating at https://givealittle. co. nz/cause/help-us-fight-for-melinke-give-her-another-chance

New Zealand backed US co-funding port on former Cook Islands military base without a formal business case

New Zealand Herald November 15, 2026

End of dialog window.

New Zealand supported the United States co-funding a major port upgrade on a former American military base in the Cook Islands without a business case.

The port upgrade in Penrhyn, part of the northern Cook Islands, is on track to be co-funded with the US Government.

The latter is intending to contribute about $84 million, and the New Zealand Government is topping up the investment with a further $17.5m.

The partnership was announced by the US Government, Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown and Foreign Minister Winston Peters at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders’ meeting in Palau in early September.

Documents obtained by Newstalk ZB under the Official Information Act show Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) officials said while there was no business case, the project was a “priority” and there were “strong reasons to support it”.

A briefing from MFAT officials to the Foreign Minister in May 2026 noted Cabinet consideration of a project of this scale would usually come with a business case.

“Major New Zealand development activity would ordinarily be supported by a detailed business case prepared over a number of years with firm cost estimates,” officials admitted.

Officials added it would not be possible to complete a feasibility study or business case in the time available before the proposed announcement at PIF, meaning Cabinet would have to make a decision “based on more preliminary information”.

The agency noted a 2023 study commissioned by the Australian Government was considered out of date and high-level. Later advice added construction costs have increased since then.

A separate batch of talking points prepared by MFAT said if all three countries were supportive, the project would be announced at PIF.

Officials said it was their intention for a feasibility study to begin.

MFAT looked at three options to support the co-funding of Penrhyn port, including supporting it via the agency’s baseline funding, providing $10m or $17.5m – the latter was supported.

Officials said larger funding contributions “would be an option for New Zealand”, but would require more substantial trade-offs.

Peters was told there was scope in the Cook Islands development programme for a “reasonably significant” investment in infrastructure, after funding was paused during a “difficult period” in the Cook Islands-New Zealand relationship.

Funding was restored in April after the Cook Islands signed an agreement with the New Zealand Government to consult New Zealand on significant defence and security matters, ending a disagreement sparked by China’s interest in the area.

The May briefing said officials “have already advised the US that New Zealand will be willing to fund an initial feasibility study and take on implementation of the [Penryhn port] project”.

Anna Powles, Massey University associate professor in defence and security studies, told Newstalk ZB the port upgrade sends a “very strong message” about US interest in the Pacific and sends a signal to China.

Powles said the fact the project was approved without a business case “speaks to the sense of urgency” from the US, specifically US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, who has made numerous visits to the region.

The academic said critical minerals had been the heart of the US’ strategic competition with China, and also seemed to align with the Cook Islands’ economic development goals.

Powles added when Brown hosted the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ meeting several years ago, he presented leaders with nodules from the seabed, sending “strong signals” that the Cook Islands was “open for business”.

An MFAT concept note for the port extension, also obtained under the OIA, described the project as high risk.

The agency’s concept note said the port would be upgraded from December 2026 to December 2031.

Officials also recounted the historical significance of Penrhyn, once used as a World War II military base. US forces established a military camp on Penrhyn and constructed a port and airstrip in 1942.

The area, also referred to as Tongareva, is the northernmost Cook Islands atoll, described by MFAT officials as “one of the most remote and difficult-to-access islands in the country”.

An existing port at Omoka, on the islet of Moananui, serves as the main entry point for goods into Penrhyn and is in “poor condition”.

Officials suggested without the upgrade, the reliability of shops being able to deliver essential supplies would “continue to degrade”, capacity would reduce, and operational safety risks would increase.

Despite endorsing the merits of the project, MFAT officials noted potential adverse effects in the concept note.

The agency warned construction activity in the area could harm coral reefs and “may temporarily disrupt feeding, nesting, breeding, or migration patterns of fish, seabirds, turtles, and other species that depend on the lagoon environment”.

Powles added there was some strong opposition to deep-sea mining in the Cook Islands as well, and said critical seabed mining does not have broad support across the Pacific Islands Forum membership.

A growing number of countries are pushing for a moratorium on mining, while other nations are speaking openly about the economic benefits it will realise for the blue continent.

MFAT officials added any disruption to shipping services would need to be mitigated, as residents rely on food delivered through its port.

The concept note gave a timeline suggesting an indicative business case would be completed in February 2028, and a detailed one would come through in June 2029.

An MFAT statement said the milestones dates were “indicative only”.

“New Zealand is very pleased to be partnering with the United States and the Cook Islands Governments to deliver the Penrhyn port upgrade.

“The project is a Cook Islands priority, which will deliver economic, security and resilience benefits to the Penrhyn community and the wider region,” MFAT said.

“MFAT supported the project because of the unique opportunity it presented to secure a significant combined US/New Zealand investment for a long-standing Cook Islands development objective.

“The first stage of the project is a feasibility study. Further decisions about the scope of the project will be taken by the partners at the conclusion of the study,” the agency added.

A separate proactively released Cabinet paper authorised ministers to confirm the project should proceed, provided a detailed business case confirms it can be implemented within budget.

When co-funding was announced, Peters said the project was “a positive and hugely significant initiative that demonstrates the strength of New Zealand’s partnerships with both the Cook Islands and the United States”.

Landau said the upgrade “underscores the United States’ strong commitment to our partners in the Pacific and builds on the Critical Minerals Framework the United States and the Cook Islands agreed to earlier this year”.

Azaria Howell is a multimedia reporter working from Parliament’s press gallery. She joined NZME in 2022 and became a Newstalk ZB political reporter in late 2024, with a keen interest in public service agency reform and government spending.

Sydney Morning Herald November 16, 2026

Come walk with me through Scarborough, as blissful a place as you might find.

It won’t take long, for it’s not a huge slab of land. It’s actually only a fragment of the larger Redcliffe Peninsula, the seaside locale to Brisbane’s north-east where two bridges – one named for the famed engineer Manuel Hornibrook, the other for the WWI veteran Ted Smout – shoot across Hays Inlet in Bramble Bay.

Like any peninsula, Scarborough has water on three sides, with the ceaseless ripples of Moreton Bay kissing its beaches.

As majestic as that sounds – and there’s plenty of natural beauty to celebrate in this part of the world – it would be folly to ignore the humans who have called it home.

Think footballers like Artie Beetson, Bunny Pearce and Petero Civoniceva, and actor William McInnes. Then there’s the Bullivants, Vaughan and Carmel – once owners of the Nature’s Own vitamin and supplements business. They built neighbouring his and hers mansions on Prince Edward Parade after amalgamating a few smaller allotments on one of the suburb’s more salubrious boulevards, with its groves of towering Moreton Bay figs.

Snoops were often seen snapping photos of the homes, one an ostentatious triple-storey structure, and the other more like a doll’s house on steroids, where life-sized animals appeared to cavort in a lush, poolside garden.

If Scarborough has celebrity runs on the board though, it’s mainly courtesy of the Bee Gees. The suburb of Redcliffe to the south even has a laneway named after them, decorated with statues of brothers Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb. But it was in Scarby, as some locals call it, that the siblings (including youngest brother Andy, a star in his own right) actually lived.

When the Gibb clan migrated from England in 1958, they moved into a guest house in Oxley Avenue then settled in Fifth Avenue. Imagine being a neighbour to their early rehearsals for gigs at Redcliffe Speedway and Queensland coastal resorts, before the trio decamped to the Gold Coast, and then Sydney in 1963.

Putting all that aside, there’s plenty to love about Scarby: clean air, friendly residents who are passionate about the district, accessible and safe beaches, good schools and shops, and a low crime rate.

I’ve lived in Scarborough for the past two years, but my connection stretches back to the ’70s when my parents moved from Brisbane’s inner north with my youngest brother and me in tow. Sadly, mum and dad have checked out, but both are interred on the peninsula, as are an aunty and uncle.

As your guide, I’ll first lead you east along Eversleigh Road, beginning where it intersects with Ashmole Road, virtually in the shadow of Kayo Stadium, where the Dolphins rule. The road is mysteriously wide, the architecture eclectic. Where Eversleigh Road bisects Scarborough Road, we avoid a left turn, where we would catch sight of the sprawling Southern Cross Catholic College campus.

Instead, we stay true to our course and walk by the suburb’s eponymous primary school and then on to Queens Beach, a sliver of paradise where pooches run free and kite surfers defy gravity as they race past Drury Point towards Scarborough Beach.

Now watch your step, because this is where the magic happens.

Scarborough Beach Park abuts Moreton Bay on its eastern flank and to the west, Landsborough Avenue, which zigs one way, then zags another. I walk this way every day accompanied by my better half and our dog. The birdsong, the gentle swoosh of ripples breaking the shore, and countless greetings from passers-by are the soundtrack to our life.

Council workers tend to the park as if it were their own, cleaning public areas with almost military precision, much to the appreciation of visitors, who descend on the area each weekend and holiday period with the type of zeal a chip-hungry seagull could admire. Grab a picnic table or spread a blanket and watch as boats bob along between the shore and Moreton Island.

Some residents yearn for quieter days when Scarborough was still a secret, its streets were less cluttered, and no building was taller than any of the Norfolk pines, standing to attention where grass gives way to sand.

The aroma of coffee rides the breeze from Landing, a family-run cafe on the ground level of The Oscar, a multi-rise residential and commercial development on the former site of the movie theatre. With its oxide-coloured tables, Landing pays homage to the red cliffs that James Cook noticed in 1770, and its designer sausage rolls are next level. Not to mention the Breton buns, the croissants and brownies.

Contributor

Scarborough is awash with dining options. Choose between any number of Asian or continental-themed restaurants, including Vietnamese, Indian, Japanese and Italian. Drop by the Friendly Grocer and they’ll prove the name is not misused.

Wander further around to Thurecht Parade, where sunsets roll on forever. Morgans offers muddies, sweet lip and prawns so fresh, it’s easy to think these little treasures should still be swimming. Dine in alongside the trawlers, or skip across to Jamieson Park, where Deception Bay reveals itself, and breathe in the beauty. Drop by the Scarborough Harbour Brewing Company and quench your thirst.

I can vouch for each and every one, which probably explains my expanding girth.

The Bee Gees’ old wooden house on Fifth Avenue is still standing, and Barry Gibb returned for a nostalgic visit as recently as 2024. “We fell into paradise when we got off that ship,” Gibb said at the time. “We didn’t know what hit us.”

Like Barry, I too feel the bliss.

‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 19:40:23 GMT

Professor urges ministers to use awareness triggered by Russell Brand conviction to examine use of rape myths in trials

The debate triggered by high-profile cases must “pull back the curtain” on the treatment of people making allegations of sexual offences in the criminal justice system in England and Wales, the government’s independent adviser on rape has told the Guardian.

Prof Katrin Hohl, who has advised the government in an overhaul of how rape is treated by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the government should use the public awareness triggered by Russell Brand’s conviction for rape to examine the use of rape myths and jury direction in trials.

“So many things are going wrong in our justice system when it comes to the treatment of victims of rape and sexual assault, but most of the time no one ever finds out what has happened during the investigation process or during a trial,” she said.

Hohl said that despite “significant progress” made by police forces and the CPS – who have been directed to make investigations more focused on suspects rather than victim behaviour under a system known as Operation Soteria – the court system was being left behind.

A report published by Hohl last month suggested sexual assault cases prepared under the new system were experiencing “a cliff edge” when they came to trial, and were potentially coming up against practices such as the use of rape myths by defence barristers.

“We essentially know very little about how rape and sexual assault cases play out in England and Wales and it is time to pull back the curtain,” said Hohl.

“We need proper research into the actions of barristers, judges and juries during trials so that victims can actually get the justice the law says they should achieve.”

Hohl’s remarks come after the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, called for a new legal duty on judges to direct juries, if rape myths have been ventured during a trial, stating: “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

During the Brand trial, which saw the comedian sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, his barrister, Ian Winter, said Brand’s accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Government ministers are also understood to be considering calls for a “staggered” consent law, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds, after a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 launched a campaign for the law to be changed.

Mia Latter, who says she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16, told the Sunday Times: “I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

On Sunday, Pat McFadden said ministers would discuss the issue. Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the work and pensions secretary said questions over a staggered age of consent have “been raised and will be discussed”, adding: “[I] can’t tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights.”

Since the trial, several support services for victims of sexual assault and rape said they had been experiencing a significant increase in the number of calls and messages to helplines.

Rape Crisis centres are experiencing “very significant demand” and phonelines have been inundated with calls since Brand was convicted of rape, said Ciara Bergman, chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.

Many women are also now questioning their own experiences with older men, she said, after separate allegations were made public that David Walliams preyed on young women for sex.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sexual offence allegations against Walliams were being looked at by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Bergman said calls to the 24/7 rape and sexual abuse support line had quadrupled since the start of the month, while rape crisis centres were reporting a massive rise in demand for help.

“That demand comes from a range of places,” she said. “There are people who see the news and are reminded of their own experiences and people who are retraumatised by seeing this issue in the news.

“But there are people who may have experienced predation and exploitation at vulnerable times in their lives, and they’re now beginning to question their own experiences.”

She echoed calls for greater transparency in trials, and argued the coverage of high profile cases had highlighted the gap in the public knowledge around the experience of going to trial and issues around consent.

“Our centres are adept at responding to victims but they are under very significant pressure,” she said. “When you look at these stories and the response to them there is no question about the need for more comprehensive support and more rape crisis centres so victims and survivors can get the justice they deserve.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We are always looking at ways we can improve how the justice system treats victims of sexual violence.

“That’s why we are changing the law to stop irrelevant evidence that relies on myths being weaponised against victims, rolling out specialist courtrooms for rape and serious sexual offences and improving support for victims, backed by our record £550m investment in support services.”

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse and childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

Texas puts to death man who beheaded three children, hours after Oklahoma execution

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 19:27:24 GMT

Oklahoma man, 73, executed for killing ex’s estranged husband, as US nears 40 executions for second straight year

A Texas man convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading his three young children in a squalid, windowless apartment in 2003 was recently executed.

John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6.47 pm on Thursday after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville, Texas. His killings of his baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville on the US border with Mexico that the apartment building was later demolished – and the land turned into a park and community garden.

After a spiritual adviser prayed over him briefly, Rubio thanked friends and family for their “love and understanding” and said he was “not the same person I once was”. He thanked prison staff for teaching him how to find God and also expressed love for Angela Camacho, his common-law wife who is serving life in prison for her role in the slayings.

“I want to say I’m sorry to my wife’s family,” he said. “I can’t change the past but I can tell you my life is going to be over. But that’s not going to make you happy.”

“I’m going to be with my kids in a little bit,” he added. “I’m ready to go to heaven to be with my lord and savior.”

As the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital began taking effect, Rubio took three breaths and began what sounded like snoring. All movement ceased after, and a physician pronounced him dead 21 minutes after the injection began.

Also on Thursday, 73-year-old James Pavatt received a lethal injection at an Oklahoma prison for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband in 2001. The victim was killed as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving.

Thursday’s executions were the 36th and 37th this year, with the US on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year – a pace driven by Florida.

The death penalty has drawn renewed attention since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September. And on 5 November, California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office in January – what experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.

In Texas, Rubio and Camacho were accused of killing three-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E Rubio and two-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the apartment they shared in Brownsville. Camacho received a life sentence after pleading guilty.

An appeals court overturned Rubio’s first capital murder conviction, ruling Camacho’s statements were improperly admitted as evidence in his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but again was convicted and sentenced to death.

According to court records, Rubio wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but raised them as his own.

At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world.

Defense experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, a finding prosecution experts rejected. The defense experts also testified his childhood – marked by violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution – damaged him developmentally.

Meanwhile, in Oklahoma, Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the killing of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is the only woman currently on Oklahoma’s death row.

Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.

Pavatt and Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while re-entering the US.

On Thursday, when he was asked if he had any last words before his execution, Pavatt shook his head no. As a chaplain read from the Bible, Pavatt appeared to mouth some words that couldn’t be heard.

Also on Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December.

Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after nearly 30 years in prison. He had been awaiting a retrial after the US supreme court overturned his conviction.

Ronaldinho makes debut for Italian side Ravenna after 11-year hiatus in playing career

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 19:20:08 GMT

Brazil legend plays first half for Serie C club at age 46

‘Is this my last one? I don’t know,’ Ronaldinho says

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting line-up as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì.

Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.

The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.

Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.

“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”

Climate crisis gave Cheltenham a major headache – and more pain is coming

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:55:55 GMT

There is little Cheltenham’s bosses could have done to prevent the chaos on and off the track this weekend

Even after two days of racing afflicted by dozens of non‑runners because of the fast ground, the elements still had not quite finished with Cheltenham on Sunday, when the third day of the track’s November meeting went ahead only after a late inspection – to assess standing water on the course after several hours of rain.

A crowd of more than 10,000 racegoers, swelled by a big contingent of students from the specialist racing events organiser Invades, had largely assembled when the inspection was announced, and while the course was passed fit for racing 15 minutes later, it was another uncomfortable moment for all concerned at the end of a tricky three days in the West Country.

The November meeting is second only to the festival here in March in terms of its significance and popularity, and its crowd figures have also held up well at a time when the festival has been struggling to maintain its attendance. The crowd on Saturday of 32,618 was 2,000 up on last year but they did not get entirely what they were expecting as there were no fewer than 29 non-runners on the day, almost all of which were ground‑related.

That followed nine non-runners on Friday and there were another 15 on Sunday.

Friday’s card also saw three slips by runners on the final bend, while several hurdles were omitted in a later race because of the low-lying sun. And all this after Cheltenham cancelled its final three racedays last season and then spent a significant sum to replace a drainage pipe in the home straight after a hole appeared in the track at the Trials meeting in late January.

The extent to which the racegoers allowed any of this to impinge on their day out is difficult to say. They certainly seemed to be having a good time, not least when Meetmebythesea, the favourite, landed some meaty bets in the Paddy Power Gold Cup on Saturday. The ever-popular Jonbon’s win in the Shloer Chase a day earlier was a heartwarmer, too, and my guess at least would be that a significant proportion of Saturday’s crowd were already planning to return in 12 months’ time as they headed for home.

But for the owners and trainers of horses that missed out – because a track with a top-end watering system had good-to-firm in the going description in mid-November – the memory may be harder to shift.

Cheltenham is the home of National Hunt racing and there will never be another track to match it, but that also means any runner there is the subject of huge excitement and anticipation for its owners for weeks, or probably months, beforehand. If they then find themselves having to withdraw a fit horse because the ground is too fast, the frustration could be such that, as Willie Mullins warned last week, owners will start to look towards Aintree and Punchestown in the spring instead.

Perhaps a greater concern for Cheltenham, though, after its “one-thing-after-another” weekend, is that it is very hard to point to anything that Jon Pullin, the clerk of the course, could have done to avoid it. He could not water the course on Thursday or Friday evening because the temperatures were forecast to get well below freezing – which they did – while the slips on Friday were apparently down to moisture brought to the surface by a light overnight frost.

Pullin cannot change the ambient or overnight temperature, or the amount of rainfall at a track where the gauges at different parts have been known to register different readings.

“It’s another acknowledgment that we as a racing industry have that the climate is changing,” Pullin told ITV Racing over the weekend. And the really bad news for Pullin and all his fellow clerks of the course is that climate science does not simply predict that the planet is warming up, but also that this will result in more extreme weather patterns. Cheltenham’s problems over the weekend were not simply the result of low rainfall over the past two weeks, but over the past six months or more.

When ground changes, meanwhile, it can change rapidly, and the jockeys were coming home caked in mud at the end of the card on Sunday. That was, at least in part, down to the 8mm of water applied overnight on Saturday, but also because a forecast of 2-3mm of natural rainfall ahead of racing turned out to be 12mm.

Again, it is hard to see what else Pullin could have done. It is not like ordering a steak medium-rare and then sending it back for another minute each side if it arrives looking too bloody. Watering remains a controversial topic for some punters, but it is a vital part of the clerk’s armoury to ensure that racing takes place at all, and will become more important still due to the climate crisis.

Ludlow abandoned its entire 2026-27 season last week due to the effects of the summer drought. Exeter and Wincanton both lost their biggest days of the season for the same reason. Taunton, Kempton and Leicester have lost meetings too. So while it looked a little touch-and-go on Sunday lunchtime, Cheltenham got all three days into the form book and thin fields or not, many racegoers left with memories to treasure.

Plumpton 12.45 Ginolo 1.15 Prairie Diamond 1.45 Clap Of Thunder 2.15 Kamille Au Kanada 2.45 Of Corse I Can 3.15 Daring Plan 3.45 Kotari

Wolverhampton 4.30 Roosike 5.00 Desert Romance 5.30 Leading Role 6.00 Al Lahbab 6.30 Rhythm N Hooves 7.00 Split Elevens (nb) 7.30 Lahan Kingman 8.00 Sea The Light (nap) 8.30 Haveachoc

We live, sadly, in a blame culture where somebody needs to be held accountable for every setback or disappointment, but Pullin is working with a very delicate balance of competing risks using the best information at his disposal, in order to reach what is, in fact, quite a narrow window of success.

And that information not only proves to be way off the mark on a regular basis, but is also predicted to see wilder variations still over the years to come.

It is, quite simply, an impossible job, and while there were plenty of keyboard warriors boasting 20/20 hindsight queueing up to opine on Pullin’s actions over the weekend, my bet would be that few of them, were they in his shoes, would have done anything radically different.

Mary Earps frustrates Arsenal as London City Lionesses earn battling draw

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:53:08 GMT

Arsenal’s fifth draw from five home games in the Women’s Super League left them frustrated once again but this was a wholly different story to the previous four, as they played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with a ­London City Lionesses side inspired by their goalkeeper Mary Earps.

Aston Villa, Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Manchester United all came to this stadium for a point, defending resolutely and exposing Arsenal’s inability to break down low blocks, whereas London City came to play and were rewarded with a draw that maintains their six‑point advantage over Arsenal in the race for a European place, and moving within six points of the leaders Chelsea.

Earps, producing her best performance to date for the team she joined in the summer, repeatedly denied Frida Maanum and Lisa Baum and was named player of the match in a contest where both goals were scored inside the space of 99 seconds. The impressive Maanum finished off a superb team move for Arsenal to open the ­scoring in the 10th minute but her goal was cancelled out by a terrific finish from Isobel Goodwin whose head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “We came here to take risks. We really wanted to win.

“Our identity is playing with ­bravery – we were brave today. We weren’t scared about the context, the opponent, the stadium, nothing. We tried to play as we play at home.”

Arsenal had secured an impressive result in Barcelona on ­Thursday, drawing with the European cham­pions, but this game against the WSL’s third-placed side felt as though it was of even greater importance, particularly if Arsenal wish to continue ­visiting venues such as the Camp Nou next season, and they were unable to find a way past Earps to win and close the gap in the table.

Just like they had done away at Anfield last weekend, Renée Slegers’s team made a bright start with energy, pace and the threat of Alessia Russo. Emily Fox’s shot was deflected wide, after a good move that included some excellent Maanum build-up play, before Ona Batlle’s long-range effort bounced wide. It was not long before Maanum tucked in the opening goal after an intelligent cutback from Russo.

The visitors struck back almost immediately, though, as Goodwin did superbly to turn inside Leah ­Williamson and then ­demonstrated strength and composure to hold off Baum and fire a lethal finish past Misa ­Rodríguez with power and ­precision. It was a timely moment of class from the English striker in front of the England head coach, Sarina Wiegman, who was in the stands before naming her next England squad on Tuesday morning.

Earps then twice saved from Baum from range. After the break, Earps did well again to dive low to her left to divert a Caitlin Foord strike wide, and what followed was a sustained spell of London City possession, ­territory and chances. Maestre’s team spent a good part of 20 minutes firmly camped in ­Arsenal’s half and they carved open a good chance for Kadidiatou Diani but her relatively tame, low, near-post effort was saved by Rodríguez.

Diani’s 62nd-minute ­replacement from the substitutes’ bench, ­Delphine Cascarino, drew gasps from the crowd as she unleashed a dipping strike that bounced off the top of the crossbar. It was a lucky escape for Arsenal, who had won all seven of their previous meetings with London City across all competitions but were denied by two more fine Earps stops, firstly from a Maanum close-range effort and then from Maanum’s curler, which looked destined for the top corner before Earps touched it on to the bar.

‘If you don’t shower, so what?’ The western diplomats staying put in under-attack Kyiv

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:52:25 GMT

Ambassadors say presence sends powerful signal of solidarity and support amid escalation in Russian strikes and warnings

The warning from Moscow was blunt. Western diplomats should immediately leave the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. If they failed to do so they would be “in mortal danger”. The statement added that Russia would not be responsible for any “potential negative consequences” if its advice was ignored.

European envoys in Kyiv responded to the Kremlin’s threat last month with a loud raspberry. Denmark’s ambassador to Ukraine, Thomas Lund-Sørensen, took to social media to say that he was staying. So did the ambassadors from Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden, France, Poland and Estonia. Even the Americans indicated they would not be budging.

Speaking at his embassy office, decorated with a Lego Cossack warrior, Lund-Sørensen said the Russians were trying to spook Europeans in order to undermine support for Ukraine. “It’s cognitive warfare. These attacks have been going on for a long time. They are trying to influence public opinion in my country. Of course we will continue here,” he said.

The ambassador admitted that his job had scary moments, shared by all in Kyiv. “If you don’t find it frightening when 10 ballistic missiles hit within a couple of minutes you should probably go and see someone,” he said, but added: “There is a difference between being in uncomfortable and life-threatening situations. If you don’t shower, so what?”

The decision to remain in a city under fire is not without risk. On Friday, a drone crashed into a hospital in central Kyiv, the institute for orthopaedics and traumatology, a few hundred metres from Lund-Sørensen’s workplace. The bang could be heard for miles around.

Russia has dramatically stepped up its attacks since August, hurling missiles and hundreds of jet-powered drones. Major urban centres such as Kharkiv and Odesa have suffered, too. Seemingly frustrated by failure to progress on the battlefield, the Kremlin has intensified its all-out campaign against civilians.

It has targeted bridges across the Dnipro river, thermal heating plants and substations, as well as trains and railway stations. Power cuts last most of the day. In the past week, there was no water for 24 hours. The bombing has reached the historic centre of Kyiv, where many embassies are located. A strike in September hit a building a couple of hundred metres from the German embassy. In October 2022, the embassy’s visa office was damaged in an attack that killed eight people.

In 2025, two missiles landed in the car park next to the EU delegation building. Deadly metal cubes perforated its ground floor, shattering armoured windows. The strike was at dawn, before staff arrived. Nobody was hurt. This September, a drone exploded 500 metres away. Debris ravaged the ninth-floor, bringing down glass, ceiling panels and the ventilation system.

“I was in a meeting with seven colleagues. We ran to the corridor,” said Katarína Mathernová, the EU’s ambassador in Kyiv. “I’ve never heard anything that loud in my life. There were plumes of smoke. It was shocking.” The delegation is now reinforcing its outer walls with sandbags. It has put beanbags in corridors, for staff to use during air raids. There are foldable beds and extra showers.

Asked whether the Kremlin wanted to murder diplomats, as opposed to merely scaring them a little, Mathernová replied with a quote from Catch 22, Joseph Heller’s famous satirical novel. “As Yossarian says: ‘They are trying to kill me! They are lobbing bombs at us!’ I think they are warning shots. They [the Russians] are more and more brazen and callous.”

Vladimir Putin’s strategic goal, she added, was to destroy the EU. She described Russia’s latest threat as “intimidation”, made in the hope that some diplomats from the global south might abandon Kyiv. Meanwhile, the city was creaking. “The level of attacks are much higher than last year, and the power cuts earlier. We’ve had no water in our building. The soft underbelly of a modern city is its sewage system,” she said.

As the capital braces for winter, ambassadors say their continued presence sends a powerful signal of solidarity to Ukraine’s embattled leadership. “They tell us thank you for being here,” Lund-Sørensen said. A fellow ambassador added: “We would all like to stay. We feel conscious that our presence is politically and psychologically important for Ukraine and its resilience.”

The envoy said that in his view the Russians were not hitting foreign missions “by design”. He thought, however, that “sooner or later” a diplomat would be killed by a drone “falling in the wrong place” – an act that would plunge that country’s government into crisis, as it mulled how to respond to Putin’s violence and disregard for international law.

For visiting prime ministers and presidents, getting to and from Kyiv has become more dangerous. The capital’s airport has been shut since the 2022 invasion. Train or car are the only options. On a recent journey from Poland, the envoy said he had to leave his rail compartment twice because of marauding drones. “I sat in the woods for one and a half hours. The train staff gave me a biscuit,” he said.

Frequent air alerts and attacks on bridges have disrupted embassy business and made it difficult for local Ukrainian staff to get to work, he added. The envoy acknowledged: “I have a privileged existence. An alarm goes off and I go and sleep in the basement. Ukrainians have adapted their security protocols. But it’s more inconvenient. There’s a degree of nervousness.”

Mathernová said she sleeps on a mattress in the bathroom of her hotel suite during Russian strikes. She pointed out that millions of Ukrainians are forced to do the same thing – kipping down in bomb shelters, corridors and on the cold floors of metro stations. “There is nothing funny about using winter as a weapon of mass destruction,” she posted earlier this year, after a Kremlin official mocked a photo of her in pyjamas.

Kyiv is classified as a hardship role. Western ambassadors typically stay for two years, separated from families. Lund-Sørensen said there was not exactly “a queue” of colleagues wanting to work in Ukraine but enough “right people” volunteered. “It’s really hard to imagine as a diplomat a more meaningful posting than Ukraine. Its struggle against Russia is personal to me and my country,” he said.

At weekends the envoy relaxes by going on long cycle rides. Mathernová said she enjoyed Nordic walking in the botanical gardens, as well as saunas and dinners with friends. “Kyiv has an unbelievable array of amazing restaurants. One of the things I will miss most is its culinary scene. And it’s can-do attitude. Everything is possible. It’s a big contrast with Brussels,” she said.

Trident nuclear submarine concludes record underwater deployment

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:50:33 GMT

HMS Vengeance’s seven-month patrol prompts fears over slow pace of maintenance of ageing fleet and strain on crew

A Trident nuclear submarine has concluded a record seven-month deployment, returning to the Faslane naval base in Scotland where its crew was greeted by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting.

HMS Vengeance began its patrol on 12 April and spent 217 days submerged before returning on Sunday, having left the country when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street and Manchester United were third in the Premier League.

Its tour surpasses the previous 205-day record set by HMS Vanguard, and has raised questions about the strains placed on sailors and the reliability of ageing submarines sent on the extended missions.

“Patrols are getting longer and longer,” said David Cullen, a nuclear expert with the Basic thinktank. “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world.”

The increase in the time spent at sea reflects the slow pace of submarine maintenance, prompting Labour to blame spending cuts implemented by the Conservatives, though naval chiefs insist there is a plan for improvement.

Streeting said the length of time the crew had spent submerged did not “sit lightly” with him.

Streeting, who was accompanied in Faslane by the first secretary of state, Lou Haigh, added: “It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they’ve given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise.

“I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent.”

He described the nuclear patrols as the “ultimate national endeavour” and thanked the returning submariners for their “dedicated, heroic service” which he said was the model of patriotism.

HMS Vengeance is one of four submarines that carryBritain’s Trident nuclear missiles. A boat is at sea at all times, so the UK could launch strikes even if land-based systems had been destroyed in a nuclear war.

When the Vanguard class of submarines was brought into service in the 1990s, they were designed to carry three to four months of food for the crew of about 140, and deployments of more than 100 days were considered highly exceptional. Missions now start with tinned food crammed into corridors and other available spaces.

Each submarine has to keep its location secret so it cannot be targeted, meaning it also cannot be resupplied. The boats maintain radio silence and so the crew cannot message out on the long deployments, though they can receive news and other information.

Such is the length of the patrols that the return of a Trident submarine, known as a “day zero”, has become a political event. Starmer made an unannounced visit when the last patrol ended in April, praising the crew on their return.

There have been worries about the psychological impact of the patrols on the crew members, who have to spend seven months underwater in a boat 150 metres long, at a time when the Royal Navy is struggling to recruit new personnel.

Last week, the head of the Royal Navy, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for the Trident sailors, but added that the UK needed to “improve our submarine maintenance” to allow faster turnaround.

The submarine service, in line with the rest of the navy, has a “no touching rule” – prohibiting physical intimacy on board – though the service has had to contend with allegations of sexual abuse and harassment during deployments.

after newsletter promotion

In October 2024, the then first sea lord was forced to issue an apology to women – who make up about 10% of the navy – who had suffered “misogyny, bullying and other unacceptable behaviours” in the submarine service.

The navy conducted an inquiry after a whistleblower, Sophie Brook, complained of a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” from male sailors. Reports of rape, physical and verbal abuse were examined in a heavily redacted report.

Trident submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities, and a letter from the prime minister to tell the captain how to proceed in the event it is determined the UK no longer exists after an all-out nuclear attack.

Such is the length of the boat’s patrol it will still be carrying Starmer’s letter, though the replacement submarine on rotation will have Andy Burnham’s instructions, written in longhand in the days after he took over at Downing Street.

In July, Labour announced a £26bn, 10-year plan to invest in Britain’s three main naval bases, at Faslane, the operational home of the Trident submarines, Devonport and Portsmouth, as part of a wider increase in defence spending.

However, the first of the replacements for the four Vanguard class submarines, HMS Dreadnought, is not expected to be ready until about 2032, meaning that the old boats have at least five more years to remain in service.

“The inherent risks of operating submarines are being pushed by them being run as they are. At the end of the submarines’ design life they should be run gently, not as hard as they are,” Cullen said.

Labour rebellion over Rosebank oilfield expected to top 100 MPs

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:35:10 GMT

Total of 75 have already signed letter to Burnham opposing plans as discontent also grows over Europe and welfare changes

As many as 100 Labour MPs could sign a letter opposing the giant Rosebank oilfield, as discontent among backbenchers looks likely to surge this week, with rebellions also brewing over Europe and welfare changes.

A total of 75 MPs have already signed the private letter, which is expected to be delivered in the next fortnight to Andy Burnham as part of a campaign in which Labour MPs from the party’s 2024 intake are playing a significant role.

While the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is said to be minded to reject the controversial oilfield, she could still be overruled by the prime minister, amid a cabinet split in which the chancellor, John Healy, is in favour of the plans.

The letter, first reported by the Sunday Times, says Britain’s credibility as a global climate leader would be destroyed if drilling went ahead off the Scottish coast, and argues that it would not reduce energy bills.

“We’re at a point where Reform and the Greens are on the back foot and Labour is enjoying a bounce, but a lot of people are very worried about Rosebank,” said one Labour MP who signed the letter.

“Andy’s big problem is also that he has let three fights start at the same time, which could prove to be very awkward. Rows about this and what our position should be on European relations have come at the same time as the debates that will come this week over [Alan Milburn’s] proposals on out-of-work benefits for young people. If control of the narrative on one issue is lost it could lead to panic about another.”

Another Labour MP said: “The interest in this is not just from the 2024 MPs. There are a good number of colleagues who just don’t sign letters like this normally, but who are concerned. It’s about staying true to what we told voters, and the fact that a lot of people after the summer we’ve had are really now making a link between the climate crisis and what their experience was when it comes to temperatures or flooding.

“The prospect of government resignations also looms if the drilling licence is granted. While the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is unlikely to go, such a decision would also put [him] in an awkward position given his past description of Rosebank as a ‘colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism’.”

Instrumental in organising the letter is Sera, an affiliate and member-led environmental organisation within Labour, whose members include Miliband as well as ministers such as Luke Pollard, Georgia Gould, Matthew Pennycook and others.

Some who have signed the letter include those who had reluctantly backed the smaller Jackdaw field on the basis that it was primarily gas.

The company operating both fields said on Sunday that gas had begun to flow from the Jackdaw platform, “bringing vital UK energy resources ashore in time for winter”.

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at the North Sea oil and gas producer Adura, said Rosebank and Jackdaw were expected to generate £1.4bn in tax revenues before the end of this parliament, rising to £3.8bn by the end of the next.

“With Jackdaw now producing, and other major projects including Rosebank in our pipeline, we have an opportunity to build a bright future for the North Sea, supporting jobs, investment and Britain’s energy security for years to come,” she added.

Heavy backing for Rosebank is also coming from Labour-supporting unions the GMB and Unite, which have considerable influence over Burnham’s operation, and who are also expressing concern at his talk of rejoining the EU.

The letter opposing Rosebank is modelled on the one that derailed Keir Starmer’s welfare overhaul plans, which spanned the new intake and veterans. Yet one of its signatories pointed out stark differences.

“I do think it will probably get to around 100 MPs and may go beyond it, but the welfare rebels were willing to be much more ruthless. The other thing is that some of the people behind that rebellion are now in government and they are wise to these things.”

Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:23:12 GMT

Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.

Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.

The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.

He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine,” Michal said.

The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”

Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.

It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have attributed to Russia, following an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.

In September, Kapo said it was confident that incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”. The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.

At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.

Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks against defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries on messaging platforms online to carry out acts of sabotage.

Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told state news agency Tass: “... If ‌these are ‌their real plans, then ‌they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia”.

Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:03:56 GMT

Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation

Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.

Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.

The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.

US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.

Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.

A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.

There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.

The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.

The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.

“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.

The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.

A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

Electric vehicle targets and reality are now on a collision course

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:01:19 GMT

Paul English says the cheap home charging that makes EVs economical is out of reach for many, while Mike Hawes wonders if consumers are ready to switch. Plus letters from Ben Plowden and Anne Maclennan

George Monbiot is right that European carmakers have dragged their feet, but his column describes only half the problem (Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them, 11 November). About 40% of UK households have no off-street parking, rising to around 60% in urban areas.

For us, the cheap home charging that makes electric vehicles (EVs) economical is out of reach. Ministers may have removed the need for planning permission for cross-pavement charging channels, yet more than 20 councils still refuse them, while others, like my own Green-run council, dither and leave residents waiting for a policy. (I have been waiting for over two years.)

China did not rely on mandates alone. It paired purchase-tax exemptions with licence-plate privileges and parking and charging discounts: a coherent carrot-and-stick policy approach. Britain offers a patchwork instead. We need national leadership: cheaper parking and VAT-free public charging for EVs, heavier charges on the most polluting vehicles, and one national rule on pavement charging.

Telling carmakers to “move or get squashed” is easy from a house with a driveway. Until families on terraced streets can charge as cheaply as their wealthier neighbours, the transition will feel like something done to them, not for them. Paul English Bristol

George Monbiot claims that the western automotive industry has failed to keep pace with Chinese and other counterparts, and that government should not bend to requests to have the zero-emission vehicle mandate amended.

However, these “foot-dragging, planet-trashing car companies” have actually helped create a new car market with more than 180 electric models available, with more to come, whatever happens to regulation. Average range exceeds 300 miles, enough for at least two weeks’ average driving. And most electric vehicles sold in the UK are actually from European brands.

Consumers have every reason to switch: massive manufacturer discounting, heavy promotional spend, a government grant and sky-high fuel prices; and, as Mr Monbiot says, they are cheaper to run if you can charge at home. Despite these advantages, fewer than three in 10 new car buyers in the UK will choose a pure electric car this year. Rather than western carmakers not being ready, perhaps it’s the consumer? Mike Hawes Chief executive, Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders

Relaxing zero-emission vehicle targets would send entirely the wrong signal at a time when climate action needs to be accelerated, not delayed (Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests, 8 November). As the prime minister himself has acknowledged (British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it, 17 September), the impacts of climate change are no longer a distant threat; they are already being felt across the UK. Yet the government continues to fall short of the pace of action needed.

The Climate Change Committee has repeatedly warned that progress on transport emissions is too slow. Transport remains the UK’s largest source of greenhouse gas emissions, but the good news is that we know what to do to cut those emissions. Electrifying cars and vans through the zero-emission vehicle mandate is the single most important tool available for decarbonising road transport. Weakening those targets would make it significantly harder to meet future carbon budgets and legally binding climate goals.

At the same time, we cannot rely on vehicle technology alone. Improving public transport, increasing car-sharing and making walking and cycling easier are more important than ever if we are to cut emissions while giving people the affordable, sustainable travel choices they need to create prosperity in every postcode. Ben Plowden Chief executive, Campaign for Better Transport

George Monbiot’s article focuses on Britain, but the issues apply equally elsewhere. As usual in this debate, little mention is made of those on a limited income, who cannot change their car on a whim. I bought mine before retiring, at a price I could afford, so that I could hope not to have to change it again.

Mr Monbiot writes “electric cars, if you can charge at home, are much cheaper to run”. This may well be so, but first there is the added expense of installing the system for charging them at home.

The article also states: “We should be reducing transport demand, through a shift towards the 15-minute city model of which Paris is an exemplar. We need better and safer provision for cyclists and pedestrians. We need more investment in public transport.”

This would be ideal if we all lived in cities; we do not. There is one bus service from my local village to the nearest town; the bus stop is 4km from my home. There are two buses into town, one early in the morning and one at lunchtime. The one return journey is scheduled to suit commuters returning by rail in the evening. The terminus (the railway station) is a half-hour’s walk from the shops. How can I, on foot, carry 7kg-12kg sacks of animal food and all my weekly groceries from the town centre to the bus stop and from the bus stop to home? Mr Monbiot, answer me that, if you please. Anne Maclennan Cuguen, France

Ordnance Survey maps go the extra mile

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:01:06 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial which argues that the agency’s maps are still a superior way to navigate the landscape

I loved your homage to the original mapmakers of the Ordnance Survey, giving credit to those who hauled their theodolites around the country to take their measurements (Editorial, 8 November).

Credit also should be given to the mathematicians, and especially the computers (people who did the arithmetic for hour after hour) who took the field measurements and converted them to coordinates to plot on a paper map.

I could just about cope with the sine rule and the books of log tables needed for a simple triangulation, but the computational effort needed to deal with even a simple map projection such as the Cassini-Soldner one used by the OS until the 1940s would fill me with dread. They require the use of sines, cosines and tangents in multiple calculations to get a single x, y coordinate pair.

It’s easy to praise the people who did the glamorous cartography such as displacement, simplification, drawing etc, but miss out on the hard work the surveyors and mathematicians do. John Elgy Redditch, Worcestershire

An Ordnance Survey map does indeed provide cultural enrichment and pleasure, as do various products of the OS shop such as puzzle books and personalised maps. However, for a deeper experience, try orienteering. It is a sport that can be enjoyed competitively, or by simply walking in a scenic setting. Events have courses suitable for all ages.

Many clubs across the UK stage orienteering events. These may take place in forests, on moorland, in interesting historic urban areas, and even indoors in an Ikea store. Many clubs offer come-and-try-it events in local parks for beginners. Doug Edwards Withington, Manchester

For hikers and off-roaders, Ordnance Survey maps are indeed still a genuinely useful – as well as nostalgic – way to navigate, especially using the OS’s GPS-enabled app. But their usefulness is significantly degraded by something that I only discovered (the hard way) relatively recently: that they do not reliably show public rights of way.

Only local authorities hold the so-called “definitive” public right of way route maps, more often than not in paper form only, which you can inspect only by visiting the local town hall.

More to the point, with a lack of coordination typical of the British public sector, they are under no obligation to tell Ordnance Survey if the public right of way routes change or are extinguished (which is a regular occurrence). Some authorities do, some don’t. So: caveat navigator. Stephen Psallidas Newcastle

Folding OS maps have a distinct role that will preserve their relevance: on the phone app, the little red arrow shows you exactly where you are – the paper map spread on the pub table later settles the argument over the mistake that got you there. Jonathan Hauxwell Crosshills, North Yorkshire

Chickens are great characters, not cowards

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:00:54 GMT

Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny

Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).

I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

They display a wide range of emotions, including empathy for members of their flock that were ill, and grief at their passing. They also took great delight in terrorising my cats and stealing food from the plates of small children.

Branding chicken-kind broadly as cowardly removes their individuality and, as with labelling foxes as cunning or sheep as stupid, merely serves to justify our treatment of these “dumb” animals. Jo Barlow Torquay, Devon

The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:00:46 GMT

Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes.

Importantly, the Norwegian research cited does not demonstrate that eagles cause the “wipeout” of seabird colonies. Rather, it documents how eagle disturbance, largely involving immature eagles from an established population, can accelerate declines in colonies already experiencing food shortages. This distinction matters. If impacts are greatest where seabirds are struggling to find sufficient food, protecting prey availability must be central to conservation efforts.

Of course, seabirds face considerable additional pressures, including climate change, declining prey availability and disease. These vulnerabilities must inform reintroduction planning. However, impacts on individual colonies do not necessarily demonstrate population-level consequences, particularly for mobile species.

Through the Cumbrian White-tailed Eagle Project, we are exploring these questions, combining ecological research with community engagement to assess the opportunities and risks of restoration. The appropriate response is rigorous ecological assessment and adaptive management, not an assumption that restoring a native predator represents an unacceptable conservation risk. Prof Ian Convery University of Cumbria

Your article distracts from the real causes of seabird decline. Britain’s seabird numbers are collapsing primarily due to overfishing, seabed degradation and climate change, which have reduced fish stocks, leaving seabirds struggling to find enough food to raise their chicks. Extreme weather has also put pressure on remaining colonies.

Of course, the return of any species, including white-tailed eagles, needs careful consideration – with strict licensing following rigorous ecological feasibility and community engagement. But it is wrong to portray the reintroduction of a native predator as a major conservation threat while giving so little attention to human-driven decline of the food chain on which seabirds depend.

By restoring natural habitat and ecological processes, rebuilding food chains and reintroducing lost native species through rewilding, we can give nature the chance to recover and thrive. Framing native species’ return as a threat delays vital recovery and traps ecosystems in a degraded state. Rather than blaming native predators, our focus must remain on restoring the healthy ecosystems on which all wildlife depends. Rebecca Wrigley Founder and chief executive, Rewilding Britain
