England handed boost for All Blacks clash with Furbank leading return of cavalry

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:00:19 GMT

Chessum, Atkinson and full-back Furbank back from injury

England expect backlash after New Zealand defeat in Wales

England have welcomed back the cavalry for the crunch clash with the All Blacks on Saturday with George Furbank, Ollie Chessum and Seb Atkinson all returning to the squad from injury.

Steve Borthwick’s team are braced for a backlash after New Zealand’s first defeat by Wales in 73 years, but the England head coach is boosted with three key men on course to make their comebacks this weekend.

Furbank shone in his first England appearance in two years against Australia, but sat out the 78-15 win against Japan on Saturday with a groin problem. Chessum, the vice-captain, was also absent against Eddie Jones’s side with a shoulder injury, as was the inside-centre Atkinson with a groin complaint. All three were named on Sunday in the 36-man squad, however.

England are looking for their fifth successive win in the Nations Championship and clinched their first home victory against the All Blacks since 2012 this time last year. Jones predicted a “violent” response from New Zealand after they were toppled in Cardiff, but victory for England would put them top of the northern hemisphere table and pile the pressure on Ireland and France before their matches.

Since the 33-19 win against the All Blacks last year, Scott Robertson has been sacked as their head coach with Dave Rennie appointed and overseeing an upturn in form, before the defeat by Wales the weekend.

The tighthead prop Joe Heyes said, however, that England now have a taste for beating the All Blacks.

“We’d expect the best of New Zealand every time we face them,” he said. “They know it’s a big game and it’s obviously a huge rivalry as well. So regardless of what the result was for this week or last week or whatever, we’re going to get the best of New Zealand. I just had two mint choc chip ice-creams in [the changing room]. And the first was as good as the second and the second will be as good as the third. So I’m actually still incredibly excited. It’s a whole different game and every rugby game is different.”

The captain, Maro Itoje, has beaten New Zealand on three occasions – twice with England and once with the British & Irish Lions – and has called on his side to carry the fight to the All Blacks. He said: “You’ve just got to attack the game. New Zealand are one of these teams … At Premiership level and with some international teams it’s like: ‘OK, they’re not very good at this, they’re not very good at that.’ New Zealand’s not like that. They’re actually very good at pretty much all aspects of the game.

“It’s not often you look at their team and think they have an obvious weakness and therefore you just have to attack everything. Every scrum, every lineout, every breakdown, every collision, everything. You just have to go after everything.

“That’s just the mindset. We just need to attack the game from minute one. If you start poorly, it’s very difficult for you. If you’re ill‑disciplined, it’s very difficult for you. But if you’re aggressive, if you’re disciplined, if you have that mindset to attack everything, then things can open up.”

Scotland hold off late Australia rally to secure narrow victory

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 17:37:08 GMT

Scotland 15-12 Australia

Fagerson and Dempsey touch down in Murrayfiield

After the pyrotechnics in Paris on Friday and a wondrous Welsh win in Cardiff on Saturday, this was a much more prosaic affair. Not that the stakes were low: both teams badly needed a positive result and Gregor Townsend’s side got one by dealing with the quintessentially Scottish conditions better than their opponents.

Scotland could scarcely afford another patchy performance like last weekend, when they excelled in the first half against New Zealand before capitulating in the second. They ultimately edged across the line at a sodden Murrayfield, but might have fallen to a calamitous defeat had Darcy Graham not foiled a last-ditch Wallabies attack.

“If Darcy hadn’t made that tackle it would have been a tricky time,” Townsend said of the dramatic final play. “I’m proud of the players that they helped each other out. We knew Australia were going to run it from deep, so that’s the frustrating thing … But I think we deserved the win given the effort that had gone in and given we’d led throughout.”

Thus the hosts narrowly won a match that Les Kiss, the Wallabies head coach, described as “turgid”. But the limitations of this Australia side are well known and the visitors would have hoped for anything but heavy rain. Australia have lost four in a row and will go to Wales next week even more desperate for victory. Scotland leapfrog Wales to move fourth in the northern hemisphere table on points difference.

A knee injury to the captain, Sione Tuipulotu, prompted a late reshuffle: Bristol’s Tom Jordan started at No 12, with the openside flanker Rory Darge taking the armband. Flower of Scotland sung at Murrayfield always stirs the spirit, and as smoke from pre-match fireworks hung in the air, the teams set about each other under leaden skies. Australia repeatedly repelled Scotland on their try-line but became fatally narrow in defence, allowing Ben White to chuck a pass right for Matt Fagerson to dive over on eight minutes.

Harry Potter’s excellent try had the Wallabies back on terms: Carter Gordon sparked an attack down the visitors’ left before Fraser McReight supplied a pass for the former Leicester back to score. The Australia scrum‑half Ryan Lonergan attempted a drop goal but pulled it: a scruffy effort that summed up the overall mood. Graham then touched down on 24 minutes, after a clever pass by Darge, but Kyle Steyn had put a foot in touch. The second-row Scott Cummings then trudged off with a thigh injury, Max Williamson replacing him.

When Australia were penalised for not rolling away, Finn Russell kicked for the corner, and the No 8 Jack Dempsey burrowed over. Russell’s conversion, making it a seven-point game, felt significant. But Australia came again. Billy Pollard was shoved over, only for the score to be disallowed for obstruction by Jeremy Williams after a check by the television match official. Scotland thus nursed their seven-point lead to the interval.

Pollard’s afternoon worsened five minutes after half-time, when an upright tackle and clash of heads with Blair Kinghorn brought a trip to the sin-bin. It stayed a yellow card on review, thankfully for the Wallabies hooker, but when he returned the scoreboard stubbornly remained at 12-5.

The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 17:30:19 GMT

Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks

The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.

While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “it’s make or bake time”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.

Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves, while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition.

Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser, Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field, must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing.

A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays.

A large majority of the global public recognises the threat from global heating and wants action by governments. Of course, this takes courage and leadership: people may back a green transition in the abstract, but be more resistant to changes that affect their lives. But those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, at Cop31 and at a national level, should be emboldened by the way that public awareness and support have grown: they are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past.

The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 17:25:19 GMT

Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked

The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”

This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “human bandwidth”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

Trust in institutions is waning. Reliability and fair outcomes matter. But the public also need ways to challenge decisions. Learning from business must not mean treating public scrutiny as “frictions” or neglecting the people whom markets fail to serve. Dame Antonia correctly identifies poor incentives, churn and inadequate training as issues. But who gets to the top also matters. A 2025 paper by Oxford University’s Erzsébet Bukodi and John H Goldthorpe, with Nottingham University’s Inga Steinberg, says access to elite civil service posts remains skewed to people from advantaged backgrounds. Progress towards widening access has reversed in the last 20 years. Whitehall risks overlooking the talent to govern an increasingly complex country.

The academics traced the backgrounds of 476 public service leaders between 1945 and 2022. Among officials reaching the top, the share from higher professional and managerial families fell from 56% before 1960 to 45% in 1980-99, then rose again. Those reaching senior posts in 2000‑22 resembled their pre-1960 predecessors in class origins. The paper also highlights how few people at the top have qualifications in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) or quantitatively oriented disciplines such as sociology and demography. The latter could help officials understand the lives affected by policies they implement. Such a “cultural disconnect”, experts say, has caused major policy blunders.

Class privilege is linked to Whitehall’s cult of the generalist: those valued for intellectual dexterity rather than expertise. Privately schooled Oxford graduates dominated among top officials from privileged families, the vast majority of whom had studied humanities – the traditional grounding for Whitehall generalists. State-school entrants from other universities were more likely to have Stem or social science degrees. Better recruitment and promotion could help with the specialist knowledge Dame Antonia wants. Kate Bingham, the former vaccine taskforce chair, has warned that too few scientists are being recruited to shift Whitehall’s skillset. It’s time to look at the social selection that determines who gets to the top as well as reforming the system that shapes officials’ behaviour.

Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools.

Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”.

He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade.

Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer, Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”.

“If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham.

Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit.

The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year.

Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it.

Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront.

Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.”

Pat McFadden acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently.

The work and pensions secretary said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work.

But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said.

The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 17:00:18 GMT

Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change

Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis

A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.

We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.

Sixteen years ago, the Conservative government took a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt of the cuts they chose to make. Those becoming adults today are the children of austerity. At four years old, with Sure Start centres closed, too many were already beginning school behind, without the support they needed to catch up. By 12, too many had seen youth clubs shut down and had fewer places to go in their communities with the closure of libraries and leisure centres. Teenagers in need of mental health support were told to wait months or even years. And, by 18, millions had passed through an education system that told them their technical talents were not worth as much as the abilities of their academic peers.

A country focused on the future would make young people its priority for investment – not the target for cuts. It would give all young people a path in life, giving them confidence and hope for the future. Britain has done neither. It is time to acknowledge that this failure has left too many young people ill-prepared for the challenging world they now face. And, of course, that has costs. Under the Conservatives, the welfare bill shot up by £114bn.

What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again. The crude cuts they are proposing to the welfare bill would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.

The way I see it is that we have two choices: we can either invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on; or we can continue to pay the price for failure.

I choose the first. The time has come for a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world. To bring down the welfare bill for good, we have to act at the different stages where young people can fall behind. We must intervene long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state.

Next week, Alan Milburn’s review into young people and work will be published. I want it to be a watershed moment. We have an opportunity to change the way we think about welfare and the way we think about childhood. Because the two cannot be separated.

For too long, we have waited until young people reach adulthood and then tried to deal with the problems that have built up over the years. Under this government, we will start much earlier, making sure children have the support they need at the moments that matter most.

It is what I call a whole-childhood approach. It means, in the early years, giving every child a proper start. Those who start school behind too often never catch up. To stop these children from falling through the cracks, we must build an education system which offers support with wider needs, such as mental health, and values all talents.

This brings me to a change I am determined to make as prime minister. I will build an education system in England based on the principle of parity between academic and technical routes, that gives all young people a path in life, a confidence in their abilities and tells them they are equally valued.

For too long, Britain has praised the graduation cap and looked down on the hard hat. New technical pathways in school will start to put that right. We will open up opportunities for young people to learn new skills and get good jobs where they live. When they approach adulthood, we will make sure they do not face a cliff edge. We will guarantee good work experience and employment opportunities.

The government will consider Milburn’s recommendations carefully and respond in full in the coming weeks. But I can say now that our response will not be in the manner of traditional Department for Work and Pensions reform. It will be societal and generational. We will rethink supporting childhood – shifting government spending from paying for failure to investing in success.

Of course, that support will have to come with responsibilities. If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can.

Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point. The system will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to receive. It will understand their ambitions and identify the help they need to achieve them.

This is the sustainable way to get the welfare bill down for good. It is how we build a more preventive and productive state and a country which allows every young person to grow up with hope.

Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 15:31:08 GMT

Ulster Hall, BelfastWith two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

All 12 album tracks are played, shuffled in among later hits such as Hundred Mile High City and Profit in Peace. The six-piece have become a family firm: Steve Cradock’s son Cass switches between guitar and keys; drummer Oscar Harrison’s son Leon works congas and tambourine and sings backing vocals. On The Circle, the first big singalong, father and son drum as one.

Fleeting Mind is pure refraction, Cradock’s lead all glacial pull-offs and slow runs, as if he’s still finding colours in a palette he mixed when MiniDiscs were the future. Get Away still welds, then transcends, Dear Prudence and When the Levee Breaks. Wistful craft and maximum R&B are their two modes, and nobody in their class moves between them so easily, or soulfully. One for the Road’s closing refrain, “I’ll sing my sorrow”, is longing worn without embarrassment. That’s the gift: songs about fragile feelings, sung back by people seldom licensed to have them.

The ballads cluster early on, trading a little momentum for some of the night’s finest singing. Alone on stage for the encore, Fowler introduces Robin Hood as “the night I came face to face with Christ, all for £2.50”, and Belfast takes it from him. The Day We Caught the Train closes, as it must: a Beatles-schooled heirloom few have bettered in the 30 years since, and seismic with it.

Consensus has lazily filed them under dad-rock. With two dads and two sons on stage, the term has never sounded less like an insult. Their flowers are overdue. There are 20 more nights to send them.

Ocean Colour Scene play Ulster Hall, Belfast, on 15 November; then tour Ireland and the UK until 12 December

When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 15:00:16 GMT

Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat

From Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart, Bill Gates and Bill Clinton, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang.

These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well …

We all love a bit of schadenfreude now and again. But it’s not so fun for the employees, shareholders, partners and others who work alongside these men. And it’s deeply unpleasant for their families, particularly when they work in the same business.

Jensen Huang’s family is feeling that right now. His son, daughter and son-in-law all have prominent positions at his company. His daughter is married to another Nvidia executive. And they’re not alone. And when it happens at a smaller business, the impact is even worse.

Huang’s company is so well known that the world knows of his indiscretions. But people live in their own worlds, and in my client’s world, pretty much everyone in the company knows what’s going on with the cheating spouse.

Some surveys claim that as many as 20% of people have admitted to cheating on their partners. There are 34m small businesses in the US with almost a third being family owned. So the odds are that there are other moms and dads (probably dads, given that 61% of businesses are still owned by men) making the same mistakes. I have clients in this position. And their children working in their businesses are going through the same horrible experience.

Hopefully, the children working in family businesses have positions where they are not directly reporting to mom and dad. Hopefully there’s an organizational structure and policies in place that separates them from ownership and treats them as any other employee. Whether the owner of the company – even if it’s the mom or dad (again probably the dad) – is having dalliances on the side should be of no matter. They’re doing a job in the company. They’re not a part of this.

But unfortunately they are. It’s still their parents. There’s still an unsaid thing amongst the rest of the employees that not only are they the kids but they’re also likely to be the future owners of the company. Their behavior inside the company walls is being watched as closely as their parents. Suddenly, their parents’ behavior is now reflected on them. Can they also be trusted?

And yet I don’t feel entirely sorry for the Jensen kids or any kids working for their parents where a similar situation occurs. They’ve enjoyed the perks of being the owners’ offspring. They’ve likely been given opportunities they wouldn’t necessarily get if they worked for someone else. They know what they signed up for.

The hope is that Huang’s children, and the children of any business owner going through the same situation, learn and turn it to their favor. When a responsible CEO cheats on their spouse, it calls into question their overall ethics. When the affairs become a circus like Jensen’s – or even in the smaller world of my clients – the ridicule it creates undermines their authority. People look at my cheating clients like they’re a joke. They wonder how they could do something so blatantly stupid like having an affair with an employee in an environment where their children work? They question the judgment of the very leader who runs the company that provides their livelihood.

The kids should stand by both their parents, accept that mistakes were made, but show to the world that it’s still their family and that they love them. But they should also take the opportunity to show their fellow employees, and the world, that they wouldn’t behave the same way.

After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays

We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving.

I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.

Grocery retailers are keen to take advantage of holiday-related binge eating, developing and releasing ever-more-depraved festive novelty foods to subdue us into carb-induced slumber.

In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk, affectionately known as “picky bits”, to prevent your digestive system from ever idling into park. “Ham and Barber’s Cheddar Crumpets”. “Twelve Mini Chicken Kyivs”. “British Melton Mowbray pork pie”. These dishes either sound like a thing a tertiary character orders in a Harry Potter novel or the last meal of a 60s British gangster.

In America, we have Trader Joe’s. There’s no fun name like “picky bits” for the plastic tubs of slop they sell in the refrigerator section. Instead, we turn to our spouses and partners and mumble: “Pick me up some of that crap.” Toffee-flavored cheddar cheese. Pumpkin spice yogurt dip. An advent calendar … for dogs.

I don’t begrudge anyone for cramming their shopping carts with intentionally whimsical perishable food products for depressed people. Overeating is a better use of your hibernation time than drunk-driving into an Arby’s at 2am. This is a holiday rite of passage: the junk food gauntlet. It’s as crucial to the festive season as a decorated tree and a surplus of good cheer.

But what if I told you that with the press of a button, the entire picky bits industrial complex could collapse before we even have a chance to open our canine advent calendars?

In France last month, supermarket refrigerators across the country were shut off remotely by Iranian terrorists. Other European countries have been hit with similar attacks, which occasionally lead to food having to be thrown out.

My entire body goes numb thinking about what it would do to US and British citizens if their supermarkets were similarly affected during the holidays. Can I muddle through another family get-together without a large, rapidly-warming bowl of chicken uncured bacon ranch dip to soothe my anxiety? Doubtful. The chaos would be unprecedented. It’d be like Judge Dredd, Blade Runner and The Purge rolled into one, but with worse catering.

You might be wondering how someone even hacks a fridge. Well, industrial fridges like the ones hacked in France are operated remotely via computer.

It makes some sense that large-scale operations like grocery stores need to have the ability to make temperature changes quickly, without a bunch of fumbling around with knobs and buttons. But internet-connected fridges are available to consumers, too. Refrigerators from brands such as LG and Samsung allow regular people to change the temperature of their fridge from a smartphone app.

My house is not nearly big enough to require me to adjust the settings on my appliances from another room. I only have six rooms (counting the bathrooms, with which I am very familiar during the holidays). Once again, technology aims to solve a problem that doesn’t exist.

All we’re doing is trying to get closer to the God-level control of everything at the push of a button. The issue with that is: if we are God to our machines, then the devil also exists, and he knows how to code.

Maybe there are a few useful applications of this technology for those of us who are supremely lazy. Some fridges have cameras and AI capabilities that tell you what food is inside, so that you might maintain a clean, tidy food storage system – one that tells you when your groceries are about to go bad.

As though your actual human eyes and hands don’t work. That old broccoli is in there. Do I need a computer to tell me what my poisoned nose already can sense? Yup, that’s rotten food. Confirmed. Until there’s a robot that can take the food out for me, move it to the compost bin, and hose down the interior, I’ll pass on the smart fridge.

I’ve already pointed out that computers have overwhelmed our cars, but this feels far more ominous. I need my holiday trash. I need my 2,000-calorie tandoori chicken bites. I can’t function without uncured ham and swiss cheese pockets.

This is existential. It goes beyond mere sustenance. This is my emotional support during trying times. If black-hat hackers can shut off my fridge and spoil my food, I might start picking my hair out or nibbling on one of my less crucial digits. If my mouth isn’t full of goop and slop, then I might be forced to have a conversation with an uncle. These are the things nightmares are made of.

The calamity is coming. Someone with more computer savvy will realize that the most vulnerable moment in our society is right now, during the holidays. The time when we need our buffalo chicken garlic bread bites the most.

The only solution is to rip the computers out and go back to the switches, toggles and tactile buttons that used to maintain our civilization. The alternative is risking a holiday season without parmesan-crusted chocolate chip cookies or peppermint orange chicken.

If you’re sweating right now, your blood pressure rising like a crimson tide, then you’re a normal human being. This is the proper response to a doomsday scenario otherwise unfathomable by the average mind.

Alternatively, we could go back to digging holes in the backyard and filling them with ice and food. Hackers can’t access your refrigeration hole. They can’t melt ice from thousands of miles away. We must go back to nature – potato cheese sticks and cookie dough ice cream bites preserved as the Lord intended.

Grab a shovel and get to work. Just make sure you have a functioning microwave.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 14:00:16 GMT

About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?

Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.

“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”

Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.

High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”

The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”

It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”

In the UK, Europe and the US, gout afflicts 2%-4% of the population. In the UK that equates to about 1.6 million people. “That is an awful lot more people in this country, for example, than have rheumatoid arthritis,” says Lucy Donaldson, director of research at Arthritis UK. She thinks persistent misunderstandings about gout can be a barrier to effective treatment. “There’s a lack of recognition about how common it is, and therefore people think it’s more isolated,” she says. “And, there’s a very judgmental attitude.”

Most sufferers will experience their first attack in the big toe, but if left untreated gout can spread to other joints in the foot and ankle, or the knee, or even hands, wrists and elbows. “You start to recruit different joints, and the flares become more common,” says Roddy. “Trying to avoid that happening is one of the important justifications for earlier treatment.”

Across the world gout affects about three times as many men as women (it is especially rare in pre-menopausal women). Certain ethnic groups, including Maori people, have a high susceptibility. “Some people may have gene variants that predispose them to having less tight control over urate levels in blood,” says Donaldson. But the genetic predisposition to gout is not perfectly understood. “Most of the focus has been on the genetics of uric acid levels,” says Roddy, “but we know less about the genetics determining crystal formation and inflammatory processes.”

Global incidence of gout is predicted to increase by 70% from 2020 to 2050; this is largely due to population growth and ageing. It’s more common among older people, but it’s also possible to suffer a first attack in one’s 20s. “There are reports coming in suggesting that the age of people developing gout is coming down,” says Donaldson.

If we still don’t hear too much about younger people getting gout, it could be because they often don’t seek treatment for the first flare. Painful as it is, gout tends to subside quickly.

“I just waited and eventually, a couple of days later, it went away,” says McAllister-Byrne, who is now 40. “A year or two after that, it would come back, and I’d wait for it to go. It’s only in the last two or three years that I went to the doctor.”

Historically, gout was understood as an affliction of leisure, of indulgence, even of quality. The Georgians thought it “a disease of the better sort, a superiority tax, a celebrity complaint,” according to the book Gout: The Patrician Malady. “Gout is the distemper of a gentleman,” Lord Chesterfield said, “whereas rheumatism is the distemper of a hackney coachman.” Gout was a hereditary trait that ran in good families; a badge of honour; a mark of distinction.

To some extent, those beliefs still colour our view of gout as a comical malady brought on by excess and idleness. “We’ve got the history of seeing pictures of people with a bandaged big toe in a bath chair,” says Donaldson. “And it often looks to be somebody who’s quite well off and clearly has quite a rich diet.”

“It definitely isn’t treated very seriously by other people,” says McAllister-Byrne, who says he had to endure unflattering comparisons to Henry VIII. “That’s what everyone always says, insinuating that it’s self-inflicted, from drinking lots of red wine and eating red meat.” He is in fact mostly vegetarian, and doesn’t drink regularly. McAllister-Byrne’s gout was probably part of his inheritance, however. “That’s what I think, because my dad has it.”

The National Institute for Heath and Care Excellence (Nice) guidelines for gout treatment call for patients with persistent flare-ups to be given urate-lowering therapy on a treat-to-target basis: that is, to establish a level of medication that will work and adjust the dose as required. Allopurinol is the most common prescription; febuxostat is another that will keep blood uric acid levels below a prescribed target of 360 micromoles per litre. Under that level, new crystals are prevented from forming and existing crystals in the joints should eventually dissolve. The risk of further gout attacks can be effectively eliminated.

That’s the theory, but it’s not always common practice in primary care. “Changing practice is like stopping a juggernaut sometimes,” says Roddy, who was instrumental in establishing the Nice guidelines in 2022.

“Not everybody’s treating to target,” says Donaldson. “They’re just giving a dose that they think is appropriate, but not then testing to see if it’s having the right effect. People were getting about 50% of what the effective dose should be in many cases.”

Very often the patients themselves do not follow up their initial treatment once the symptoms have abated, at least not until they’ve had several more painful flare-ups. As Roddy puts it: “The episodic nature of the condition contributes to suboptimal management.”

Then, of course, the stigma associated with gout can inhibit people from seeking treatment. It’s still regarded as a lifestyle disease, a consequence of a rich diet and too much drink. And while there are certain dietary risk factors – alcohol and foods rich in purine such as red meat and seafood can increase urate levels – the whole picture is much more complicated.

“Moderate wine consumption doesn’t really increase your risk,” says Roddy. “The risk is greatest with beer, and the reason for that is that beer is very rich in a compound called guanosine that the body breaks down to make urates.” But ultimately dietary precautions will not, on their own, alleviate gout. “There’s no good evidence that dietary modification makes much difference to urate levels,” says Roddy.

Apart from treatment, McAllister-Byrne hasn’t made any changes to his lifestyle. “When I was desperate during last year, I looked into it and I was like: I’m pretty much doing most of that,” he says.

The true causes of gout are a complex interplay of genetics, ethnicity, diet and related conditions including obesity, heart disease and poor kidney function. But the stigma associated with the historical disease persists. Could that be because, centuries on, we still call it gout?

We don’t diagnose people with apoplexy or dropsy any more, but we still have no better name for gout than gout, with all its ancient associations, misunderstandings and prejudices. A 2018 study found that when members of the public completed a questionnaire about gout, they were likely to believe it was caused by the patient’s own behaviour, but when it was called “urate crystal arthritis” (UCA), they were more likely to attribute it to ageing. Participants also considered UCA a more serious condition requiring medication, while gout was seen as more socially embarrassing.

Since starting treatment with allopurinol at the beginning of the year, McAllister-Byrne has had no further flare-ups of the disease. He is, however, reluctant to consider himself cured. “It’s managed, but it’s a sort of niggle in the back of my mind – if there were ever any issues, climate change or whatever, that stopped supply chains,” he says. “It’s made me think: should I stockpile some? Because quite quickly, I would be hobbling around.”

Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 14:00:15 GMT

People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated?

I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies, on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”.

Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders?

Apparently: only 41% of the 1970 cohort rated their health excellent or very good compared with 50% of the 1958 lot surveyed in 2008, when they were in their early 50s. Meanwhile, a higher proportion of gen X reported having diabetes (9% v 6%) and were obese (32% v 26%). We also reported more symptoms of psychological distress.

Assuming we can discount fuzzy peach bath pearls or plaid shirts turning out to be mysteriously toxic, what’s happening to gen X? I have theories. For a start, this study uses self-reported health data. Maybe we’re more inclined to admit weakness and health worries? That might not be all bad – 10% more gen X than boomer women consulting a doctor about their mental health could, actually, reflect our greater openness rather than the fact we’re falling apart (it’s probably both).

A recent US study also found we’re the only generation currently drinking more now than before Covid. The researchers theorised it’s a stress-related hangover from the pandemic. And speaking of stress, demographic shifts mean many gen Xers are squished in a caring “triple-decker sandwich”: 56% have adult children at home (I bet all 56% are worried about their future); 34% with kids under 18 are also caring for ageing parents.

We also grew up in the golden age of UPFs. My husband’s madeleine de Proust is tinned ravioli and I remember my busy working mother gleefully buying our first M&S ready meal – chicken kiev, my madeleine. We might be fibremaxxing now, but we’re products of the era that birthed the Pop Tart: maybe the (kiev) chickens are coming home to roost?

But my strongest, grimmest hunch is that gen X aren’t special: we’re all less healthy. A 2024 UCL study found that while boomers are living longer, they’re doing so in poorer health than their parents, living with more chronic disease and a higher incidence of cancer, lung disease, type 2 diabetes and other serious conditions, a phenomenon the lead author, Laura Gimeno, described as “generational health drift”.

Down the cohorts, there’s the worrying rise in cancers among under-50s: in England, prostate cancer rates have quadrupled and bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses have more than doubled. This summer a damning report by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health warned that without drastic action, the UK is risking “raising one of the unhealthiest generations of children ever”. A King’s Fund analysis this year found that healthy life expectancy in England was more than two years lower in 2022–24 than in 2017-19.

This is compounded by income inequality (which in the UK is among the highest in Europe) and financial insecurity. Deprivation is starkly correlated with poor health outcomes across all generations – the same King’s Fund study showed a difference of almost 20 years of healthy life between the least and most deprived areas (69.2 and 49.8). In 2023, the Institute for Public Policy Research reported the UK was getting “poorer and sicker”, and while the economy is reportedly picking up, we’re still pretty poor and sick.

The gen X responders in the 1970 British Cohort Study rated health as more important than money. Hopefully our (mostly gen X) politicians feel the same and tackle the underlying issues – health and care services at breaking point, poverty, poor housing, pollution – with the urgency they need. The Centre for Longitudinal Studies started a new study this month following 30,000 UK babies. It would be wonderful if a few decades from now, as gen X staggers into decrepitude (if we’re lucky), it had good news to report.

Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:00:14 GMT

From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair?

For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

Dupes are products that claim to offer a similar experience to a high-end item though do not claim to be that product. They were originally a Gen Z obsession but have become a mainstream shopping trend at a time of strained household finances.

“No matter what age you are, how much money you’ve got to spend, everyone wants to ‘luxe it up’ with a dupe,” says Catherine Shuttleworth, a retail consultant and chief executive of Savvy Marketing.

“The message is ‘why not be smart like me saving cash but still looking good’,” she says.

“In the case of homewares, a high street dupe of a luxury branded candle can look and smell just as good as the real thing, and will your visitors really notice that your table lamps are from B&M not the White Company?”

Dupe culture is being supercharged by social media, particularly TikTok. More than 30 million people across the UK now use TikTok each month, according to the company, with Gen-Z’ers admitting that seeing products sell out or go viral makes them more likely to buy them.

Data firm YPulse has been tracking consumer attitudes to dupes for several years and Tori D’Amico, managing content editor, says: “The idea that a dupe can be a true replacement for a luxury item is still prevalent. Dupes are not shameful or embarrassing to own. Young consumers brag online about finding a good deal and share it with the masses.”

YPulse’s most recent research found that 44% of UK 13- to 39-year-olds have bought a dupe in the past year. When asked, just over half (53%) of this age group agreed that “the quality of dupe/fake luxury items makes me less likely to want to purchase a real luxury item”.

Dupes are particularly prominent in the beauty world but are also found in other sectors including food, furniture, homeware and designer fashion.

US “dupe” retailer Quince, which sells upmarket products ranging from candles to cashmere sweaters, has just launched in the UK. Alongside each product on its website it suggests the saving you are making against more expensive brands. A £50 woman’s red cashmere jumper, for example, is pictured alongside graphics comparing it with jumpers from Cos and Reiss costing three times as much.

Fragrance, in particular, is a popular target. There are more than 50,000 videos on TikTok under the combined hashtag #perfumedupe and #perfumedupes, where influencers rate imitation fragrances against famous names and tell viewers where to find them.

With fragrances a sought-after Christmas gift the platform is awash with content extolling these cheaper scents. Instead of spending nearly £130 on Mugler’s Alien try Zara’s Violet Blossom for £15.99, suggests one. Or, if you can’t afford Le Labo’s Another 13, try Marks & Spencer’s Aura Ambrette, a snip at £22.50.

In TikTok Dupeland budget supermarket Aldi is lauded as a perfume house with its Lacura brand tipped to offer substitutes for high-end favourites ranging from Paradoxe to Flowerbomb and Baccarat Rouge – for £7 a bottle.

“These cut-price products are in focus right now as consumers look for cheaper alternatives in response to rising prices,” says Eric Mills from market research firm NielsenIQ. In a recent survey, 38% of UK consumers said that in the past 12 months they had switched to lower-priced brands to manage their shopping bills.

“The buyers of these brands are often thought of as only younger consumers, but while Gen Z are key spenders, it’s millennials who account for the greatest proportion of sales,” he adds.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

In a microcosm of what is likely happening elsewhere in the market, the number of people buying dupe fragrances online is up 17% in the past year which is ahead of the overall market.

With the continued adoption of AI tools, Mills says: “It’s easy to imagine dupes gaining further traction, as consumers can simply ask a chatbot for a cheaper alternative to their favourite luxury scent.”

With dupes copying well-known brands without pretending to be the real thing they occupy a space somewhere between authentic and fake. While consumers might love dupes, the targets are less enthusiastic.

Celebrity makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury, whose £350m fortune stems from the sale of her eponymous beauty empire to Spanish fragrance and fashion group Puig, recently told the BBC that “when you dupe, you dupe the consumer”.

“It is not Charlotte Tilbury … and it is not performing the way that my products do,” Tilbury says of cheaper imitations. “If I could do them for those prices I would.”

Charlotte Tilbury has had some success pushing back and, in 2019, brought a successful copyright case against Aldi over the designs on its Filmstar Bronze & Glow palette which the supermarket had copied.

Claire Breheny, partner and head of trade marks at Mathys & Squire suggests that business owners should be requesting that dupes be taken down from online platforms or social media. Brand owners “need to protect their packaging and get-up, not just their name.

“The risk for consumers is that similar packaging doesn’t guarantee similar quality, ingredients or performance – although a cheaper alternative isn’t necessarily always going to be inferior.”

With the cost of living crisis only making dupes more attractive to shoppers, Savvy Marketing’s Shuttleworth says that nearly 80% of shoppers its survey polled were happy to selectively spend more on treats and luxuries where they think it’s worth it.

“The challenge for top brands like Charlotte Tilbury, is that they need to be able to convince shoppers the quality difference is always worth paying for.”

The 14 best men’s boots for winter, from chelseas and lace-ups to wellies

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:00:13 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Whether you want minimalist or heritage, waterproof or suede, our menswear expert has rounded up the most stylish pairs for every occasion and outfit The best men’s coats for autumn and winter

I haven’t always worn boots. For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. All anyone sees is a smart pair of shoes that happens to keep your ankles warm.

Here’s the thing: boots needn’t be intimidating. They’re just the wintry version of the leather shoes you already own. A chelsea is your loafer – it goes with pretty much everything in your wardrobe and every event in your diary, Christmas parties included. A derby boot is laced up, a bit sturdier and just as happy with jeans. The chukka is your weekend trainer. And the chunky, rubber-soled ones? Just think of them as an umbrella for your feet.

Whatever you go for, my advice stays the same: keep it classic. Trend-led boots tend to look tired by the following winter, whereas a well-made, time-tested silhouette in full-grain leather will see you through years of wear. And if you want to know whether a pair is worth the money, flip it over. A stitched-on sole (look for “Goodyear welted”) means a solid structure, and, most importantly, that a cobbler can put a fresh sole on when the original wears out.

These are the 14 best you can buy now, from high-street stores to heritage footwear experts.

Barbour chukka boots

Barbour has spent more than a century dressing people for the outdoors, so it makes sense that its boots are just as tough as its jackets. I’d recommend these for anyone who wants a single pair that does everything. A boardroom meeting; drinks after work; a muddy trail walk: these boots can handle plenty of winter outings. Now all you need is the wax jacket.

M&S leather boots

Marks & Spencer menswear just keeps getting better. Just look at its London fashion week runway debut in September: Kit Butler walked the Design museum runway in a proper rain mac with stylish straight-leg jeans, while Lennon Gallagher’s grey suit and tonal knit would give Savile Row a run for its money. Not bad from the place you buy Colin the Caterpillar. These Autograph (M&S’s upmarket line) lace-ups are another example: they’re the kind of boots you’d expect on your well-dressed uncle, whether with jeans at the pub or chinos on Christmas Day. And they’ll only look even better a few winters in.

Schuh Dice boots

Schuh is hard to beat for high-street footwear, especially chelsea boots. These tick a lot of boxes: all the smartness of a chelsea, a rubber sole that can handle a slippy pavement, and real leather. If you’re shopping on a budget, the material is a corner you really shouldn’t cut. Synthetic uppers tend to crack and wear much faster than leather, and once they go, there’s no saving them.

Dr Martens 1460 Ambassador

Everyone knows the yellow stitching. It’s Dr Martens’ calling card, often spotted on the kind of guy who knows the bouncer at every gig in Camden. The OG is the 1460, an eight-eye boot that’s barely changed since the 60s and has been through everything from punk and ska to Britpop and grunge. The catch has always been the break-in period – but these bypass that, made from a tumbled leather that feels worn-in from the box. It’s probably best to keep some Compeed blister plasters on you anyway, just in case.

Brian boots

Good-quality, no-fuss footwear is Vagabond’s MO. It sells all the staples in shades of dark brown and black, with clean lines and zero (noticeable) logos. Suede is where the brand shines. These are the colour of a good espresso – and they’ll make a pair of indigo jeans and a chunky knit look like an outfit you’ve spent time thinking about. They’re also so light you’ll barely notice you’re wearing boots at all – just give them a spray of suede protector before you let them loose.

Grenson Richie

Yes, Grenson is on the more expensive side, but you really can’t fault the quality. It’s where almost all of my favourite leather shoes come from, and they’ve all lasted for years without needing repairs. These are my pick this season – an understated zip-up with a wide, flat toe that sits nicely under straight-leg jeans or work trousers. And because the sole is Goodyear welted (stitched rather than glued), when you do wear them down, you can send them back to Grenson’s Northamptonshire factory to be resoled for a fee.

Asos leather boots

If you like the look of the Grensons but not the price, Asos has an affordable alternative. These are the same sleek zip-up idea, and they’re real leather too. Unlike the Grensons, though, they’re not Goodyear welted, so it’s unlikely they’ll last you a lifetime. They may last a few seasons, but a pair you can properly resole is usually best in the long run.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Muck Boot Woodland Pro

Living in London, I don’t have much use for wellies. My dad, on the other hand, does. He lives in the Forest of Dean, so we’re talking two dog walks a day through muddy woodland, often in the rain. Since swapping his Hunters for Muck Boots, he hasn’t stopped going on about them: warm feet when it’s frosty, cushioning that makes them feel more like trainers, and an adjustable calf that allows space for trousers – basically, in his eyes, they can do no wrong. Hunter will always be the stylish choice, but for practicality, Muck Boots clearly take gold.

Blundstone x Finisterre lace-up boots

Blundstone has become something of a national treasure, despite its Australian roots: the original chelsea has gone from Tasmania to just about every festival field and school run across the UK. For something fresh, though, you could try the new collab with Cornish brand Finisterre. It’s a lace-up in dark brown waxed suede, well suited to brisk clifftop walks, as well as the lunch reservation that follows. Best of all, they feel far more stylish than most walking boots, so nobody will mistake you for someone who’s about to take on the Pennines.

Camper Dean

If you know Camper, you probably know it for its playful side – most of the collection looks like it could’ve wandered out of a cartoon. My favourite pair right now, though, is actually fairly normal – at least at first glance. It’s a suede chukka, just scaled up, with a structured upper, a rounder toe and a thick black sole that gives it some heft. So, if colour isn’t your thing, let shape do the heavy lifting.

NPS walnut brown calf

You might not know NPS from the name, but you’ll almost certainly be familiar with its history. The company has been making boots in Northamptonshire since 1881 – and, for 35 years, it made Dr Martens under licence. These days, though, it makes boots under its own labels, including the better-known Solovair (a portmanteau of sole of air). These derby boots are classics from the NPS Heritage line: they could take you from a book launch in Bloomsbury to a farm shop in Suffolk and dinner at a fancy restaurant without an outfit change. They’re Goodyear welted, too, so they can be resoled rather than replaced.

Clarks Walla Orkhon

The Wallabee has had more lives than most cats. It went from 60s counterculture to Wu-Tang Clan, who essentially wore them as a uniform, and it’s been a go-to for insider menswear nerds ever since. Purists might argue the OG is barely a boot, but this new winter-ready version settles the debate: it keeps the moccasin upper but now sits on a chunky sole, and swaps the delicate suede for a hardy leather. The cherry brown is a considered finish among a sea of chocolate and black.

Cos leather boots

Every man needs one pair of boots that can stand in for smart shoes at formal events. This is it: Cos’s slim chelsea with a flat, barely there sole that’s a sophisticated match for tailoring or smart trousers. Unlike most formal boots, which come on slippery leather soles, these have rubber underfoot, meaning you can leave the function with your dignity intact – no matter how many times you visit the free bar.

Timberland Premium 6-Inch

Few boots have a CV quite like Timberland’s six-inchers. They started out on building sites in the 70s – where they’re still very much a workwear staple – before being adopted by the hip-hop scene in the 90s (Biggie name-checked them so often that the brand eventually released a tribute pair). But you don’t need to wear them with baggy jeans in 2026: this burgundy version is a grown-up take that lends itself to anything from dark denim to black trousers. They’re also waterproof and insulated, so should see you through the wet and cold months of winter.

Obama portrait artist draws Burnham for Big Issue cover to highlight rough sleeping vow

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:00:15 GMT

Exclusive: Shepard Fairey says image will hold PM accountable over promise to get people off the streets

The “Hope” portrait of Barack Obama by the US street artist Shepard Fairey came to symbolise a historic 2008 presidential campaign, became one of the most ubiquitous and reproduced political portraits of modern times, and ended up in the Smithsonian.

Fairey’s latest work, of the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, may not elicit the same response but will, he hopes, deliver a hard-hitting message: one of a promise made.

The portrait, “Home”, captures Burnham in a red Big Issue tabard when, as Greater Manchester mayor, he sold copies with vendor Colin in 2023, and is the front cover of a new collectors’ edition of the magazine.

Designed exclusively for the Big Issue, it’s a reminder to the new prime minister of his pledge to tackle rough sleeping. From Monday, it will be sold on streets, and also be unveiled on the walls of the Saatchi Gallery in London as part of a six-month street culture exhibition, Beyond the Streets.

Fairey said: “The thread that runs through all my work is a push for justice. This portrait reminds us of the pledge Burnham made. Politicians often want people to forget to hold them accountable for the promises they’ve made. This is harder to do when a symbol of that promise is in thousands of people’s hands.”

The art work was created after the Big Issue approached Fairey, who said he was “overjoyed” that the portrait would be in the public sphere. “What I wanted to convey was simply warmth, and a reminder that he has actually been out on the streets promoting and selling the Big Issue, even before he was prime minister,” he said.

The magazine also carries an exclusive interview with Burnham. In it, the prime minister said: “I don’t think anyone should sleep rough in this country … I’m not going to be naive. I can offer people a route off the streets, but not everybody will take it.

“What I can say though is, I can ask every council as part of the funding we’ve given to provide an offer to everyone. And that’s what we’re confident of now …

“Big Issue knows better than anybody. You get a surge of sentiment around rough sleeping later in the year, for really good reasons, but when you hit the earlier months of the new year it falls away. What I’m saying is that public money won’t fall away. That’s the only way to do it. Stop-start is not fair to the organisations that are out there working with rough sleepers. This is a fixable problem and it’s about a national effort to fix it.”

Occupation Design director at a healthcare company

Voting record Campaigned for the Lib Dems, but is not eligible to vote in UK general elections

Amuse bouche Ilyan was nine when communism fell in his native Bulgaria. It was a gruesome time of rationing and hyperinflation, but it was also full of opportunity. He built Bulgaria’s first website, and its first advertising agency, in his early 20s

Occupation Works at a thinktank

Voting record Conservative and, recently, Reform. If Reform professionalise, for example by getting a shadow foreign secretary, he will consider voting for them again

Amuse bouche Daniel was president of his university Conservative association and lived with a communist as an undergrad. They spent all the time they were meant to be studying arguing about grammar schools

Daniel He was a lovely guy, very amicable. He’d cycled in.

Ilyan I was pleasantly surprised to see such an inquisitive young person.

Daniel I had the cod brandade ravioli with smoked eel, then we both had the guinea fowl. Dessert was a chocolate bombe with honeycomb mousse and ice-cream on top. It was all delicious.

Ilyan I had a fascinating thing with a crispy egg. The place was fantastic.

Daniel I think immigration policy in the 80s and 90s was quite sensible, and we should go back to that. Ilyan I come from a country where you couldn’t even move from a town to a city without a permit. I treasure the right to move, whether out of a village or from Bulgaria to London. You’re a happier person, you give more, and the world is better. But that didn’t work on Daniel. He went back to the topic of uncontrolled immigration; he was fixated with Tower Hamlets. I hold Britain as an example of good integration – I know in France they’re not as good, and in Germany they have these Turkish enclaves. I think in this country we do a pretty good job.

Daniel If you go to Tower Hamlets, there’s sectarianism there. It’s no longer diverse. Look, in my extended family, there are rightwing people who voted Reform, there are people who voted Labour, Lib Dem, possibly for the Greens. I don’t know anyone who’s decided to vote for independent Muslim candidates. I don’t have any shared opinions with them, there’s nothing that we have in common.

Ilyan I’ve had Muslim friends who opened a whole new world to me. I was telling him about a friend who took me to Tooting High Street, how it was like going to another country – an incredible experience. I thought that might be a way to challenge his perceptions – but they were all rooted in deeply personal, emotional experiences. He talked about how his wife used to live in a Bangladeshi area and didn’t feel as if she was in Britain. It’s very hard to move an argument so viscerally held.

Daniel I don’t think Brexit has done massive economic harm, the problem is we haven’t taken advantage of the economic benefits we could have had.

Ilyan He said Boris Johnson was a traitor to the cause – never a real Brexiter. Europe would have been great, according to Daniel, if it didn’t have the free movement of people. But the free movement of people is what makes the EU meaningful.

Daniel Assisted dying, I would call assisted suicide. It’s been a massive coup by Dignity in Dying to change the lexicon. If there isn’t proper hospice care around the country, surely that choice – either assisted suicide or a difficult death – is a scandal?

Ilyan He just came back to sanctity of life – and in my view, sanctity of life is being able to end it on your own terms. I cannot fathom putting a loved one through suffering and not being able to help them end it. Then we hit a wall; we were just restating our views.

Daniel We both agreed it was good to chat to someone who disagreed.

Ilyan It was futile, but it was a nice meal and we didn’t offend each other.

Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:00:13 GMT

Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn, announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social homes target of 60%. But this was leavened with another bit of old-time Labour religion: “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.”

The clock, however, is loudly ticking. John Healey’s underwhelming budget could only find an extra £1.5bn for social and “affordable” housing – which, apart from anything else, once again underlined the fact that the latter term is often all but meaningless. Thanks partly to a downturn in private housebuilding, Labour’s manifesto promise to oversee the building of 1.5m new homes of all kinds in this government’s first term is simply not going to happen. All this feels as if it symbolises how swaths of Burnham’s policy agenda still seem to be missing, fiscally strangled, or in a frustratingly early stage of development. But hope remains alive: the unveiling of his 10-year plan – which he insists will appear this year – could conceivably flesh out the kind of ambition we heard from him over the summer, as could next year’s spending review (note: I try hard to sound optimistic sometimes, and that is this week’s attempt).

At root, this is a story about people’s lives. It centres on depressed and anxious families living out of carrier bags and constantly moving from one friend or relative’s home to another, and thousands of children trying to lead relatively orderly lives amid the chaos of temporary accommodation. About 1.7 million children live in damp, mouldy, cold, or otherwise non-decent accommodation. Given that Alan Milburn’s report about young people and employment will apparently be published on Tuesday, we should also remember that the sheer impossibility of owning or even renting a secure home is a huge part of the reason why 16- to 24-year-olds feel so estranged and alienated from the everyday world of work, earning and somehow making a life. As Aneurin Bevan famously said, the language of priorities is the religion of socialism, and this one is self-evident.

So where are we? Since Labour took office it has made some good moves: introducing restrictions – with more to come – on the right to buy scheme whose various iterations have so depleted our housing stock, increasing rents to boost social housing revenues and, perhaps most significantly of all, returning at least part of the political conversation to such matters. The biggest step of all, though, is the SAHP, and the billions beginning to be spent on it.

That may sound impressive, but the first results of that programme are unlikely to even start to be seen until 2029 or so. Besides, the consensus among housing insiders is that on the optimistic reading, even if everything works out – which is dependent, among other things, on Labour winning another election – the result will be about 19,000 new social homes a year, totalling just under 200,000 in all. I am sure that everyone who works at the housing charity Shelter is now sick to death of reciting this statistical counterpoint, but they believe, quite rightly, that in order to meet the UK’s dire level of housing need, at least 90,000 new social homes need to be built each year between now and 2036, which is some indication of the gap between official policy and cold reality.

History, moreover, suggests that our ambitions should be even greater. I have spent the last week immersed in Michael Foot’s magisterial biography of Bevan, the postwar Labour government’s health and housing secretary. Before you read one of its more head-turning passages, imagine a distant world of Bakelite phones and bombsites: the kind of place we now would imagine moved chronically slowly. “At the Blackpool conference of the Conservative party in 1950, when the Labour housing programme was running at the rate of just over 200,000 houses a year,” Foot writes, “the floor forced on the platform a target of 300,000 houses a year.” Most of these would be council houses. Foot goes on: “Within two years, under Harold Macmillan’s direction at the Ministry of Housing, the figure was attained.” Those two sentences shame both our main parties.

I recently had long conversations with Martin Wicks, and Charlie Berry, respectively a leading light in the redoubtable Labour Campaign for Council Housing, and a policy manager at Shelter. Once you look under the bonnet of housing policy, they both explained, the mind boggles. For instance, thanks to an arcane agreement struck between Whitehall and local authorities back in 2012, councils now hold £31.8bn in unsustainable debt, the servicing of which inhibits the building and acquisition of new homes (as one London council leader told me earlier this year, “We have sites with planning permission, but we can’t build on them because of the state of our finances.”) Given that it represents a tranche of money owed by one part of the public sector to another, writing it off would be fiscally neutral. So why not just do it?

More such questions abound. Why is it that councils must take out 30-year maturity loans for housebuilding from the Public Works Loans Board at an interest rate of more than 6%, whereas the government has offered an interest rate of 0.1% to housing associations and “for profit registered providers”, claiming that it has refused the offer to councils “because of the fiscal implications”? Given that private housebuilding is in such a slump, does the government not therefore realise that now would be the perfect time to hire construction workers and acquire what the building industry calls stalled sites?

And one last one. If answering our housing crisis demands additional borrowing, could ministers not sell the idea to those infamous bond vigilantes through a simple enough pitch, reflective of the basic idea of investment? As a recent Shelter report put it: “the government must wholeheartedly recognise that large-scale social housebuilding is a safe investment and presents minimal market risk even in today’s climate … it improves public finances by supporting economic activity and generating substantial public sector savings and revenue.”
