‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 12:00:12 GMT

A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back

Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes.

“But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

Highsmith, who was born in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1921, had a hit with her 1950 debut, Strangers on a Train, boosted by Alfred Hitchcock’s film. A perfect second novel, lesbian road trip The Price of Salt (later republished as Carol), sold a million copies under the pseudonym Claire Morgan, and The Talented Mr Ripley (1955) was a critical success. But around the mid-1960s, Highsmith’s American luck ran out: her agent wrote that her books were “too subtle”, her characters too unlikable, to make it into paperback. By 1984 she was without an American publisher.

“She never found a home because she was so unpleasant,” Penzler says. “I don’t think anybody said, ‘Oh look, we’re losing money but I love her so much, let’s keep her.’” Not yet knowing this, he signed a six-book deal with Highsmith, creating a new imprint in the process. “Pat didn’t want to be identified as a mystery writer, so I started Penzler Books.” He knew Highsmith’s first editor, Joan Kahn. “When I told her I’d bought Pat, she said: ‘God, what’s wrong with you?’ Later we agreed she was a monster.”

In Anton Corbijn’s new film A Talent for Murder, adapted from Joanna Murray-Smith’s 2014 play, Switzerland, a dying Highsmith is played by Helen Mirren, who nails her physicality with dark contact lenses, a wig and a way of seeming to make her neck disappear. By 1995, when the film is set, Highsmith had lived alone for years, ending her last relationship with the translator Monique Buffet, then 27, when she was 66. Tortured by her sexuality, unrequited love and a poisonous mother, happiness largely eluded her.

The film’s premise is that a young American editor must persuade Highsmith to write one last Ripley novel: if she signs, his job is guaranteed and her uncertain legacy assured. It’s a fiction, of course, though lovingly built on real details, from the water glasses filled with cigarettes to her tank of pet snails and the Bond villain bunker she designed.

The image of the misanthrope has helped keep Highsmith’s legacy alive, with Ripley recently remade by Netflix, but has the knife-collecting sadist become a caricature? Did she deserve greater recognition in America? She hated publicity, which made life tricky for her champions. Penzler remembers that on one book tour, “my wife and I took her to our most beloved Italian restaurant. A young publicist, whose job it was to take Pat to all the interviews, came with two long-stemmed roses. My wife said, ‘Oh, what a sweet thing!’ Pat threw hers on the floor without making eye contact. You can’t imagine a person like this.”

After that, Penzler took on chaperoning duties. The interviews were brief and sometimes never published. “The one time Pat said something positive was when I asked if she’d like to stop for a drink. She said, ‘I would have a beer. I like beer.’” Highsmith’s Swiss editor, Anna von Planta, recalled a similar first encounter in 1984: “Pat greeted me coolly, disregarding my extended hand. She then ordered a beer and fell silent.”

By 1967, Highsmith had begun a lifelong relationship with the Swiss publisher Diogenes, who took control of her literary estate when she died – as well as 56 volumes of unpublished diaries, letters and stories, neatly filed at the back of her linen cupboard. Those diaries laid bare Highsmith’s antisemitism and racism. In her introduction to a published edition of them, in 2021, Von Planta writes that Highsmith’s views have been represented faithfully, even where offensive, but that “in a handful of more extreme instances [we did] feel it our editorial duty to deny Pat a stage for them, in the same way we did while she was still alive”. Did Penzler ever feel she crossed a line? “She hated so much, including women. If there was antisemitism in her stories, I probably missed it because it was mild compared to the other things.”

Even those who were repelled by Highsmith’s prejudices shared an appreciation of her work – its strangeness, precision, gift for character and its unfashionable darkness. The horror of the Tom Ripley novels lies not so much in their violence (though there is plenty of that), as in his increasing enjoyment of it. Does he mean to murder an art collector with a bottle of Margaux in Ripley Under Ground? “Tom simply could not answer that. And did it matter, much?”, she writes. That bleakness sold better in Europe: even a weak late novel, Found in the Street, sold 40,000 copies in Germany compared with 4,000 in America.

Gary Fisketjon was Highsmith’s next and final American editor, at Atlantic and then Knopf. He died suddenly of a stroke on 7 November, aged 72, but when I spoke to him a week earlier he had nothing but good memories of her. She was no pussycat but nor were his other authors — among them Jay McInerney, Donna Tartt and Cormac McCarthy. He still had regrets over a lunch that never quite came together with Highsmith, Bret Easton Ellis and Michel Houellebecq, which would have been quite the nihilist triumvirate: you can draw a direct line from Tom Ripley to Patrick Bateman.

“We never had a cross word,” Fisketjon said on the phone from Oregon. “I took Pat for dinner at the Odeon, which was very popular. Kind of a chic, downtown, artistic crowd and whatnot, and she was just captivated. She was studying everybody in the room.” In a 1984 diary entry, Highsmith wrote that “it will be interesting to see what good writers come from the cocaine takers”, and in the mid-80s literary scene she had her answer.

At the Frankfurt book fair, she and Fisketjon talked about their cats. “She was a superstar in Germany, and she was careful to instruct me on the best way to drink their beer, with the foam on top.” Fisketjon published Found in the Street (1987) and the final Ripley novel, Ripley Under Water (1991), giving notes in the same way he would for anyone else. “The ideal was, and this happened a few times with Pat – she’d say, ‘I see what you’re getting at, but here’s a better way of improving it.’” When Hollywood scouts took him for lunch, he told them to look at Highsmith’s backlist. “But the notion of getting in touch with a Swiss publisher to make a deal was unusual. She was an outlier, living abroad.”

Fisketjon had passed on her final novel, Small g: A Summer Idyll, feeling he “couldn’t publish it as fervently as Pat deserved. She took it better than I feared.” They stayed friends, trading letters and cat news. He had seen A Talent for Murder a couple of days earlier, and liked it, while finding the plot implausible. “Dame Mirren’s expressions reminded me vividly of Pat, even if her personality was a lot darker than I ever saw.”

Liz Calder looked after Highsmith at Bloomsbury in the late 1980s until the author’s death, and gets a mention in her diaries: a dinner in Hampstead in 1992, with her “parrot called Jon-Jon – maybe 38, light green”. “Actually it was Juju,” Calder says, “but they communicated quite well. I think she was more interested in the parrot than any of us.”

Now 88, she remembers Highsmith as “very, very unusual. She would comment a lot on things around her – ‘look, something’s happening over there’ – or on what I was wearing. She was almost unsocialised.” At the same time, she had close friends in London, France and Switzerland. “People who were nothing to do with her work. She loosened up with me over time but I never met them.”

Highsmith died of lung cancer and anaemia on 4 February 1995, aged 74. The American papers ran obituaries but there was no bump in sales. When editor Robert Weil approached Diogenes about publishing a couple of her books at WW Norton in 1998, they insisted he acquire all 14 that were then out of print in America, including Strangers on a Train. “I was new at Norton. They said, ‘This is folly, the sales don’t bear up.’ But I was persistent.” He agreed to Diogenes’s terms, eventually taking on her last unpublished novel, Small g, as well as the Ripleys, Carol and dozens of unpublished stories.

Now an executive editor at the Norton imprint Liveright, Weil speaks from a New York office lined with Highsmith box sets. Actor Alden Ehrenreich spent time here while researching A Talent for Murder (“he was a wonderful fly on the wall”) and Weil thinks there is still more to be done with Highsmith. Small g was “not her best work”, but a new collection of short stories got “thundering reviews” in 2001. By then, Anthony Minghella’s 1999 film adaptation of The Talented Mr Ripley had renewed interest in her writing.

“What she could do in 12 pages was amazing,” says Weil. “Highsmith can write these stories where you feel stabbed at the end – she knows how to finish something.” He reckons there are at least five potential screenplays in a 2002 collection, Nothing That Meets the Eye, which must include A Girl Like Phyl, about a man who meets his lost love’s daughter on a plane (“The girl looked at him, happened to lift her eyes straight toward him, and Jeff felt as if he had been shot”) and the title story, about a woman who bewitches every man in a ski resort before jumping from a mountain. Highsmith follows the body all the way down, to the “dark and final click” of death.

“There are a few happy stories,” Weil adds. “There’s an evocation of New York in the late 40s which is so precise and loving. But she had a gimlet eye for hypocrisy.” Exile gave her clarity. “She learned to skin and savage America. She never left it psychologically.” In her understanding of greed, she is like Edith Wharton, Weil says. “But in terms of psychological manipulation, there are very few like Highsmith. She was so far from the mainstream, and she should have been a debutante from Dallas.”

Highsmith was rude and sometimes bigoted. She also had a capacity for friendship, and for work that would have been impossible without empathy. Both things can be true, as her favourite creation Ripley attests – beneath the good man lies an evil one; beneath her cruel exterior lay someone capable of kindness.

In March 1995 Liz Calder caught a train to Highsmith’s memorial service at the Chiesa di Tegna in Switzerland, accompanied by her UK agent Tanja Howarth. They had both found Highsmith difficult. “But we wanted to go. And it was very strange – it was well attended but not by many publishing people. Tanja and I didn’t know anybody.” The Highsmith they knew was not the one her friends mourned. She was a mystery to the last.

A Talent for Murder is released in cinemas on 20 November.

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 11:51:53 GMT

Australia’s sandpaper soap opera has become one of alternative facts, but recollections of the second game in this one-day international series are unlikely to differ too greatly. For Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson, architects of an emphatic 135-run victory for England under lights on Sunday it was a match to remember.

Banton was sublime after England were asked to bat, unfurling a crisp 121 from 99 balls to underpin an imposing total of 355 for six. No touring side had gone bigger against Australia in their own back yard – the ideal platform for Harry Brook’s pace attack to release the handbrake and level the three‑match series.

Not that it felt a done deal at halfway, with the pitch true, the square boundaries short, and two dangerous openers in Mitch Marsh and Travis Head. England failed to defend 429 during their tri-series blowout against Sri Lanka in Pakistan, while Adil Rashid, middle overs maestro for the past 11 years, was once again ferrying drinks.

But up stepped Atkinson with a sizzling three-wicket new-ball burst that derailed Australia’s chase and a career‑best four for 28 followed. From their initial 29 for four, half‑centuries from Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw spared Australia’s blushes. That said, their 220 all out owed plenty to three dropped catches.

“I’ve watched a lot of cricket in Australia over the years – the Ashes and white-ball series – so to perform here today is a pretty special feeling,” Banton said, having earlier shared a run‑a‑ball stand of 137 with Joe Root to start the fightback after Perth. “To be able to stand at the other end and watch [Root] go about his business is pretty cool.”

The two teams travel to Hobart for a decider on Wednesday and the kind of scenario that Brook’s team have been craving a year before the World Cup. They are far from the finished product, clearly, but Banton’s second century since his recall in the summer sits among the positives.

Conditions were a world away from the bounce of Perth, while Mahli Beardman, the six-wicket star 48 hours earlier, was rested. After shaking off an early blow to the head from Spencer Johnson, and the loss of Ben Duckett, Banton enjoyed punching fours through cover and used the ground’s dimensions to propel four sixes.

Another plus was that England’s batting fired without Brook contributing and his dismissal, bowled for five trying to ramp Riley Meredith, will not have changed his reputation in this part of the world. Root had just departed for a fluent 62 to make it 156 for two in the 28th over, while Banton was motoring at the other end.

Even with fine leg up, it was a poor option, and after Banton holed out Brook was shown up by Jordan Cox and Will Jacks in a stand of 102 from just 70 balls. Cox had been happy to tick along at first, with his 49-ball 67 a case of blossoming when set. It also featured one absurd reverse-scooped four with both knees on the turf.

Jacks likewise built towards a climax with an unbeaten 54 from 40 balls, while Atkinson cracked a couple of late sixes. The latter was just getting started, it turned out, wiping out Head, Cooper Connolly and Josh Inglis cheaply in a seven-over spell and the recalled Sonny Baker striking at the other end.

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

As well as the stash of runs staring back down from the Adelaide Oval’s historic scoreboard, there was a bit more zip for both men under lights. They make for a contrasting new‑ball pair, too, with the quietly spoken Atkinson tight in on the stumps and the more outgoing Baker sending down fast, late outswing.

Baker’s removal of the in-form Marsh for two – one of two fine slip catches by Root –justified his ousting of Jamie Overton from the XI, as well as being preferred to Jofra Archer up top. Archer bowled well through the middle – it looks a good blend overall – even if he had to wait until the very end for his reward.

Renshaw and Green profited from early lives as England’s hands suddenly went from adhesive to Teflon, before the pair rebuilt with a 98‑run stand that briefly raised Australian hopes. These were doused by Liam Dawson trapping Renshaw lbw from around the wicket and the hosts subsided once more.

Most eye-catching among the second collapse of four for 46 was Sam Curran bowling the giant Jack Edwards with a truly glacial slower ball before inflicting a first-baller on Xavier Bartlett. By the time Dawson had Green stumped, a 31,000-strong crowd had largely evaporated and the win was sealed in near silence.

A day to forget for Australia, therefore. Albeit with Chadd Sayers giving a public account of events in South Africa eight years ago before play and slightly undermining that of Pat Cummins last week, it is unlikely to be.

Reclaiming Mary Cassatt: putting overlooked American artist back at heart of impressionism

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 11:29:58 GMT

New exhibition restores painter’s place as leading figure in French movement that revolutionised art

As a painter, friend, and collaborator of Edgar Degas, who exhibited with impressionist artists including Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, Mary Cassatt was at the heart of the 19th-century movement that emerged in France and revolutionised art.

She was also a woman and foreign – “American, American through and through” is how she described herself. As a result, in the 100 years since her death, Cassatt has been frequently overlooked in the country where she produced her best work.

An exhibition at Paris’s Musée d’Orsay, which comes to London early next year, aims to change that and place Cassatt back in her role as an active member and pillar of France’s impressionist group.

It features 80 paintings, pastels and prints covering her career, many from private European and US collections and previously unseen, along with unpublished private letters.

Caroline Corbeau-Parsons, an exhibition curator, said: “She was overlooked because she was a woman and a foreigner.”

She added that Cassatt’s choice of subjects – mostly women and children – means she was also stereotyped.

“We hope this exhibition will put Mary Cassatt back in her rightful place in the history of impressionism.”

Cassatt specialised in mother-and-child paintings, a genre in great demand in 19th-century Paris, and women, depicting their social and private lives, often severely constricted by conventions of the time. She was a lifelong advocate for women’s rights.

Sadly, the work of which she was most proud, Modern Woman, a commission to produce a monumental 4-metre by 18-metre mural to decorate the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago, has long disappeared. The Musée d’Orsay exhibition features a digital representation of the work.

Cassatt, born into a wealthy Pennsylvania banking family with French Huguenot roots, first visited France with her parents and siblings in 1854, when she was just 10 years old and fell in love with the country.

On her return to the US, she later enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and learned to paint. As a woman, there were restrictions in an era when painting was considered a social skill, not a career option. She was only allowed to paint reproductions based on statues and was forbidden from painting nudes.

Her father, Robert, was vehemently opposed to her becoming a painter and abhorred the bohemian lifestyle associated with the artistic world, but did not stop her moving to Paris in 1866, aged 21, with her mother and various female relatives as chaperones.

Unable to enter the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts, where women would not be admitted until 1897, Cassatt took private lessons with masters from the prestigious school and spent her days copying masterpieces in the Louvre museum.

Sign up to Art Weekly

Your weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitions

after newsletter promotion

She later sought out communities of artists outside the French capital whose atmosphere she described as “stifling and petty” and acquired a chateau in the Oise department north of Paris.

Cassatt met Degas at an exhibition held by rebel artists, who had rejected the formal strictures of the Beaux-Arts academy. Known as “the intransigents”, they included Claude Monet, Berthe Morisot, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Édouard Manet, Alfred Sisley and Camille Pissarro. Degas invited her to exhibit with the group, nicknamed impressionists by the press.

Degas and Cassatt subsequently collaborated on several works, including Cassatt’s Little Girl in a Blue Armchair, one of her best-known paintings. The relationship was fruitful for both. Cassatt introduced America to Degas and other impressionist artists.

While recognised during her lifetime, in the century after her death only one retrospective has been held in France, where she lived for 32 years. After her death in June 1926, several exhibitions were organised to commemorate her life and work. In France, she was largely forgotten.

Anne Robbins, who curated the exhibition, said Cassatt was overlooked in France because she was a foreign woman. As most of her paintings were sold to US collectors, with few remaining in France, she added.

“Although Mary Cassatt’s work is represented in the Musée d’Orsay collection, her presence there is significantly less prominent than that of her fellow impressionists, including Berthe Morisot and Marie Bracquemond, the two other ‘ladies of impressionism’, to use the words of art critic Gustave Geffroy in 1894.

“Furthermore, she was not part of the major French collections of her time, so her paintings were not included in the catalogues of national museums.”

The Musée d’Orsay’s exhibition will transfer to the National Portrait Gallery in London in January and then to the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.

Lucy Beaumont thought she’d never work in TV again after speaking up on David Walliams. Something different happened

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:00:11 GMT

Book sells out and tour tickets in demand after comedian reveals she contributed to Walliams investigation

When the comedian Lucy Beaumont revealed she had intervened to support a junior TV worker concerned about David Walliams’ behaviour, she feared it would brand her as a troublemaker and ensure she would never work in television again.

The immediate response to her actions, however, has been more heartening. Her book Drinking Custard: The Diary of a Confused Mum sold out online soon after she talked about her fears for her career. There was also a flurry of online posts from fans buying tickets to her current tour, with many posting messages of praise and support.

Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors, has been accused by multiple women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. He denies any wrongdoing.

Many TV insiders share Beaumont’s belief that there is still a professional price paid in the industry for speaking out against the behaviour of high-profile figures. However, Beaumont revealed she had spoken to the Guardian and ITV News in their three-year joint investigation.

Beaumont has explained that she was approached by a young TV worker, who alleged that he was asked to take young women to Walliams’ dressing room. Similar allegations emerged during the Guardian’s investigation. Beaumont did not witness any such behaviour herself.

Beaumont said that she was speaking out even though “I know everyone I know knows this, and I don’t hear anybody talking about it”.

“And honestly, I don’t think I’ll work in telly again, I honestly don’t,” she told Sky News this week, joking that she would become a pilates teacher instead.

Beaumont expressed her fears about the impact on her career despite having established herself in the comedy and television worlds. She has appeared on the biggest show on TV, the BBC’s Celebrity Traitors, as well as Taskmaster and Michael McIntyre’s The Wheel.

However, after talking about her involvement in highlighting concerning behaviour, Beaumont’s book sold out in paperback and hardback on Amazon, while a flurry of fans booked tickets for her shows, citing her decision to speak out.

Beaumont said in a Guardian article this week that she had been receiving thousands of messages in response to her intervention. “I’ve been flooded with support because people felt something,” she wrote. “They feel the same about these young women as I do and for a lot of women watching and reading, they’ve been in their shoes.”

She said she did not believe there was a widespread problem with harassment in the television world, but said she had spoken to journalists because there was “no HR department in TV”.

“The reason high-profile people aren’t saying anything is because they lose work, you’re seen as, you might be a trouble-causer,” she said. “I will slowly start getting less work, we’re all paid really well … no one wants to mess that up.”

Beaumont has said she used to work in schools and had been trained in safeguarding issues. “Whenever I’ve heard a rumour about anyone, I’ve done everything I can,” she said.

The comedian has previously raised concerns about the behaviour of some men on the comedy circuit. In 2023, she told a podcast that “predatory male behaviour” had held her back.

“I’ve had quite a few incidents where if you’re in any other workforce you would go to HR, but there isn’t one,” she said. “I think it’s just everywhere and it’s not talked about enough.”

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse and childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:00:10 GMT

The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date.

For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles.

There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts. The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside.

Today, Kolbe is sitting in front of me with Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and one of the three creative leads on GTA VI, showing me what the studio has spent more than a decade and, by independent estimates that Rockstar will not confirm, more than $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off.

After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde.

Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s. For some acts of this game you are locked into one character’s perspective, but most of the time you can switch freely between them. When they are apart, you can ensure they text and call each other. When they’re together, you can take them on little dates: to the gym, out to a bar, to a meditation retreat or to a liquor-store stick-up. You as the player become the steward of their relationship, and if you neglect it then there will be consequences. “You’re dropped into their lives,” Nelson explains, as Lucia speeds along a highway, Jason leaning out of the window to shoot at the tyres of the cop car pursuing them. “The relationship is yours to nurture or yours to lose. Whether it remains a romantic relationship is in your hands.”

This dynamic is not merely interesting – it is transformational for Grand Theft Auto. The series made its name on black humour and directionless violent mayhem, setting players free in virtual pastiches of New York, Miami or Los Angeles to crash stolen cars and terrorise pedestrians. GTA V in particular was an extravagant equal-opportunity offender, taking aim at everyone and everything from the US government to narcissistic tech bros, spoilt LA brats to hillbillies, the ultra-rich to caravan-dwelling wasters. Nobody has ever cared about anybody very much in a GTA game. Here, though, we are being asked not just to care about these characters, but to act out how they care for each other. When they are together, you can press a button to make them hold hands.

It is faintly unbelievable to see this game in action after it has existed for so long only as fervent rumour. GTA VI has been in development in some form since 2015, when the team took their first research trips to Miami (at this time, the game’s codename was Project Americas, reflecting a later abandoned ambition to set it across two continents). But it was only announced in December 2023, and has been delayed twice since. I get the impression that the people at Rockstar have basically been forced to put their metaphorical paintbrushes down. “They would never stop working on this game if they had the choice,” Kolbe says, somewhat ruefully. “It’s really hard to close it down,” Nelson admits. “If you step away and get a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: ‘I’m proud of what we’ve done’. But ultimately, it is being taken away from you, and you do the best you can to finish it in the time that you’re told.”

Usually when shown a video game ahead of release, one is taken through a highly choreographed slice of the action designed to show it at its best, but that’s not what’s happening here. We’re simply tooling about in a densely populated Vice City, and almost anything I suggest, we can do. Walking out from Jason and Lucia’s flamingo-wallpapered apartment into the Florida sunshine, the first thing we see is a woman walking a dog. I ask if we can pet it; Nelson presses a button and Jason says: “Is it cool if I pet your dog?” “Course, she loves to greet her public,” the woman replies, before Jason stoops to give the pup a fuss. You can overhear pedestrians’ conversations as you pass by, and interrupting them might result in a bemused “Have we met?” or a stream of invective. Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.

Of course we also do some crime. This is still Grand Theft Auto. But those who enjoy playing these games as a chaotic violent sociopath are in for a surprise here, because you have to be more careful than ever before. Jason and Lucia can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank; at the start they can only hotwire low-end vehicles and pick basic locks, working their way up to the higher-value jobs later. “These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall,” Nelson says. “Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.” Instead of whipping out an assault rifle in the middle of a crowded street and sending everyone scattering, you have to scope out your targets, whether it’s a gas station or an upscale mall boutique. You can disable security cameras or steal the footage, find back doors and safe codes so that you can get in without pulling a gun on anyone, and get out before witnesses arrive.

Fail to do these things and chaos ramps up quickly. After a couple of small-time crime sprees, we take Jason and Lucia to a well-protected jewellery store, where Lucia turns her pistol on the security guards for a few tense seconds before they surrender. Upstairs, though, where Jason is shoving money from the safe into a holdall, another guard decides to shoot rather than surrender. A desperate scramble ensues, in which Jason smacks the guy with the butt of a gun to knock him out while Lucia yells from the front of the store, and as they climb on to a stolen motorbike to make their getaway, the police arrive. The chase takes us halfway around the district, followed by cop cars and helicopters. When they eventually make it back to their car, Jason and Lucia stow the cash, change their clothes, and lie low in the outskirts of the city for a while to wait out the heat.

GTA VI is still very much a game about crime and criminals, but it strongly encourages you towards playing in-character and avoiding directionless rampages. In this way it is heavily inspired by Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018), in which you play an outlaw in the old west who comes to regret his life of violence. For Nelson, one of the greatest challenges of GTA VI’s development has been figuring out how to encourage players to behave differently without restricting their freedom, which would be antithetical to Rockstar’s creative philosophy. Even with an unlimited budget, you can’t solve the central tension of the form: the balance between the story that developers are trying to tell, and the random whims of any given player.

“Crime is a fundamental part of GTA – at least, up until now, it has been. We’re trying to make sure we’re not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out.” I ask whether this is the first GTA game that tries to encourage a measure of empathy. “I would say so,” Nelson replies. “I would say that it’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell. We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”

Grand Theft Auto has forever been a lightning rod for moral panic over video game violence. In GTA III, infamously, you could hire a sex worker and then run her over to steal your money back. In the 00s the discovery of an explicit sex minigame hidden in the code of GTA San Andreas prompted class action lawsuits in the US. Haitian-American groups attempted to halt the sale of 2002’s GTA Vice City, VI’s spiritual predecessor, over its depictions of violence against those groups. US courts have consistently upheld Rockstar’s first amendment rights, but this history hints at a cultural double standard. It is widely accepted that film and TV can depict violence without endorsing it – few would seriously venture that Breaking Bad endorses cooking meth – but when it comes to video games, where the player takes an active role, they are often seen to be lionising the behaviour they depict.

As video game graphics have got more realistic – it is hard to see, in retrospect, how the now comically low-resolution puppet characters of 00s GTA games provoked such outrage – Grand Theft Auto has sought to contextualise its violence. Its cinematic storytelling and character development ambitions have grown exponentially, as have its budget and team size, which has quadrupled since GTA V. The entire history of games is a story of talented technical and creative people finding ways to work around technological constraints and make things that were never possible before, working magic with blocky characters and limited graphical power. But now the limitations that defined the scope of previous GTA games are essentially gone. The leash is off.

“What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints,” Nelson says. “Like, how much can we physically build? You can keep going for ever … People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it’s no guarantee of making something good.”

It’s true that with all that time, effort and money, Rockstar has been able to achieve a level of detail in GTA VI that is beyond anything I’ve ever seen in a game – even beyond Red Dead Redemption 2, which was so extravagantly, naturalistically detailed that someone went to the trouble of modelling horse testicles that retract in cold weather. In a GTA VI gas station, Nelson takes evident pleasure in showing me detailed eating and drinking animations as Jason wanders around with a doughnut in one hand and a six-pack of beer in the other – the liquid inside the bottles sloshes realistically as he walks, and the racks are stocked with fully illustrated magazines that you can take off the shelf and read through. Every one of the pedestrians you see outside has been designed by someone, even down to their clothes.

Why go to this trouble? In the PlayStation 2 era, Rockstar was releasing a new GTA game every couple of years; they weren’t radically different from one another in terms of gameplay, but their shifting settings and characters allowed the series’ makers to stretch their creative muscles. By contrast, it’s now been 13 years and two console generations since the last GTA. Why spend all this time on a single, ostentatiously gigantic project? It comes down to this, Nelson says: if you were a developer with these resources, the only developer with these resources, wouldn’t you go for the most ambitious thing you could?

“They could have made GTA 5.5, and done it faster,” says Kolbe. “Ultimately, that’s not what they wanted.”

Nelson nods: “You have to take big swings. It can’t be just more of the same.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November.

Russell Brand accuser waives anonymity to call for consent law change

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 09:58:50 GMT

Mia Latter says she was in an abusive relationship with the convicted rapist when he was 30 and she was 16

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent.

Mia Latter says she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16.

Previously identified using the pseudonym “Alice”, Latter said in an interview with the Sunday Times that she had been inspired by Gisèle Pelicot to give up her lifelong right to anonymity. “It’s not my shame,” she said. “It’s not my burden to carry any more. It’s not me lying, and I didn’t commit any crimes.”

Latter is calling on the UK government to introduce a “staggered” consent law, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said that Latter’s “heartbreaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.

She told the Sunday Times: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.

“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”

Under UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with consenting 16- and 17-year-olds.

Latter told the paper: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about [Brand], it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.

“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

Latter, now 37, was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip. He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.

She said that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had told him her age.

Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship. Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.

Latter spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court.

Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sexual offence allegations against the comedian David Walliams were being looked at by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’ accusers was asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.

“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”

It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.

Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.

“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”

Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She said it was “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”

Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape was ongoing. A spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 08:00:08 GMT

In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem

In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.

The majority studying in the department were young women, and a few of us were of African descent. Some classmates and I raised concerns within the department at the time, but nothing was ever done: his “freedom” of speech was something we had to just accept. Years after we left Leeds, a group of us felt so strongly about what we had experienced – and the university’s failure in its duty of care – that we wrote a letter about it.

I have been transported back to those Leeds seminar rooms after reading of the decision of Oriel College at the University of Oxford to allow Dr Nathan Cofnas to speak at an event organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society, a student group that supports Reform UK. Much like Ellis, Cofnas has persistently espoused views associated with scientific racism.

A blogpost published by Cofnas while he worked at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, claimed that “in a meritocracy, Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%” and that Black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. Though Cofnas’s right to his views were upheld by a tribunal, it found that the blogpost “created a hostile, intimidating, unwelcoming and degrading environment for members of the college, particularly black students”. Cofnas’s claims against Prof Jason Arday also led to the professor facing intense media scrutiny in the runup to his death.

For me, this story is a painful and sobering reminder that little has changed when it comes to universities’ care for their students, particularly Black students. In a statement regarding the Cofnas event, Oriel College said that the institution is “committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive.”

Perhaps the argument that platforming racist ideas is merely a “freedom of expression” issue persists because of a disconnect with the real experience of Black students – and faculty – who have to navigate university campuses under such circumstances. Nearly three decades on, I can still remember preparing myself for tutorials with Ellis. Trying to defend my right to exist, to be in that space. And I wasn’t the only one. Rehearsing arguments, sharpening comebacks, compiling data. Anything I could do to try to push back at whatever derogatory comment he would slip into his lecture.

I was brought up to be conscious, proud of my heritage and culture. Maybe I landed a blow or two, but the upshot was that it was exhausting. It was never enough. I was never going to change his mind, but I was not mature enough to realise that. And it chip, chip, chipped away at me, my self-esteem, my emotional wellbeing. At a time when I should have felt liberated, encouraged – and, yes, challenged – to explore, interrogate, critically analyse, I was being pushed into a box. The message was clear: know your place, Ebony.

Advocates of free speech may think that what I endured was OK, and similarly that Black and global-majority students at Oxford must simply suck it up with regard to Cofnas. But as a young Black woman on the receiving end of anti-Black as well as misogynistic speech from a person who had power over me, it felt like abuse.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

And as for Oxford, while freedom of speech is indeed a fundamental human right, it also sits alongside an obligation, according to the UN, to “ensure the equal and non-discriminatory participation of all individuals in public life”. This means that universities must balance academic freedom with their duties under UK equality legislation.

It may be that Oriel College has considered both these obligations and done the necessary equality analysis, in which case it should share it transparently with students, academics and high-profile figures who have raised legitimate concerns. But otherwise, this just looks like yet another case of disregarding the safety of Black people who simply want to study, work and live their lives without their intelligence being questioned.

Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme

Britain’s veto could stop the UAE’s choice from running the United Nations. Miliband must use it

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:07 GMT

Lana Nusseibeh appears to have the support of Russia and the US, but her role glossing the horror in Sudan makes her unsuitable – and we should say so

Since the devastating war in Sudan began in 2023, some of the best investigative work uncovering those responsible has been carried out by the UN panel of experts. Its reports have revealed clear evidence that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been funnelling weapons and providing mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide.

It is these reports, produced by UN-funded investigators, that the UN secretary general, António Guterres, cites whenever he speaks about Sudan.

Every time a report has been published or leaked, one person has tended to take the lead in pushing back: Lana Nusseibeh. For more than a decade she has been one of the UAE’s top diplomats, spent almost 11 years as its representative to the UN and more recently as a Foreign Office minister. She has repeatedly denied the UAE’s involvement in fuelling the conflict and has publicly disputed the findings of the UN panel of experts.

But there is a high chance that in the coming weeks, Nusseibeh will replace Guterres and become the next UN secretary general. The representative of an authoritarian regime with a terrible human rights record that has been accused – by the UN, no less – of fuelling one of the world’s worst conflicts would become the voice of the dispossessed.

A few weeks ago, Nusseibeh was not even in the running. But for months the race to succeed Guterres has been in stasis as the declared candidates have struggled to win support from the major powers. The late entry allowed Nusseibeh to escape months of hustings and interviews around the world that would have placed her under more sustained scrutiny. It also ensured there was little time for her opponents to mobilise against her candidacy.

Choosing a new secretary general is a secretive business. There are hustings and the “vision statements”, but the decision is made behind closed doors and rests, ultimately, with the five permanent members of the security council: the US, Russia, China, France and the UK, also known as the P5. Only once all five have agreed can that name be passed on to the general assembly of all 193 nations, who will then vote to approve the P5’s choice.

In the most recent security council straw poll, Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice-president of Costa Rica and the secretary general of UN trade and development, had the most votes, but at least two P5 members appear to be opposed.

While all the major powers have been careful to avoid publicly indicating who they are backing, several UN watchers and diplomats I’ve spoken to believe Nusseibeh’s candidacy is backed by both the US and Russia, sparking fears that the election is being stitched up by those most opposed to the very idea of the UN.

The election comes at a bleak moment. Multilateralism is under attack, authoritarianism is on the rise, and the world is becoming more dangerous and volatile every day. One of the few consistent strains of Trumpism is the undermining of the UN, from the US’s withdrawal from numerous UN bodies to the creation of the rival Board of Peace. As I’ve written before, the US president would far prefer a world split into spheres of influence, where military and economic might counts for everything – and democracy and human rights for nothing.

A world of transactionalism suits the UAE too. For years it has used its oil wealth to build relationships across the world, whether that’s buying defence systems, building ports or investing in other nation’s cultural institutions. It is worth noting that it has major dealings with all five permanent members of the security council.

In the past month, France revived plans to jointly develop a new Rafale fighter jet with the UAE after the French president, Emmanuel Macron, met the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin ​Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi; meanwhile, a trade deal between UAE and Russia, which both sides hope will increase annual trade to $50bn a year by 2032, has come into force. One of Donald Trump’s first foreign visits in his second term was to the UAE, where he announced new deals between the two countries worth $200bn, while China is the UAE’s largest trading partner.

Then there is the UK. Its relations with the UAE have been described recently as “frosty”, but the coolness has been coming only from Abu Dhabi. UK officials appear keen to do what they can to keep the UAE sweet. Unlike the UN panel of experts, no UK foreign secretary has been willing to name the UAE as one of those fuelling the conflict in Sudan, let alone point the finger at Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE’s vice-president, who has been accused by activists of playing a leading role in the country’s support for the RSF.

Mansour, of course, is also the owner of Manchester City. In September, the Premier League’s independent commission found the club guilty of serious breaches of its financial rules. It is the biggest scandal in English football, bringing into question the validity of more than a decade of Premier League football. Put simply, a foreign power corrupted our national game. But much of the commentary in the weeks after the verdict has focused on how the UAE will react if the club faces a severe punishment. The UAE, it seems, is simply too powerful – or the UK simply too in need of its investment – to rock the boat.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

All of this has made civil society groups and NGOs fearful that the UK will not stand in the UAE’s way, smoothing the path to Nusseibeh becoming secretary general.

When Ed Miliband became foreign secretary in July, he made clear that he would “fight for … our values of democracy, freedom and the rule of law on the world stage”. His announcement of economic sanctions against Israeli settlers, plus his description of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as “unlawful”, showed these were not empty words.

But fighting for “democracy, freedom and the rule of law” is a continuous battle. If Miliband is serious about restoring international law and placing human rights at the heart of foreign policy, then he cannot go along with Trump and Vladimir Putin and give the UK’s backing to Nusseibeh. It may have an impact on relations with the UAE, but that’s no excuse. It may mean that no other candidate can be agreed upon, leaving the UN leaderless from January. That, too, is no excuse.

The UN simply cannot be run by a mouthpiece for an authoritarian regime. The UK has a veto – it needs to use it.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:06 GMT

Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.

“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”

As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised.

OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal. Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years.

Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies.

“The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable.

“I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added.

OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”.

The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not.

Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage.

During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet intelligence officers operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco as they carried out spying operations, according to former FBI special agent Rick Smith, who spent over two decades in the Bay Area working in counterintelligence. US officials estimated at the time that the Moscow Kremlin had mobilized thousands of spies in the country with the intent to steal intellectual property and help the Soviet Union copy American technology they could not produce themselves.

“Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985.

Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI.

In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms.

A report from the nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies found at least 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in the US between 2000 and 2022, with over half of the plots directed at the theft of commercial technologies. In January, a federal jury in California convicted a former Google engineer of stealing confidential company information to benefit the Chinese government.

Some operations linked to China have even involved honeypot-style schemes where a suspected spy has pursued personal or sexual relationships with politicians and executives. The Washington Post obtained declassified FBI documents in August that showed that former California congressman Eric Swalwell admitted to “occasionally hooking up” with suspected Chinese operative Christine Fang.

The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success.

Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China.

“As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.”

Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”.

The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported, despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed.

Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders.

In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security.

“Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.”

Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability.

Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers.

“They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.”

Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror.

Dealing with C-suite executives like Huang tends to pose its own unique challenges for security and threat assessment firms, experts said. Top leadership at companies possesses far more autonomy and authority than the average employee, making it harder for underlings to confront them about misconduct or potential risks. CEOs can also be hostile to seeing themselves as fallible, with consultants having to sensitively approach the idea that their personal relationships may not be what they seem.

“These are really smart, accomplished people and you don’t want to come across telling them that they don’t know how to behave themselves or that they’re not sophisticated enough to know that they’re being taken advantage of,” said Brian Stephens, president of security risk advisory at the CEO advisory firm Teneo.

Executives can also protest that they’re not important enough to be a target or that everything about them is already public.

“It’s a defense mechanism to being told that the way you live your life is going to have to change,” said Elizabeth Buckley, Teneo’s head of cyber and technical solutions.

In addition to educating staff on protecting themselves from being exploited, security and risk experts emphasized that companies need robust mechanisms to flag concerns about misconduct or outside threats. One question facing Nvidia is who within the company knew about Huang’s relationships and whether any concerns were raised internally. Several corporate intelligence and security experts said it is unfathomable that someone at Nvidia would not be tracking the CEO’s whereabouts and who he was meeting with, especially on trips abroad.

Yet for all the training, oversight and security protocols companies can put in place, experts said that no amount of safeguards can totally replace personal judgment. While looming investigations will seek to answer what went wrong at Nvidia to lead to the current disaster, Huang’s downfall was of his own making.

“Jensen Huang lost his mind here,” Smith, the former counterintelligence agent, said. “But that often happens with romantic relationships.”

At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now

The Guardian Sun, 15 Nov 2026 05:00:04 GMT

As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light

It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us. Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé. We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience.

A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may. My friends, it should be noted, felt the same. Thank God the heroic woman forced to endure Brand’s attack knew better.

After this week, much in my rear-view mirror looks different. For example, the brief relationship – although the word relationship is doing a lot of heavy lifting – I had with a 36-year-old man when I was 17. He was the DJ at the local high street nightclub that I was able to frequent, thanks to a terrible fake ID that was never closely inspected and a tangled web of lies to my parents about sleepovers at a friend’s. A group of us, all the same age, went to the nightclub as regularly as we could sneak out, as did a group of the DJ’s mates, all about 20 years our senior. We paired off and no one batted an eyelid. Boys of 17 were so childish: it was common knowledge that they matured more slowly than we did. It made sense that we were with older men.

Like most teenage girls, I was desperate to be treated as an adult, and the DJ obviously did that, with bells on. My association with him made me feel unbelievably cool, special and grownup, fully the sophisticated, worldly wise woman I had become, rather than the little girl my parents still saw me as. He had his own flat and a car, and he could come and go as he pleased. It seemed impossibly glamorous. I never for one second questioned what this man approaching 40 wanted with a kid, which is, much as I would have furiously denied it, what I was. Nor did I ever wonder why he wasn’t going out with women his own age, or what they sensed about him that I was blind to. I didn’t worry that what I was doing was dangerous, or ask myself if I was being exploited. Genuinely, until last week, it was just another tale in the folder marked idiotic teenage exploits. My friends were doing it too, it wasn’t unusual and no laws were being broken. It would have been illegal for the DJ to buy me an alcoholic drink in the club where we met, but there was no issue with him taking me home to spend the night with him after he played his last record.

Now, decades later, beyond belatedly, the person I’m most angry with is myself. Why didn’t I know better? It’s the same as when I heard from the Brand trial what women who were simply trying to get on with their jobs were subjected to, and it took me back to my time as a waitress. The male bosses would come up behind us waitresses when we had a stack of plates in each arm, and run their hands all over our bodies. None of the other teenage staff made a fuss about it, so I didn’t either. That was just what happened there. Oh, and to some degree, almost everywhere I’ve ever worked. I got used to dodging a grope, laughing off a suggestive remark, pretending not to understand advances from men with wives and kids at home, so as not to be seen as a troublemaker, difficult, someone uptight, who can’t take a bit of banter. Throughout all this, rather than doubt the men’s behaviour, the only actions I doubted were my own – what I’d worn, whether I’d given the wrong signals, or been too friendly. The misogyny is coming from inside the house.

I feel as if I’ve been blundering through life with my eyes closed. In light of the testimonies I’ve heard, the information I’ve taken in, so many intimate encounters are now reframed, blurry, uncertain. Blokes from my past who I thought were fine are rebranded – no pun intended – as dodgy and problematic. There were times when I felt bad or confused afterwards, thought that something wasn’t right, but I told myself I was being silly, oversensitive, weird. There were occasions when I ignored my intuition and my emotions and abandoned myself in favour of some man whose surname I probably no longer remember. It isn’t a case of not being brave enough to speak up: it’s much worse than that. It’s not even being aware there was anything to speak up about. I wish I could go back to the young woman I was then and apologise, for not taking better care of her, for letting her down so badly.

One way to reconcile how so many women’s histories have been altered in the wake of Brand and Walliams is to focus on hope, the positives. On what can change, now that some women, who are far more courageous than I am, have taught all of us how to know better.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer
