Five Great Reads: Sleep paralysis, parakeets and problematic laundry

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:21:43 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

If you’ve spent any time looking at the big headlines this week then you’ll know it’s high time for a good old break from the news. Take a breath, and bliss out with some long reads (mostly) a long way away from the doom cycle.

The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has spent his life studying the unfathomable depths of the human brain. His passion is sleep paralysis, “a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma”. While one in five people have experienced this frightening experience, very little is known about why the brain creates such terrifying images in the subconscious. Jalal has experienced sleep paralysis himself, and he thinks it may be a pathway to a deeper understanding of our minds.

What does it feel like? Some describe it as “the moment of peak fear in a horror movie”. Others describe being frozen in their own bodies while some evil force approaches them in their bed. It’s not uncommon for people to be able to open their eyes, which can often heighten the fear.

Around the world: Stories around sleep paralysis are more common in some countries and cultures than others. “Your grandmother might say: ‘There’s this monster that comes at night. It looks like this,’” Jalal says. In countries like Italy and Egypt, there is a long history of the phenomenon, which can cause it to happen more and for longer.

Notable quote: “When you are paralysed, and you can’t speak, your thoughts will go to a potential predator, somebody trying to hurt you. You feel very vulnerable.”

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: Do you like sleep? Try lazymaxxing.

Their existence is loud – and myths abound as to how these Himalayan birds came to be a common feature over London’s skies. Loved for its green plumage, the ring-necked parakeet has been making itself at home in Britain for decades. But more recently the birds have been recast as an ecological threat, prompting deeper questions about the idea of invasive species.

‘Invaders’: Evidence from Belgium and Spain suggests parakeets may outcompete several species, most significantly the Eurasian nuthatch, leading to local declines in areas with large parakeet populations

Opinions are split: They might be a nuisance to fruit farmers, or to nesting nuthatches. But to many Britons the birds are a welcome addition to otherwise grey cityscapes. “Everything is about diminishment and decline, but the parakeets are thriving, and they’re doing it in style. It’s a joyous thing to witness,” says Nick Hunt, the author of the 2019 “gonzo ornithology” work The Parakeeting of London.

How long will it take to read: You’ll have your beak in this story for nine minutes.

Further reading: This volunteer army is plotting to wipe out Britain’s grey squirrels.

For the past few weeks, fridges and freezers across Europe have been encountering the same problem. Temperatures inside the ice boxes have shot up, some reaching as high as 50C. Alex Pearce, who owns a fruit and vegetable business in London, discovered the malfunction was a cyber-attack when he walked over to the cable connecting the units to the internet and pulled the plug. As the rise of AI makes it easier to hack IT systems, experts say cyber-attacks could become more common.

Notable quote: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.” – Richard Horne, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), says we are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape.

Not just fridges: Blood banks in France, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, even Ukraine’s emergency alert app. And by 2028 the NCSC predicts AI-powered malicious software will “highly likely” be used to hack UK power stations, airports and hospitals.

How long will it take to read: About four minutes.

Further reading: The fridge hacks provided fairly little disruption, but what would raise the stakes?

after newsletter promotion

Bluey, the Australian series about a six-year-old dog and her sister Bandit (and, of course, their ridiculously unflappable and time-rich parents), has become a worldwide hit. Now one of the founders of the studio behind it is making headlines of his own.

Packed with nostalgia: Daley Pearson, co-founder of the Brisbane production company Ludo Studio, has created a new Netflix family film called Allen, which by his own account is topped to the brim with his own childhood nostalgia, including the things that feel impossible to let go. It centres on a character called Petey who befriends, for one blissful month, a bug-eyed extraterrestrial – Allen. But decades later, Petey is trapped in a state of arrested development and obsession.

Notable quote: “I was using the stuff that I love to tell the story of not being able to let go of the stuff you love, and how it maybe holds you back,” Pearson says.

How long will it take to read: Just over two nostalgia-filled minutes.

Further reading: The Bluey composer shares the trick to music that “hits you in the feels”.

The news cycle can be depressing at times, but that doesn’t mean your wash cycle has to be. Could there be hope for your washing in an online rabbit hole? Victoria Turk tumbled down the r/laundry subreddit in search for answers to 10 stubborn laundry problems.

Sud-based science: We’ve all been there. A coffee stain on a white shirt. Pasta sauce on a new pair of pants. Try as we might, wash after wash, stain remover, baking soda – nothing works. Eric Thompson, better known by his online avatar KismaiAesthetics, preaches a science-based approach to cleaning clothes. TikTok trends and Instagram hacks are out. Green chemistry and “the magic of water and time” are in.

Take a spa day: Thompson’s answer to persistent stains and lingering odours sounds relaxing. Famous online for its efficacy, his “last-ditch effort” to save an essential wardrobe item is described as a “spa day”. The power comes from heat, time and the enzymes in bio-powered detergent (click through for detailed instructions).

How long will it take to read: Six minutes. You can read it while folding your laundry.

Further reading: Are you doing your washing all wrong?

Flora Willson

Louise Giovanelli White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, 20 November to 16 January One of the UK’s most exciting young painters returns with new works dealing with her favourite themes: curtains, hair, female screen idols and the cinematic kiss. It’s dramatic, dreamy, ultra-theatrical and quasi-religious art.

David Nash The Burton at Bideford, 14 November to 17 January He is best known for shaping living trees into immersive sculptural installations, but this Devon show looks at how drawing has always been central to shaping David Nash’s approach to depicting and working with the natural world.

Ryan Gander Towner Gallery, Eastbourne, 14 November to 11 April For his first UK institutional show in almost 20 years, playful conceptualist Ryan Gander turns up the humour dial with a series of installations featuring animatronic mice, repurposed toys and paintings of balloons.

Angela Harding Yorkshire Sculpture Park, near Wakefield, 14 November to 28 February Linocuts, oil paintings and decorated wooden birds by this hugely respected illustrator, returning to Yorkshire Sculpture Park 10 years after her last show with more nature-loving ecological imagery. Eddy Frankel

Rosie Holt Maidenhead, 14 November; Birmingham, 19 November; touring to 5 March Holt and her MP alter ego (originally Tory, now Labour) return to poke fun at the political classes in a madcap current affairs pastiche underpinned by a more heartfelt meditation on the sexism faced by women in the public eye. Rachel Aroesti

Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella Plymouth Theatre Royal, 16 to 21 November; touring to 8 May A revival of Bourne’s Cinderella, which turns the fairytale into a wartime romance set in London during the blitz. Dancing with the drama of Prokofiev’s fantastic score, it’s a love story that also nods to the darkness of real events. Lyndsey Winship

Nine Night Kiln theatre, London, to 2 January Amit Sharma revives Natasha Gordon’s sparkling hit, about a Jamaican family gathering in their suburban London home for the traditional nine nights of grieving after the death of beloved matriarch Gloria. Miriam Gillinson

Cranford Orange Tree theatre, London, to 16 January The Orange Tree has a reputation for brilliant festive shows that feel both cosy and contemporary. This year, Josh Roche stages Elizabeth Gaskell’s sumptuous novel, with Tamsin Grieg as the intriguing woman at the centre of 1840s Cranford. MG

Bill’s Included BBC One & iPlayer, 20 November, 9.30pm The predicaments of landlords don’t usually tug at the heartstrings, but an exception may well be made for Rob Brydon’s Bill, a lonely divorcee who tries to befriend the students he rents his spare rooms to in this cross-generational houseshare sitcom from comedy duo the Pin.

Honey BBC One & iPlayer, 14 November, 9pm Early 1980s East Berlin is the irresistibly retro setting for this zany and stylish new cold war spy thriller from Emma Moran (Extraordinary), in which a rookie MI6 agent joins forces with a CIA operative to take down a Stasi officer. When a Witness Recants HBO Max, 18 November Made in collaboration with Ta-Nehisi Coates, this devastating documentary by Dawn Porter hears from the three Baltimore men who served 36 years in prison for a murder they didn’t commit – as well as the schoolboy who was forced to provide false testimony against them. RA

Grand Theft Auto VI PS5/Xbox; out 19 November Well, it’s the big one. Thirteen years of memes in the making, Rockstar Games’s Florida-inspired crime opus is upon us. Only a game this vast could ever hope to live up to the hype.

Spirit Crossing PC, Switch, Switch 2; out now In a world above the clouds, players work together to make a home, coming together to build towns, protect them (and each other) from storms, and help guide lost spirits. A welcoming, optimistic hangout of a game. Keza MacDonald

U2 – Carnaval de Luz Out now On their first album of new material in nine years, U2 sound more invigorated than they have since popping music on people’s phones without permission back in 2014. Ragged single Silencio rattles along like a much younger band, while Street of Dreams is classic widescreen Bono.

Snoh Aalegra – Legendary Love Out now Sweden-born, LA-based Snoh Aalegra drapes her silk-soft voice over 13 new songs, headlined by beautiful lead single I Love You. Full of vintage Prince-isms in the production and a luxurious chorus, it’s very nearly matched in quality by the slowburn ballad Just Friends.

Royal Blood – Dead Company Out now Worthing rockers Royal Blood, AKA Mike Kerr and Ben Thatcher, return after a short hiatus with this fifth album. Mixed by Alan Moulder (Depeche Mode, Foo Fighters), songs such as the blistering title track and Swallow the Bomb’s sweary chorus seem ripe for next summer’s festivals.

Say Now – Say What You See Out now Since launching as Needanamebro in 2022, UK girlband Say Nowhave been searching for a sound, flitting between 90s R&B (Brick By Brick) and Raye-penned breakup anthems (Supermarket). On this six-track EP – executive produced by PinkPantheress – the trio comfortably ride a suite of punchy dance-pop bops. MC

This Is Our Story With Seth Pinnock Podcast London-based youth charity Symphony Co’s new audio series hosted by founder Seth Pinnock gets into the deep questions of purpose and creativity with celebrity guests, including the actor Billy Porter.

Antony Cooke Substack Home chef Antony Cooke’s newsletters are full of recipes that blend readily available ingredients with a touch of restaurant glamour. Follow along to make everything from a Mexican-inspired squash soup to a showstopping fish pie.

Kazakhstan’s Chess Gambit BBC World Service, 19 November, 9.32am Keen to develop their homegrown chess talent, the Kazakh government introduced state-led initiatives to encourage young people to take up the game. Journalist Zoe Strimpel investigates how chess has since become central to Kazakhstan’s nation building. Ammar Kalia

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:42:46 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Old Trafford and Selhurst Park watchers aside, the break from Premier League events – on the pitch at least – heralds a day of lively international activity. Emillia Hawkins arises bright and early with all the Nations League buildup as Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland bound into view later. There may well be follow-up from Scotland’s Friday night date with North Macedonia and anticipation for England’s clash with Spain on Sunday. Plus, a host of EFL and WSL fixtures will keep the updates flowing. Join the conversation at matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Greg Wood saddles up for a cracking ‘Super Saturday’ in the autumn’s best meeting, with the Paddy Power Gold Cup Handicap Chase front and centre and Ben Pauling’s Meetmebythesea hard to ignore. Elsewhere, Old Park Star could make a winning start over fences in the Arkle Challenge Trophy Trial Novice Chase.

Simon Burnton helms the blog as the WSL’s two unbeaten sides go head to head at lunchtime. Andrée Jeglertz’s City hold top spot after drubbing West Ham 5-0 while Chelsea were held by Everton last weekend. With two points separating the pacesetters, this is a crucial match for Chelsea – lose and their title hopes will become worryingly untethered even at this stage of the season. Suzanne Wrack reports.

England welcome their former head coach Eddie Jones’s Japan to Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, after delivering their standout performance of an otherwise poor 2026 by overrunning Australia 45-22 in the autumn opener last weekend. Ranked 12th in the world, Japan are not expected to cause Steve Borthwick’s rejigged XV to stumble before the main event of the Nations Championship pool fixtures against New Zealand. This match is of particular significance for Will Joseph, Max Ojomoh and Cadan Murley, who have been told the second of this month’s four Tests is a World Cup audition. Borthwick already knows the bulk of the squad he will pick for Australia 2027, leaving around five spots up for grabs. These fringe places are the hardest to pick and with Japan offering a rare chance for Test rookies to catch Borthwick’s attention, a strong individual display could tip the scales in their favour. Alex Reid hosts the blog, with Robert Kitson and Gerard Meagher reporting.

Scott Murray bids a hearty noswaith dda as Wales attempt to block Erling Haaland and company for the second time in six weeks. Craig Bellamy’s side stunned the World Cup quarter-finalists at the start of October with a shock 2-1 win in Cardiff. They meet again in Oslo, with the bottom two sides in Group A4 aiming to ward off the threat of relegation to League B. Haaland – the Nations League’s all-time top scorer with 22 goals – drew a rare blank at Cardiff City Stadium. On home turf and temperatures around zero degrees centigrade, Wales must hope the Manchester City striker is frozen out once more.

So much for the machinations of Sandpapergate, England were duly humbled in the first ODI against their old foes, crashing to a seven-wicket defeat in Perth on Friday morning. They were bowled out for 131 in 33.4 overs ⁠after losing the toss, ⁠and the hosts ​reached 132 for three in 23.3 overs courtesy of a quickfire 50 by captain Mitch Marsh, with a stunning six for 24 from Mahli Beardman on debut stealing the show. Tim de Lisle logs on with over-by-over commentary of the second ODI as the three-match series moves to Adelaide and concludes in Hobart on Wednesday. Ali Martin reports.

Australia and New Zealand opened the Rugby League World Cup with a humdinger of a contest four weeks ago and hopes are high for another blockbuster when they face off again with ⁠the title on the line in Brisbane. The Kangaroos fullback Reece Walsh ​and his Kiwis counterpart Kalyn Ponga were the stars of the show last month in Sydney, and their pace, footwork and handling should again be vital for their teams in the Lang Park showcase. Australia and New Zealand also meet in the women’s World Cup final earlier on Sunday at the same stadium, where the Jillaroos will be gunning for a fourth straight title against the Kiwi Ferns, who won the first three editions. Join us for live coverage of both finals.

Xaymaca Awoyungbo has breaking news and buildup at the helm of our unbeatable football live blog. He’ll be looking ahead to Spain v England: La Roja have a 100% record in Group A3 but Thomas Tuchel’s side head into Sunday evening’s Madrid meeting with a chance of toppling them after securing a 2-1 victory against Croatia at Wembley. With Italy travelling to Belgium and France facing Turkey elsewhere, there’s plenty on his radar, notwithstanding three cracking WSL fixtures.

Turin hosts the world’s best eight men’s players, with the world No 1 Alexander Zverev getting the tournament under way on Sunday. He faces Spain’s Rafael Jódar, the first man to reach the ATP Finals in the same season he made his full ATP Tour debut. The German took top spot in the men’s rankings earlier this month after winning Roland Garros and the US Open – his first grand slam titles – and he is gunning for a third finals triumph. He is expected to win the four-man John McEnroe Group, while seven-time grand-slam winner Carlos Alcaraz heads up the Ivan Lendl Group after winning the Paris Masters. Tom Bassam live blogs the opener, and we’ll be back later to cover the evening’s matches.

Graham Searles tunes in to events unfurling in Munich, Bavaria, as the New England Patriots face the Detroit Lions. Sunday’s game will be the sixth regular-season match-up in Germany, a key market for the NFL in its aggressive international push. The Patriots (5-4) have lost two of their past three games and have many injury concerns, including running back Rhamondre Stevenson. Meanwhile, the Lions, despite a 6-2 record and four straight victories, are trying to keep pace in the tight NFC North. He’ll then move on to the seven 6pm fixtures.

While the Wallabies try to fix their porous defence, their hosts are trying to shore up their own rearguard as Murrayfield prepares for two sides in dire need of uplift. The problems faced by Les Kiss’s leaky mob were highlighted in the 45-22 thrashing at Twickenham by England. Australia, once the scourge of northern hemisphere sides, have now conceded 176 points in their past four Tests, the most ever over any equivalent quartet of matches in the Wallabies’ annals. Yet the same urgent repair job is being undertaken in the Scotland camp after Gregor Townsend’s side shipped 43 points to the All Blacks at their Edinburgh fortress last weekend. Daniel Gallan dons his scrum cap for live blog coverage.

Draw specialists Arsenal step up their hunt for a European berth after last weekend’s vital defeat of Liverpool and spirits lifted further by a creditable 1-1 draw in Barcelona in midweek. By contrast, Eder Maestre’s side are unbeaten in their past three away league matches, scoring 12 goals along the way. John Brewin is our MBM blog host, with Tom Garry reporting from the Emirates.

England wind up 2026 with the chance to top their Nations League group in Sunday’s collision with world champions Spain. Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions were minutes away from securing a place in the World Cup final against Spain, who ran out 3-2 victors when they eventually did meet in September’s Nations League opener at Wembley. England will attempt to win the group, having secured their place in March’s Nations League quarter-finals with last month’s results. Harry Kane’s spot-kick settled things against Croatia on Thursday evening at Wembley after Petar Sucic cancelled out Morgan Rogers’ opener on a night when the England skipper became the most capped Englishman in history. Daniel Harris buckles up for the blog, with David Hytner and Sid Lowe reporting from Madrid.

Saudi-Backed Forces in Yemen Retreat From Red Sea as Houthis Advance

The New York Times November 15, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The move is a setback for the Yemeni government and its ally Saudi Arabia, as analysts said the balance of power in the country’s civil war was tilting toward the Iran-backed Houthi militia.

By Vivian Nereim

Reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.

A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.

Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.

The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.

“The Houthis are very determined to go to Aden,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “They don’t want to see any area controlled by the government or the Saudi side, so they want to take over everything at this moment.”

The move was a public acknowledgment that, after more than a month of fighting, the Yemeni government and its Saudi allies have failed to regain control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical waterway for global shipping at the southern end of the Red Sea.

The Houthis seized land beside the strait in a lightning advance in September, allowing Iran and its allies to menace shipping passing through maritime choke points on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

The Southern Armed Forces said that their redeployment would also allow them to focus on breaking a Houthi siege of Taiz, a major Yemeni city that has been surrounded by the militia for more than a month, restricting vital supplies of food, fuel and water.

Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis swept into Sanaa and routed the government. The following year, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates launched a disastrous military intervention to try to restore the government. Their bombing campaign helped plunge Yemen into a brutal conflict that has led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease.

A truce in 2022 halted the fighting, but the two sides never reached a sustainable peace deal. The Houthis were left in control of much of northern Yemen, where they have set up a de facto administration.

The internationally recognized government of Yemen holds nominal power over the country’s southern and eastern provinces, which are effectively controlled by a patchwork of armed groups.

The conflict reignited in July, as tensions rose across the region during the U. S.-Israel war with Iran, the Houthis’ primary backer.

In September, the Houthis staged a rapid offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking control of the strategically-located port city of Mokha as well as the strip of land beside the Bab al-Mandab. In October, they advanced toward Taiz.

Soon after, the Yemeni government said its forces were mounting a new campaign to retake all of Yemen from the Houthis, backed by Saudi warplanes. That began with a counter offensive toward the Red Sea but the gains have been limited and fleeting.

At the same time, the Houthis have carried out a series of deadly and damaging attacks in Saudi Arabia, striking the international airport in the capital of Riyadh and a tower belonging to the state oil company.

A spokesman for the Yemeni government military, Colonel Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili, said in a statement on Sunday that the government’s operation to retake the country from the Houthis would continue. He also called on world powers to aid the Yemeni government.

“The international community must assume its responsibilities by contributing to the liberation operation, given the strait’s vital importance to maritime security and international trade,” he added.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, and Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025

The New York Times November 15, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

The Singaporean company’s statement added to the timeline involving Ms. Huang, a former executive who had a relationship with Jensen Huang of Nvidia. U. S. officials say she was spying for China.

By Ali Watkins

Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center company, said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang, a former executive at the center of what U. S. officials call a Chinese spy plot targeting the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, had left the company in August 2025.

The statement, which was reported by The Associated Press, was Megaspeed’s first to directly address the status of Ms. Huang since she became the focus of international scrutiny over her ties to Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday.

News of their relationship rocked Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, as well as the global technology sector and the U. S. government.

Last month, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had a close relationship with Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A. I. boom and an adviser to President Trump.

Mr. Huang acknowledged last Sunday that he’d had an affair with Ms. Huang, and Nvidia’s board of directors said they had begun an investigation into his conduct. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that he also had an extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. He abruptly stepped down as chief executive the next day from the company he had led for more than 30 years.

The chip maker’s stock has fallen about 30 percent below its all-time high, which was set just over a month ago, erasing more than $1 trillion in market value.

The scandal has trained attention on Megaspeed, a small company that purchased billions of dollars of Nvidia’s coveted chips from 2024 to 2026.

That set off an investigation by the U. S. Department of Commerce as to whether some of the chips were funneled to China, in possible violation of American export restrictions. The United States has not lodged any formal charges against the company.

On Thursday, Megaspeed’s chief executive, James Tan, said in a statement that the company had not broken U. S. laws, had cooperated with Commerce Department investigators and was “ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U. S. government authority.”

Megaspeed’s statement on Sunday reiterated that its business was “legitimate and lawful” and for the first time mentioned Ms. Huang, who helped set up the company starting in 2023, saying she had no current role there.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters,” it told The A. P. in an emailed statement.

The company’s timeline involving Ms. Huang could not be independently verified. Its statement on Sunday came after more than a year of scrutiny by the authorities in the United States and Singapore.

“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” Megaspeed added.

Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment. China has denied the espionage claims.

The Times reported in October 2025 that Ms. Huang had stepped down from the company months earlier, citing a human resources manager, though it was unclear where she went.

Last week, the government of Singapore said it had confiscated Ms. Huang’s passport from June 2025 to February 2026 over “potential false declarations” about Megaspeed. She was ultimately released and barred from re-entering Singapore.

U. S. officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, had informed Mr. Trump of concerns about Ms. Huang and her relationship with Mr. Huang as early as October 2025.

Mr. Trump declined to take action. This May, Mr. Trump brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China, another sign of Mr. Huang’s importance to the A. I. data center boom that is a key driver of the American economy.

The scandal has touched off a new round infighting in the Trump administration over its approach to A. I. and China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a prominent voice in favor of allowing U. S. companies like Nvidia to sell products in Asia, has faced accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that his department has been too cozy with Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, said on Friday that his department and others had supported putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but that only the Commerce Department could take that step. The Commerce Department said that such a move would be an administration-wide decision.

Mr. Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look externally for a new chief executive. On “Sunday Morning Futures” on Fox News, he said that the company needs “a dramatic shake-up.”

He added that the company’s board and outside counsel within the next 10 days needed to answer questions ​about the company’s culture of compliance with export ⁠restrictions.

Adeel Hassan contributed reporting.

Ali Watkins covers international news for The Times and is based in Belfast.

She hated Epstein, but she was accustomed to pushing through pain. As long as her mother was sick, she would endure. Then, one day at the studio, wearing her leotard and tights, Danielle found she could not move her body. Her joy for ballet was gone. All she could do was cry.

Her mother had a successful surgery to remove the tumor in May 2005, and once she recovered, Danielle finally stopped answering Groff’s calls. She got a job as a door girl at a nightclub, sleeping on couches, gluing extensions into her hair, running around in Victoria’s Secret lingerie, drinking excessively to escape thinking about Epstein and what he had done to her.

Marina was 17 when Epstein told her she was “boring” and “too old” for him. He said it in a joking way, but she got the hint. She didn’t need him so much anymore, anyway. She had just married and begun working as a dancer at a strip club in New Jersey, an hour and a half commute from Astoria. She was one of their top girls. Her name was Sky. She got a better gig in Manhattan at New York Dolls, then FlashDancers, then Private Eyes, then at Rick’s Cabaret. She liked Rick’s Cabaret. She thought it was classy. You had to wear a gown.

In 2008, when Marina was 19, the F. B. I. showed up at her door asking about Jeffrey Epstein. Marina didn’t know that Epstein had been under investigation in Florida since 2005. More than 30 girls had already been interviewed by the Palm Beach police, who sought charges for unlawful sexual activity with minors, but a grand jury indicted Epstein on just a single count of soliciting a prostitute. Investigators in Palm Beach who suspected Epstein was getting special treatment referred the case to the F. B. I., setting off another wave of interviews with victims.

Marina was in the process of getting her green card and was worried about being deported. “I was petrified,” she told me. She asked the agents to leave and immediately got on the phone with Epstein. He told her not to call him. He would have a lawyer call her. He hung up.

Marina talked to a lawyer Epstein hired for the case, Brendan White. “What about the girl that brought me?” she remembers asking. “What about the girls I brought, and the girls they brought? How am I the only one getting in trouble for this?”

“They found you,” she recalls him saying. “That’s it.”

Marina agreed to be interviewed by Florida investigators and spent months preparing with White. Then one day, she says, he told her she had nothing to worry about. Go home and forget about this, he said. (White said that he never interacted directly with Epstein and acted in Marina’s best interest as his client. He acknowledged these conversations took place but does not recall what was said.)

Like most victims, Marina wasn’t getting the full story. Federal prosecutors had drawn up a 53-page indictment against Epstein, but in a deal that was later ruled to have violated the Crime Victims’ Rights Act, the U. S. attorney’s office agreed to give him immunity from federal crimes if he pleaded guilty to lesser state charges. The investigation was called off, the indictment shelved. Epstein was sentenced to 13 months at the county jail in Palm Beach.

The F. B. I. found Marina for the second time in 2019. She was still working at Rick’s Cabaret, having divorced, remarried and given birth to a daughter. They told her that Epstein had been arrested again. Ghislaine Maxwell, a former romantic partner of Epstein’s who helped him traffic and abuse underage girls, had also been arrested. The U. S. attorney for the Southern District of New York was building a new case, and the F. B. I. was searching for witnesses.

Marina reluctantly told the F. B. I. about Lisa, Lindsay and some of the other girls. Then she had to call her friends to let them know the F. B. I. was coming. They were furious, cursing at her, all asking, Why would you do that? They weren’t thinking about justice for themselves. They were thinking, Am I going to get in trouble?

Some of the women remembered what happened to a woman in Florida named Haley Robson. Robson was 16 when another girl brought her to Epstein. When she resisted his advances, he threatened and harassed her. Robson felt she had to choose between bringing girls and being sexually abused by Epstein. She introduced him to around 20 girls, some as young as 14. In 2005, during the Palm Beach investigation, the police sought charges against her, even after she agreed to cooperate. In May 2006, the police requested an arrest warrant for Robson for “lewd and lascivious acts on a victim under 16 years of age.” Her name was distributed to the press as a co-conspirator, leading to death threats that are still coming in today. In 2008, one of the girls she brought to Epstein filed a lawsuit against her for “intentional infliction of emotional distress.”

Robson’s experience showed the other victims how easy it would be for them to be treated as a perpetrator. Politicians kept calling them “recruiters” and “co-conspirators” without talking about how they themselves had been trafficked or recognizing that asking girls to bring their friends was a typical way sex traffickers built their networks and stayed in control — by sowing guilt, shame and conflict among their victims. They worried: Am I on the list of co-conspirators that’s going to come out?

When the F. B. I. called, Lindsay had just moved into a new house and was a stay-at-home mom taking care of a newborn. She went straight to a lawyer and offered everything in her family’s bank account: $10,000. She thought she might go to prison for life because she would be condemned as the next Maxwell.

Even so, Lindsay agreed to testify at Epstein’s trial. Marina also agreed to testify, appearing in the U. S. attorney’s indictment as Minor Victim-1. But Lisa wanted to be left out of it. She dodged the F. B. I. She dodged her lawyer. She dodged all her friends. She stopped listening to the news. I will never face him, Lisa remembers thinking. I’ll never go to trial. She was mad that her friends had turned on Epstein. She had seen him for close to a decade and had really cared for him. Lindsay and Marina kept asking her, “Why are you still protecting him?”

When Epstein died in his jail cell a month after his arrest, Lisa was so sad that she cried. For months, she barely slept, trying to make sense of it all. She began remembering things in the middle of the night, and when she did, she called Lindsay. They talked for hours. The memories seemed contradictory: He loved them, he trapped them, he saved them, he hurt them. Lisa’s lawyer tried to help her talk through it. She’d say, “Tell me about a time he upset you,” but Lisa couldn’t handle it. “He never upset me,” she’d say. “He didn’t do anything to me! Jeffrey was my friend!”

Marina was taking a lot of Xanax, numbing all thoughts of Epstein. She moved to Florida with her husband and daughter, but her pill supply ran dry during the pandemic. Every day felt like a heart attack. She had diarrhea, couldn’t sleep, couldn’t eat, couldn’t function. Then she had a seizure and woke up in a gurney on her way to the hospital. It took her 18 months to recover. The last thing on her mind was the news.

Lindsay worried that she had ruined other women’s lives by bringing them to Epstein. She felt her whole moral self collapse. During her first meeting with her therapist, Lindsay said: “I brought the girls. I am not a victim.” The therapist had to remind her that she had been a child. “I felt terrible,” Lindsay told me. That’s when Epstein came to her in her dreams. He was giving her money, trying to bring her back. These were “horror dreams,” she said. “You feel him coming for you.”

Lindsay wrote to apologize to girls she introduced to Epstein. She got in touch with a childhood friend who had lived in the same building as her family in Queens. The two of them used to sneak cigarettes outside. The friend was so overwhelmed by the news after Epstein’s death that she fled the country with her family. Lindsay offered to help her apply for settlement money through Epstein’s estate. It was a new program, set up by Bank of America, which had held some of Epstein’s accounts. “Not that the money’s going to compensate,” Lindsay told her, “but we are already in it. And I know you have kids. All I can do is try to help with my kind of intel and what I know, but I just want to let you know I never meant to bring any of this on you.”

Lisa was also hearing from some of the women she brought. They wanted compensation from the estate, and hoped Lisa would help their chances by signing declarations saying that she had introduced them to Epstein. They promised her she wouldn’t get in trouble, but she was too scared to sign. One of them had been abused by Epstein for years and years because he really liked her. “Without your signature,” Lisa recalls her saying, “I don’t have anything. And I think that’s fucked up. You’re the one that brought me there, and because of you I didn’t have a childhood.”

Danielle and Marina hadn’t seen each other for nearly 20 years when they unexpectedly met again in September 2025. They had both come to Washington for a rally outside the U. S. Capitol, organized by the anti-trafficking coalition World Without Exploitation, to demand the release of the Epstein files. It was the first public gathering of Epstein survivors, and many of the women were meeting for the first time.

Danielle was working as a dance instructor and choreographer after having a son and moving back to New Jersey. Until Epstein’s arrest in 2019, she hadn’t known that she was a victim of sex trafficking. She thought being trafficked meant you were kidnapped off the street and held captive. The realization that she was a victim came as some relief. Danielle went public with her story in 2021, speaking to reporters outside Ghislaine Maxwell’s arraignment, and she knew that more women planned to go public with their stories at the rally.

That day, Danielle had her blonde hair cut above her shoulders, and she wore a royal blue blazer with a brooch shaped like a butterfly. She walked up over the hill toward the Capitol and recognized Marina. Her hair was pulled back into a low bun and she was wearing a light pink silk blouse and large black sunglasses. Danielle decided she wanted to talk to Marina. “We had been friends,” she told me. “This was someone, dare I say, back in the day, I really loved.”

Danielle went to shake her hand. “Hi, I’m Dani,” she said, looking up at Marina, no longer a child of 15 but a woman of 37.

“Dani, oh, my god! I can’t believe you’re standing in front of me.” Then she asked, “Did I bring you to Jeffrey’s?”

Caught off-guard, Danielle’s first thought was to protect Marina. She blurted out: “No, no, no. It was somebody else.”

She walked away from Marina thinking: Why couldn’t I have just been honest? Why couldn’t I have told her that she’s all over my paperwork, in the F. B. I. reports. Why couldn’t I have just said, Yes, it was you.

A news conference had been planned for that morning where victims would give statements. At 10:30 a. m., Marina and Danielle joined a crowd of survivors and politicians huddled around a lectern, fanning themselves with their speeches in the heat. A lawyer for the survivors said that her team had identified hundreds of other victims, but only about 30 were public. Marina was one of eight survivors who spoke. She stepped up to the mic and shared her story with reporters for the first time.

One reason she wanted the files released, she told the crowd, was so that she could better understand what happened to her. “There are many pieces of my story I can’t remember no matter how hard I try,” she said. She lived in a constant state of wonder, fear and confusion. Her voice cracked trying to read the speech she held with shaking hands. “There are people out there who know more about my abuse than I do,” she said. “The least that they can do is give me my documents.”

Marina started to realize how much she had erased from her mind only after she reconnected with Lisa and Lindsay and they began comparing their memories. “He raped you in front of us, plenty of times,” she remembers Lindsay telling her. “He used you as an example, as a doll.”

Marina couldn’t understand how she had blocked it out. Her therapist said it was how her body protected her. That seemed true. If her therapist asked about Epstein, most of the time Marina said: “I’m not upset about what happened. I don’t remember.” She kept telling her therapist, “When Jeffrey and I had sex,” and her therapist, Randee Kogan, kept saying: “You didn’t have sex. You were a child. He sexually abused you.”

When a batch of files was released this January, Marina learned that she had brought Danielle — it was all there in the F. B. I. report. The next month, they saw each other at a congressional hearing where Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, was testifying about the Epstein files. When it was over, Marina walked up to Danielle and shared that she had read the F. B. I. report. “Why didn’t you tell me?”

Danielle explained that she had been embarrassed. She didn’t know how to talk about it. None of them did. “I was worried how you’d react,” Danielle said. But she left wondering whether Marina really didn’t remember bringing her to Epstein. Was she lying? And if she really didn’t remember, that hurt, too. How could Marina — her friend — have forgotten a moment that had derailed her entire future?

Danielle wished a victim who had brought girls would come forward and talk honestly about it. “There’s the 15-year-old recruiter who was just trying to help her family and make it,” Danielle told me. That’s different from someone like Maxwell, who was holding passports and preventing girls from leaving. But she also wondered: Where does the victimization stop and the choice begin? She knew it was distressing and triggering for so many survivors to suddenly be in the company of the women who had ensnared them, and the taboo around recruitment was making it harder to heal. “If what we are doing is working to bring secrets out of the dark,” Danielle said later, “then recruitment is the biggest secret out there.”

But it was hard for women to come forward when politicians were continuing to refer to victims who recruited as co-conspirators or traffickers. In February, outside the House Oversight Committee’s deposition of Bill Clinton, Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican from Florida, told reporters that it was “very apparent” that Epstein groomed some victims to traffic other girls, but insisted that once a victim turned 18 they were no longer victims but co-conspirators. “In my opinion, they are not to be given victim status, because they did partake in harming young girls.” In May, Representative Nancy Mace, a Republican from South Carolina, put it even more harshly: “If you’re an adult female and you’re recruiting underage girls, you’re not a victim. You’re a prostitute, a child predator, and a sex trafficker.” News outlets continued to raise the question of the possibility of criminal accomplice status in connection to a survivor.

The women were starting to blame one another, and question one another’s stories. Some wanted to create different categories for victims who brought girls their age, and victims who were young adults and brought minors. Randee Kogan, Marina’s therapist who has been working with Epstein victims since the Palm Beach investigation, told me it didn’t make sense to draw that line. “That’s not the way psychology works,” she said. Kogan emphasized that turning 18 didn’t mean you were suddenly a different person — young adults were just as vulnerable to Epstein’s manipulation. Earlier this year, one of the other Epstein victims killed herself. “And you know why?” Kogan said. “I’ll tell you this: She couldn’t handle the fact that she brought other girls and ruined other girls’ lives.”

This spring, Danielle and Marina were among a group of survivors invited to visit a public art installation in New York created by a nonprofit focused on government transparency, which displayed 3.5 million pages of partially redacted Department of Justice records from the Epstein files. As part of a publicity campaign, the exhibit’s curator asked survivors to post note cards about their experience on an enormous timeline on the wall.

Danielle wrote, “Trafficked to Epstein in 2004, 17 years old.”

Later, Marina read the note and took offense. Trafficked? Was Danielle calling her a perpetrator? “I understood that it’s never a good feeling to have the person who brought you to Jeffrey standing in the room,” Marina told me. “But I thought I was helping people, and I still do today. I didn’t forcefully bring anybody there.” She felt she had no choice but to obey Epstein because she was a child who didn’t know where food was coming from or how she was going to live. “That’s pressure,” she said. “And when you’re under pressure, you don’t realize that you’re making mistakes along the way that might hurt other people.” But she decided not to say anything to Danielle. She didn’t want to cause any trouble.

As the months passed, Danielle learned more about Marina’s story, seeing how different it was from her own. Danielle could always go back home to her mom. Marina really didn’t have anything. If she went to her mom’s she would be going back to live with a man who sexually abused her for years. Danielle told me it was hard to navigate these feelings of empathy and anger on her own. There was no playbook for dealing with this kind of betrayal. “They were victims, too,” Danielle told me. “That’s what makes it so complex.”

Danielle was not the only victim searching for answers. When Marina went public, another woman reached out to talk about how angry she was. She said Marina brought her to Epstein in 2004. She went only once, but Epstein assaulted her.

“You never told me what was going to happen,” she said.

Marina couldn’t remember this woman. She told Marina that they met at a cafe in Astoria and went to clubs together.

“I can’t remember you,” Marina said. “I don’t remember!”

They talked for hours, until slowly some of the details returned. “I’m sorry, I’m sorry,” Marina told her. “I was so young.”

Even years after Epstein’s death, the women felt his presence everywhere. Danielle had recurring dreams in which a bomb explodes or she’s driving off a cliff and can’t get the seatbelt off her son, and she just accepts what’s going to happen. She always had the feeling of having to accept what was happening and just submit to the violence. Last year, she tried to read Virginia Giuffre’s memoir, “Nobody’s Girl,” but after she got to the part about Ghislaine Maxwell, she couldn’t fall asleep. She entered a half-sleep state where she was walking the halls of the mansion over and over, not knowing what she was trying to find. She thought she was awake, because she remembered waking up, but then she was still in the massage room. “Am I awake? Am I not awake? Oh, my god.”

Epstein was so present in Lisa’s dreams that it was hard for her to believe he was dead. She and Lindsay lived with daily reminders of his power. Ever since their identities were released in unredacted files, they’ve been harassed by strangers. This summer a rock crashed through Lisa’s window. Lindsay saw men taking photos of her house and decided she had to move. She and her husband would go out for a nice dinner and somehow it always seemed as if the topic at the bar was Epstein.

Lisa told me she couldn’t have sex without massaging her partner first. “I don’t know how to get into it,” she said. She paused for a moment. “I don’t even like sex,” she said. “Honestly. I hate it.”

Marina hated sex, too. She told me her anxiety is so high that she can’t sleep through the night and obsessively cleans to avoid difficult thoughts. She found it hard to connect with other people, to be intimate with them. Sometimes she had trouble telling her boyfriend that she loves him, too afraid he’ll think she’s weak and exploit her. She didn’t want her daughter go to the movie theater or the park without her waiting nearby in case of danger.

Marina had a lot of hope that going public with her story would help people understand how Epstein manipulated victims to harm other girls. She thought her voice would be everything, speaking and getting into people’s hearts. But she was still seeing people online calling victims who brought girls co-conspirators.

“It’s OK,” Marina told me. “I think it’s going to take everybody a long time to accept that we all brought each other.”

“I don’t know how to feel about it,” Lisa told me. “I thought it was helping people, because he was helping me. Now when I look back, I’m like, That’s fucked up.” She continued: “I was grooming them, too.”

“But we had no choice,” she added. “There was no ‘I don’t want to do this.’ You know what I mean? If you don’t want to do this, then we’re going to literally be in the street living with bums and crackheads.”

“And he made us feel loved,” Lindsay said. “He did. We were cared for.”

“He would ask us about everything,” Lisa said. “He always acted like he cared to hear all the stories in our head. And so for the first time we had a voice. We didn’t have a voice at home.”

“We felt heard,” Lindsay said. “I know I did.”

“Me, too,” Lisa said. “That’s what it was. We felt heard.”

They could call him anytime and ask for help. They could say, Hey Jeffrey, we are locked out. Anytime. For any reason. “That’s what it was,” Lindsay said. “That was a nice feeling to have.”

For Marina, it helped to try to imagine what it was like to be 13 again. “I think I’m starting to understand more seeing my daughter being 13, really seeing that age and how she thinks.” When she can, Marina spends time looking at the sky, the way she did as a child, trying to remember. She lies in the hammock in her yard, beneath big oak trees, naming the shapes of clouds, asking the questions she asked as a girl: Why is the cloud following us? How are we upside-down on earth and still not falling?

She has been in therapy for a year, working on breaking down her defenses. She was still suppressing memories, trying to protect herself from the pain that would come along with them. “Do I feel bad for bringing girls to Jeffrey? Maybe after more therapy,” she told me. Every time she brought up the past, Marina admitted, she ran away from it. “I keep saying, ‘I’m not upset about what happened.’” Only in September did she find herself crying for the first time remembering Epstein. She couldn’t believe it. Why am I crying? She was starting to understand how afraid she’d been at 13. It was hard. She didn’t want to stay there for long.

Marina and Danielle still found it challenging to be in the same room, but they got along. Sometimes they didn’t talk, just felt each other’s presence, and that was all they could take for now.

Jen Percy is a contributing writer for the magazine and the author of “Girls Play Dead: Acts of Preservation,” a nonfiction book on passivity and women’s survival strategies, out in paperback on Nov. 10.

Van Hollen Says His Senate Challenge to Schumer Is Gaining Support

The New York Times November 15, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said on Sunday that he has a “wide-open” path to unseat Chuck Schumer, the long-serving Senate Democratic leader.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, contended on Sunday that he has a “wide open” path to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York to become majority leader next year, intensifying the internal leadership battle that is dividing the newly empowered Democratic caucus.

Mr. Van Hollen, who has positioned himself as a populist underdog, said he did not believe Mr. Schumer’s support was solid. Mr. Schumer, an architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate, has announced that he has locked up enough commitments to return him to the position of leader for another two years.

“I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me,” Mr. Van Hollen said on CNN’s “State Of The Union,” though it was not clear what list he was referring to. “The others are very open to the idea of change.”

Mr. Van Hollen had previously said he had more than 10 colleagues supporting him.

On Sunday, he said on “Fox News Sunday” that number was up to 15 and growing. “This is a wide-open race,” he said.

The winner needs a simple majority of the caucus to vote for him in a secret-ballot election that is scheduled for Dec. 1. Democrats will make up at least 55 seats in the Senate next year, including the independents who caucus with them.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, also accused Mr. Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats since 2016, of trying to change that date because he was not confident he had the votes.

“If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections,” Mr. Van Hollen, who appeared on three different programs on Sunday morning, said on Fox News. “They’re talking about trying to short-circuit that open debate process within the Democratic caucus.”

While there has been an internal discussion by some lawmakers of moving up the date of the election to avoid a prolonged internal battle, it is not clear that the idea has gained any traction or is being driven by Mr. Schumer himself, people familiar with the conversations said.

Mr. Van Hollen said that he differed from Mr. Schumer in his position on funding the war with Iran. He said Congress should give “not one penny more” to fund the war, using the leverage of a government shutdown next month to force the issue. Congress has a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government to avoid a shutdown.

Mr. Schumer and other top Democrats have been weighing a temporary extension of government funding with some restrictions on the military money until early 2027, when they would hold the majority and likely be able to exert more leverage against the Trump administration.

Mr. Van Hollen also said he disagreed with Mr. Schumer’s decision to try to influence Democratic primaries during the midterm elections, particularly against Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

“He joined with AIPAC and crypto to try and defeat them,” he said, referring to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which spent about $30 million in the competitive Michigan primary against Mr. El-Sayed.

While Mr. Schumer has been criticized for supporting some center-leaning candidates in primaries who ultimately lost to progressives, his allies noted that he recruited five winning candidates in states that Democrats flipped or are on track to do so: Mary Peltola in Alaska, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Josh Turek in Iowa, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Scott Colom in Mississippi.

They also noted that Senate Democrats’ campaign arm never spent money in the Minnesota Senate race.

Overall, though, Mr. Van Hollen said he was challenging Mr. Schumer because the message of the midterm elections was that the American people wanted change.

“We need to earn people’s trust, and I don’t think you do that by simply going back to business as usual,” Mr. Van Hollen said on Fox News.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.
