Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Flawed Hunt for a Missing Airman

The New York Times November 15, 2026

War in the Middle East

Times Investigation

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

Times Investigation

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

At a protest in 2025 in Tel Aviv, supporters of Israeli hostages held captive by Hamas held pictures of the hostages and of Ron Arad, who has been missing since 1986. Credit... Itai Ron/Reuters

Supported by

By Adam GoldmanRonen BergmanFarnaz Fassihi and Hwaida Saad

Ronen Bergman, Farnaz Fassihi, Adam Goldman and Hwaida Saad have spent years investigating the disappearance of the Israeli airman Ron Arad.

Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.

As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.

He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.

As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.

What did he know about Ron Arad?

Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition, to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.

The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

Mr. Arad was the only thing that interrogators asked him about, Iranian officials said.

General Saberi’s abduction and interrogation, details of which have not previously been reported, were particularly remarkable because several Israeli intelligence reports had concluded, over many years, that Iran had not been involved in Mr. Arad’s disappearance.

Yet time and again, a New York Times investigation found, Israeli intelligence officials gave greater credence to reports and assumptions that Iran must be to blame for the airman’s disappearance or knew about his whereabouts. That belief, which officials said was genuinely held, justified cross-border raids, kidnappings, harsh interrogations and more.

The Times investigation also discovered something else: the answer to one of the region’s enduring spy mysteries, the two-decade-old disappearance of an Iranian general, Alireza Asgari. In hunting for Mr. Arad, Israeli officials kidnapped the general, interrogated him about Mr. Arad and then killed him. He had no intelligence on Mr. Arad.

“It was a collective blind spot,” said Avi Kalo, a retired senior Israeli military officer who wrote a detailed report in 2016 that, like others, found no conclusive evidence of Iranian involvement. Yet operations against Iran continued.

“Iran,” Mr. Kalo said, “was the boogeyman.”

Today in Israel, after years of bloody operations targeting Iran, the prevailing thinking among people involved with the hunt for Mr. Arad is that he was never held by Iran, and that Tehran was not involved in his disappearance, officials familiar with the intelligence told The Times. Recent information collected during Israel’s wars with Iran and Hezbollah has only hardened that conclusion.

Officials who were once certain that Iran was responsible told The Times that they had most likely been wrong all along, including Raz Zimmt, a former Israeli military intelligence analyst who helped write a key 2005 report that pointed blame at Tehran. That assessment, he said in a recent interview, was probably mistaken because of “a natural inclination to pin everything on the regime in Tehran.”

In interviews, nobody suggested that Israeli intelligence officials had intentionally misled the government over the decades about Iran’s role. Rather, they said that the conclusions were based on fragmented or circumstantial evidence and were probably influenced by confirmation bias — the tendency to give more weight to conclusions that fit with previously held beliefs.

Such biases have clouded Israel’s vision before. Before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, officials were preoccupied by Iran and Hezbollah and underestimated the closer threat posed by Hamas, even as it raised millions and prepared for an assault. Israeli officials were so convinced that Hamas could not muster a coordinated attack that they doubted it despite obtaining the battle plans.

Israeli officials were again overconfident in their intelligence before the current war with Iran, when they incorrectly predicted a popular uprising that could topple the government in Tehran.

Israel’s foreign intelligence service, the Mossad, declined to comment on the intelligence that it had produced on Mr. Arad and the operations that it carried out to find him. A spokeswoman for the Israeli military said that Mr. Arad was regarded as alive and missing in action.

The Times interviewed dozens of Iranian, Israeli and American officials and others directly involved in the hunt for Mr. Arad. The Times also interviewed families, friends and associates of the two abducted Iranian generals. Some spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss military and intelligence secrets.

These interviews reveal new details about key moments, faulty assumptions and fatal costs. The hunt for Mr. Arad is, in its own way, a story of generations of mutual mistrust and violence between Israel, Iran and its proxies. The fighting and secret diplomacy have spanned nearly the entire history of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Israeli leaders, no matter their political parties, have relied on intelligence to hold Iran responsible for Mr. Arad’s disappearance.

In one indication of how the thinking has changed, Israeli commandos set out this year in the hopes of finding Mr. Arad’s body — not in Iran, but in a small Lebanese village.

That is where the saga began.

On Oct. 16, 1986, an Israeli F4-Phantom jet streaked through the sky over southern Lebanon. Mr. Arad, then a 28-year-old weapons officer, took aim at a Palestine Liberation Organization target and fired.

The bomb detonated prematurely, badly damaging the aircraft. Mr. Arad ejected.

Everyone agrees, after years of investigations, that Mr. Arad was captured by a Lebanese Shiite militia and political group known as Amal. The group’s chief of security, Mustafa Dirani, took charge of the fallen airman.

The militants offered to trade their hostage for millions of dollars and the release of Palestinian and Lebanese prisoners. But Israel’s defense minister at the time, Yitzhak Rabin, had suffered politically for a prisoner swap in 1985 and was reluctant to make a deal.

As progress stalled on locating Mr. Arad, Israeli suspicion fell on Iran and its Shiite Islamic government. It was a reasonable assumption. Iran was a major player in Lebanese politics and provided training and money to Shiite groups, including Amal.

In 1989, Mr. Arad’s wife announced that the Israeli government had told her that it had “irrevocable proof” that her husband was alive and that he had been handed over to Iranian operatives.

Iranian involvement in Mr. Arad’s disappearance quickly became conventional wisdom, despite Israeli officials’ making no progress in locating him in Iran.

The Iran theory got a major boost in 1992 inside the Mossad.

Israel Perlov, a veteran officer, figured that Mr. Arad most likely would have been wounded in his fall and would have needed medical care. Mr. Perlov set out looking for doctors who might have seen the airman.

He found an Iranian doctor who claimed to have treated Mr. Arad in both Tehran and Lebanon. This was potentially a breakthrough moment. If the doctor were credible, it would be solid evidence that Mr. Arad had indeed been taken to Iran.

But a polygraph test produced inconclusive results on the question of Iran. So Mr. Perlov tested the doctor a second time. Again, the test showed signs of “disturbances” when the doctor described seeing Mr. Arad in Iran.

“But they were not significant enough to negate the veracity of his response,” Mr. Perlov wrote in a book released last year.

He found the doctor credible, but decided to put the doctor to the test. Mr. Perlov opened a suitcase full of cash and offered it as a reward. All the doctor had to do was prove that he had treated the missing airman.

He never saw the doctor again, and Mossad agents never corroborated his story. But Mr. Perlov wrote that his encounters with the doctor bolstered the idea that the “Iranians were up to their necks in holding Ron.”

A few years later, another Mossad officer, Rami Igra, would review this encounter and come to a very different conclusion.

In his view, Mr. Igra told The Times, the doctor was a liar who had been angling for a big payday. Mr. Igra suspected that the Mossad had gone looking for proof of its own assumption, and found it.

But the doctor’s story became part of the official evidence against Iran. Mr. Igra’s contrarian assessment gained little traction.

The most explosive evidence against Iran burst into public view in 1994, and it shaped public opinion and news accounts for decades.

Israeli commandos stormed into Lebanon and kidnapped Mr. Dirani, the militia member who was last known to have held Mr. Arad. They whisked him to an underground prison in an operation known as Poisonous Sting.

Under questioning, Mr. Dirani said he had stashed Mr. Arad in a home in the Lebanese village of Nabi Chit, where a trusted family could watch him. One night, he said, the men assigned to guard Mr. Arad had left the house, probably in response to an unrelated Israeli raid nearby. When they returned, he said, Mr. Arad was gone.

Years had passed, and Mr. Dirani said he did not know where the airman was.

Mr. Dirani’s interrogator did not believe that.

“You couldn’t reason with Dirani. The only thing that worked was force,” the interrogator, Doron Zehavi, later recalled in an interview.

Mr. Dirani would later testify that he was physically and sexually tortured — claims that the Israeli government broadly denied. But it acknowledged rough treatment and that Mr. Dirani may have been threatened with sexual assault.

Under harsh interrogation, Mr. Dirani recounted a meeting with an Iranian official who told him that the Revolutionary Guards had snatched Mr. Arad and taken him to an Iranian prison camp.

“After his soul was drained out, when he spat blood, then he tells us about a massive Revolutionary Guards camp complex in Iran,” Mr. Zehavi said.

Some believed this as incriminating evidence against the Iranians. Others regarded it as coerced and too unreliable to act on. Mr. Igra, the Mossad officer, concluded that there was no evidence that Iranian officials had held Mr. Arad.

To date, no evidence has surfaced to prove Mr. Dirani’s account of Mr. Arad's being held in an Iranian prison, officials say. Some officials believe that Mr. Dirani had honestly recounted his conversation with the Iranian official, but that the information itself was bad.

Mr. Igra’s analysis did not conclude what had happened to Mr. Arad. Maybe he had been killed while trying to escape. Perhaps his captors had executed him as revenge in the tit-for-tat fighting that had defined the era.

The most logical explanation, he assessed, was that Mr. Arad’s story began and ended in Lebanon. “It was a simple solution to a complex problem,” Mr. Igra said.

But Mr. Dirani’s story was big news in Israel. It seemed to confirm years of suspicions that Iran was behind Mr. Arad’s disappearance. Journalists, analysts and top government officials repeated it for years.

“The Iranian authorities have been holding Ron Arad for more than six years,” Mr. Rabin said in 1995, “and they are directly and fully responsible for his fate.”

Convinced that Iran was to blame, the Israeli government put intense pressure on government leaders in Tehran.

“The issue of Ron Arad followed us everywhere,” Mohammad Ali Abtahi, Iran’s vice president from 1997 to 2005, told The Times in a telephone interview from Tehran. “In every international encounter we had, we were asked about Ron Arad, Ron Arad.”

The case even followed them to the Vatican. When the Iranian president at the time, Mohammad Khatami, visited Rome in 1999, Pope John Paul II presented him with a letter from Mr. Arad’s wife, pleading for information, Mr. Abtahi recalled.

“Israel was obsessed about Iran’s role in the Ron Arad case,” he said. “Our position was that this has nothing to do with us. It happened in Lebanon.”

Something about that gnawed at some Israeli intelligence officials. Iran knew that Israel would pay a hefty price for information about Mr. Arad. If Iranian leaders possessed such information, why would they not try to capitalize on it?

Finally, in 2004, it seemed like that might happen.

Israel agreed to free a high-profile Lebanese inmate in exchange for genetic evidence proving what happened to Mr. Arad. Hezbollah’s leader at the time, Hassan Nasrallah, was eager to make that happen, so he enlisted help from the Iranian government.

“I got the impression that they — Hezbollah and the Iranians — were truly trying with all their might to locate the body,” Gerhard Conrad, a German intelligence officer who helped mediate the negotiations, told The Times. “Nasrallah knew he could extract any price for him, even if he was dead.”

Iran dispatched Abdullah Saberi, a Revolutionary Guards commander who’d served many years in Lebanon, to help coordinate the search, according to former Israeli and Iranian officials.

The Hezbollah-Iranian investigation concluded with a secret report saying that Mr. Arad had died in 1988 in Nabi Chit, the village in eastern Lebanon where he had been held, according to three former Iranian officials. The document, the details of which have not been previously reported, concluded that he was most likely buried somewhere there.

The findings were considered so important that the former president of Iran Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who was involved in the search, dispatched one of his children to Germany to hand-deliver them.

“During the entire negotiations, Israel was insisting that we find information on Ron Arad, but we couldn’t find anything,” said Hossein Mousavian, a former Iranian ambassador to Germany.

The German mediators saw such high-level engagement as a sign of Iran’s seriousness and willingness to engage.

Israel read it completely differently.

Why, intelligence officers asked, would Iran have dispatched a Revolutionary Guards commander to lead the search if it had not been involved with the disappearance? To the Israelis, this was evidence of high-level Iranian complicity.

“The fact that a highly important Iranian general flew to Lebanon from Tehran to bring a unique body of knowledge and help Hezbollah locate the grave only added to our deep conviction that Iran was behind this event,” Mr. Zimmt, the former intelligence officer who participated in the review, told The Times.

Israel’s 2005 report that concluded that Mr. Arad must have been kidnapped by the Revolutionary Guards. (This landmark report remains classified, but its conclusion has been widely reported.)

Mr. Zimmt, today a highly regarded scholar who studies Iran, said that looking back, he and his colleagues had gotten tunnel vision. “And it wouldn’t be the last time,” he said.

In 2006, Yuval Diskin, the head of Israel’s domestic security agency, Shin Bet, launched a comprehensive review of the Arad case. After two decades without a breakthrough, investigators re-examined every aspect.

“We went through everything, item by item, and examined all the sources, their reliability and the way the information had been obtained,” Mr. Diskin told The Times in an interview. “We reached the conclusion that all the reports or analyses based on those reports, according to which Ron Arad had been transferred to or had reached Iran at some stage, were incorrect and were based on serious mistakes in reading the intelligence that had been collected, or on unreliable or erroneous information.”

This intelligence assessment was reported earlier by the Israeli journalist Yoav Limor in his 2023 book, “The Interrogator.”

The Shin Bet team concluded that Mr. Arad never fell into the hands of Hezbollah or the Revolutionary Guards. The answer to his disappearance, the team said, most likely rested in the village of Nabi Chit — the very place that the Hezbollah-Iranian investigation had pointed to.

That report got little traction inside the government, Mr. Diskin said.

Rather than dropping the Iran theory, the Mossad doubled down with an audacious, and previously unreported, kidnapping operation.

A general in the Quds Force of the Revolutionary Guards named Alireza Asgari had been on the Mossad’s radar for years. The general had close ties with Hezbollah leaders and had risen to be deputy Iranian defense minister. Most important, he had arrived in Lebanon shortly after Mr. Arad vanished.

In December 2006, General Asgari flew to Istanbul and checked into the Ceylan Hotel, according to his wife, Ziba Ahmadi. From there, he vanished.

General Asgari’s disappearance quickly became one of the intelligence world’s biggest whodunits.

The Israelis have steadfastly denied involvement.

Years later, as the United States and Iran negotiated a nuclear deal and prisoner swaps, the Iranians asked their American counterparts what had happened to their missing general. American officials denied involvement, but quietly began asking questions themselves.

Israeli officials told U. S. negotiators that General Asgari was dead, according to a former American official involved in the negotiations. Three other former American officials who worked closely with Israel said that Mossad operatives kidnapped him, interrogated him for weeks and killed him.

One of the former officials said that General Asgari had been questioned aboard a boat and dumped into the Black Sea. They said that the Mossad had questioned the general over potential involvement in Mr. Arad’s disappearance. Interrogators had found no such ties.

In an interview with The Times, Yitzhak Ilan, a top Shin Bet investigator, recalled a discussion with Mossad officials before General Asgari’s disappearance. Though he did not name the general, he said he had been briefed on a risky intelligence mission related to the airman’s disappearance.

“I understood, even before the operation, that the solution was not there at all,” he told The Times before his death in 2020.

It is not clear how much the Americans told Iran about what they had learned about General Asgari’s disappearance. Iran conducted its own investigation, and Ms. Ahmadi told The Times that investigators had told her that Israeli operatives had entered her husband’s hotel room, drugged him and kidnapped him.

She said that investigators had found the vehicle used in the operation abandoned by the Black Sea.

Asked why the Israelis would want to question her husband, she replied, “Have you ever heard of Ron Arad?”

General Asgari’s interrogation had failed to turn up evidence of Mr. Arad’s whereabouts. So once again, officials started from scratch.

Mr. Kalo, who led the Israeli military’s missing-in-action unit in 2014, recounted in an interview with The Times how he had examined years of intercepted communications, informant reports and analytical assessments.

He reached the same conclusion that the Shin Bet team and the Hezbollah-Iranian investigation had reached years earlier. Mr. Arad had most likely died in 1988, probably in Nabi Chit. He was never in Iran.

Mr. Kalo said he delivered his lengthy report to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in late 2016. The conclusion quickly appeared on Israel’s Channel 2 news.

By the time Mr. Kalo retired in 2019, he thought the Iran theory had been laid to rest. In discussions with his colleagues, he recommended focusing future intelligence-gathering on Nabi Chit.

Mr. Kalo said he made clear to Israeli intelligence officers that abducting Iranians would not solve the Arad case.

But two years later, nearly two decades after he helped coordinate the Hezbollah search for Mr. Arad in Lebanon, General Saberi stepped out of his apartment and ended up inside a refrigerator box and a Mossad moving van.

The Israelis never stopped suspecting that General Saberi must know something about the airman’s whereabouts.

After a lengthy interrogation, the dazed general was dumped on a street in Johannesburg, South Africa. He later said he was tortured.

As questions swirled in Israel, David Barnea, the Mossad chief at the time, said he had authorized an operation to find information on Mr. Arad. He described the mission as “courageous and daring,” but ultimately a “failure.”

After that, Mr. Barnea told Mossad members that they might as well throw everything they knew about the Arad case into the shredder, associates recall.

None of the operations, the abductions, the raids or the killings had gotten them closer to finding this missing airman. The Mossad began looking seriously at Nabi Chit.

This was the village, Mr. Dirani had told interrogators long ago, where he had stashed Mr. Arad in the care of a trusted family. Those friends had left Mr. Arad alone one night, he had said, to fight Israeli troops nearby.

It is also the village that the Hezbollah-Iranian investigation had identified as Mr. Arad’s probable resting place. At least two subsequent Israeli inquiries had reached the same conclusion.

One of the few men suspected of knowing Mr. Arad’s location back in 1988, former Israeli and current Lebanese officials said, was Ahmad Shukr, a retired Lebanese security officer. Last December, Mr. Shukr left home for a meeting about what he thought was a business deal.

He promptly disappeared, and Lebanese officials believe that he was abducted by Israeli agents. Mr. Shukr’s whereabouts remains a mystery, as does what he may have told investigators.

Israeli officials now say that the closest thing the government has to a theory is that Mr. Arad was executed as retribution for the killing of Mr. Shukr’s brother, who died battling Israeli forces that night in 1988. (Ahmad Shukr’s niece Rana Shukr said in an interview that her uncle had nothing to do with Mr. Arad.)

A few months after Mr. Shukr’s disappearance, Israeli soldiers descended on Nabi Chit in one of the deadliest clashes of this latest round of fighting with Hezbollah. Dozens of Lebanese were killed and wounded.

Israeli soldiers searched a corner of a cemetery, looking for the remains of Mr. Arad, and unearthed a grave. They found nothing, but officials say that the search continues — with a focus now on Lebanon rather than Iran.

“We should have gone there 20 years ago. It was a failure,” Mr. Kalo said. “We could not get away from the narrative that Iran was involved. We could not untie Arad from the threat of Iran. It was too deeply rooted in our obsession.”

Gal Koplewitz and Euan Ward contributed reporting.

Adam Goldman is a London-based reporter for The Times who writes about global security.

Ronen Bergman is a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine, based in Tel Aviv.

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

8 Takeaways From a Big Democratic Gathering in Denver: Democrats in Array

The New York Times November 15, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates made early pitches for themselves and their visions at what amounted to a party-wide post-election victory party.

By Shane Goldmacher and Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from Denver

Democratic spirits were higher than the altitude in Denver, where more than 3,000 party strategists, activists, lawmakers and potential presidential candidates gathered last week to strategize how the party could capitalize on its dominant showing in the midterm elections.

Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats while also securing what could be the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades.

“America is back,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-in-waiting, beamed at one welcome party.

For a party that is often fractious, there seemed little discord in Denver. Some of the loudest jeering over the three-day event came when the lights at the Ritz-Carlton hotel bar brightened and hundreds of drinking Democrats booed in unison at the thought of it closing.

Here are eight takeaways from the gathering.

More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates descended on Denver to make early pitches for themselves and their visions. They were not technically campaigning — at least not yet. But they were all eager to share how much they had to give to the country.

At one point on Friday, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania was speaking on the main stage while Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan was taking questions from reporters. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona was nearby, too, waiting to speak to the media.

Later, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia gave a speech, then stayed to listen to Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey address the crowd. And Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, was sought after — especially after a rare nationwide ground stop was issued.

The pileup of hopefuls previewed what could be a crowded campaign.

The conference was hosted by Majority Democrats, a relatively new group that espouses a less ideological brand of Democratic politics and focuses on recruiting younger candidates. The group is funded chiefly by the hedge-fund billionaire Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue. But billionaires still found themselves in the cross hairs of some progressives.

Representative Ro Khanna of California, who is considering a presidential run, called for a wealth tax on billionaires and accused Israel of a genocide to cheers.

Since Mr. Shapiro has rarely left Pennsylvania this year, his presence alone in Denver was notable. But on Friday, he spoke about his ambitions for the party — and his role in its future — both in his speech and an interview. He called it imperative for Democrats to construct a party that could win “370 electoral votes” — not just the 270 needed to win the presidency.

“We can’t be a party that is focused on sloganeering,” Mr. Shapiro said in an interview. “We have to be a party that’s focused on real deliverables.”

He said that the party can’t become “distracted by the shallow litmus test or trying to figure out where someone fits on some imaginary political spectrum.”

For many years, the Democratic presidential primary began in Iowa and New Hampshire, and then went to South Carolina. No longer.

In 2028, six early states will open the primary calendar: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

Officials in Michigan, Virginia and New Mexico are already plotting how to take advantage of the new attention, circulating among ambitious Democrats on the sidelines of the conference.

For instance, Mr. Buttigieg ate Friday night with Don Scott, the House speaker in Virginia, which will hold the final primary before Super Tuesday. Mr. Scott said he told Mr. Buttigieg to start meeting with local leaders now if he wanted to be competitive in Virginia.

Shapiro. Gallego. Warnock. Booker. Khanna. Buttigieg.

Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois had aides and advisers circulating in Denver. So did Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland.

All those potential 2028 candidates — as well as Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who was attending a climate summit in Turkey — are men.

Although women seem less certain to run, some could chase the Democratic nomination. That group includes former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ms. Slotkin, who gave the clearest indications yet that she was considering a run, saying in an interview that she was “seriously” weighing a bid.

Although she said that gender was not reason alone to run for the nation’s highest office, she added it was hard to ignore the possibility of the party being represented by only men in the primary.

“I would hate to see us go backwards by having no women enter the fray,” she said. Later, she said, “I know I want to be a part of the next generation that is helping to lead. That doesn’t necessarily mean I have to be the top dog.”

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland arrived in Denver a day after declaring his underdog candidacy to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York as the top Democrat in the Senate.

He received loud cheers when he restated his intention to the crowd, but Mr. Van Hollen is unlikely to succeed. One conference attendee came wearing a “Van Hollen For Leader” shirt modeled after the Van Halen logo but did not want to discuss on the record his support for the Maryland Democrat.

Mr. Van Hollen is an unlikely avatar of trying to upend the political status quo. He told reporters that he had “a record of running against the establishment,” while also noting in the same answer that he had served as chairman of both the House Democratic campaign arm and the Senate Democratic campaign arm.

“What has never changed about me is that I still believe we can support the underdog,” Mr. Van Hollen said.

In a small sign of frustration with the party’s old guard, Mr. Jeffries was repeatedly heckled while speaking onstage with Jessica Tarlov, a co-host of Fox News’s “The Five.” Mr. Jeffries waved off the hecklers dismissively by noting he was from Brooklyn.

“They didn’t win over a single person, but at least they got their clips for social,” Ms. Tarlov said afterward.

Ms. Slotkin said one of the most important qualities for a candidate in this media landscape was simply being compelling.

“The way citizens consume presidential elections is fundamentally changing,” she said. “I’m not sure we’ll ever have a boring president ever again.”

She just watched Abdul El-Sayed, a charismatic progressive, succeed in Michigan. And after a cycle in which a deluge of Republican cash failed to yield much return on the party’s investments, Democrats debated on the sidelines whether paid ads were as important as earning organic attention and riding the algorithm of social media.

“You can have all the great policy papers you want,” Ms. Slotkin said. “If you can’t convey authentically, that’s going to hold you back. And I think that’s actually OK.”

There was broad agreement among the could-be presidential candidates — and the Democrats who might work for them — that the time for choosing was near.

The competition for attention, donors and top staff is already steep. Many Democrats in Denver spoke of the relative dearth of top operatives who were eager to dedicate themselves to the rigors of a presidential primary campaign — especially with so many new Democratic congressional offices also staffing up.

Mr. Shapiro said he might announce his decision even before he tried to enact a robust agenda in the first 100 days with new Democratic state legislative majorities. Ms. Slotkin said she would decide early next year. And Mr. Warnock, who may have to choose between running for president and seeking Senate re-election in 2028, said nobody could dawdle.

“I don’t think there’s much time for anybody who thinks they want to do this,” he said.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Flight Delays and Cancellations Persist as Air Traffic System Recovers

The New York Times November 15, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

Operations are returning to normal after air traffic was shut down for more than 4 hours on Friday following a maintenance upgrade that crippled communications.

By Bernard Mokam

Air traffic operations over the United States continued to improve on Sunday after nearly all flights were grounded for more than 4 hours on Friday. Still, disruptions remained across the system with many flights canceled or delayed.

Nearly 90 percent of all flights left within 14 minutes of their scheduled departure time on Sunday morning, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. But some 5 percent of flights — more than 1,300 trips — had already been canceled, higher than a typical day, showing the continuing effects of the nationwide flight freeze.

Disruptions have occurred at major hubs — from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Georgia to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas — and at airports in Phoenix and Philadelphia.

The disruptions postponed college sports games and stranded professional basketball teams. Passengers slept overnight in airports and competed to rebook their flights; some canceled their trips entirely.

The logjam is the latest example of the vulnerabilities in the American air traffic system, which is facing twin crises: a shortage of air traffic controllers and an outdated infrastructure.

It was an upgrade to the system that officials have identified as the root cause of the problems that led to the shutdown on Friday. As the contractor L3 Harris was upgrading copper wires to fiber-optic cables, a router overloaded the system with data requests, disrupting communications.

As a result, tens of thousands of passengers endured a nightmare travel weekend. Some 9,000 flights were canceled on Friday, according to Cirium, while about 30 percent were delayed. As airlines worked to get back on track on Saturday, there were still 6,649 cancellations and more than half of all flights were delayed.

“Our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, wrote on social media.

Officials said Sunday that they expected schedules to return to normal by late in the day or Monday morning.

For Ashley Greiner, 45, the delays have compounded.

On Saturday, her flight from Seattle to Atlanta was rerouted to Charlotte, N. C. But her connection to Atlanta was canceled, and she spent the night in North Carolina. On Sunday, she faced two delays and a plane change.

“I’m a heart-failure patient, and my trips were for speaking engagements to share my story with health care providers,” she said in a direct-message conversation. “This has been exceptionally hard on my body.”

The disruption in the communication system forced officials at the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights at around 4 p. m. on Friday.

It was the third such ground stop this century.

Some 3,500 planes were airborne when the order went out, Secretary Duffy said on Friday.

Overall, more than 17,000 flights have been canceled since Friday, according to Cirium’s latest tally. Nearly 40 percent of the 74,696 scheduled flights since Friday have been delayed.

On Sunday, Secretary Duffy said the affected facilities in Texas and Arkansas were “secured” and diagnostic testing was underway.

“We have no indication of a foreign cyberattack, and we will continue to investigate alongside the F. B. I. and our federal law enforcement partners,” he said.

Brenda Folkerts, 59, arrived in New Orleans on Thursday for a marathon but now faces the prospect of a long trip to her home state of Washington on sore and tired legs. Her connection through Dallas was delayed by two hours on Sunday, and she missed her flight to Seattle. She does not know when or how she’ll make it home.

“My case is not unique,” she said in a direct message as her plane taxied. “Most people here have missed connections and are scrambling to figure out what to do.”

Bernard Mokam covers breaking news.

Duffy Points to Router in Arkansas as Start of Nationwide Ground Stop

The New York Times November 15, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

When asked, the transportation secretary could not guarantee on Sunday that a similar air traffic meltdown would not occur again.

By Karoun Demirjian

Reporting from Washington

The cascade of failures that led to the grounding of U. S. air traffic on Friday began with what officials say was supposed to be a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. The station was remote enough, they figured, that they could do the work without causing undue harm.

But that swiftly proved to be a gross miscalculation.

The effort to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable in Arkansas occurred as the agency officials noticed a second issue with a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, where such work had been done weeks before, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning during a blitz of appearances across network and cable television. The work in Arkansas was carried out by one contractor who is also a U. S. veteran, Mr. Duffy said.

Officials took the two facilities offline shortly after, but not before each had pinged the network with an abnormally high rate of connections. That prompted failures in other parts of the air traffic communications network that forced officials to declare a rare nationwide ground stop, Rebecca Guy, the F. A. A.’s chief technology officer, told reporters on Saturday.

But agency investigators still have not determined whether a faulty part or an error on the part of L3Harris, which owns the telecoms system in question and is responsible for upgrading and maintaining it, caused the initial problem in Arkansas. And Mr. Duffy said they are equally unsure why the facility in Amarillo failed on Friday when no upgrade work was being done there at the time.

The protracted crisis, from which airlines have yet to recover, and the lack of clarity from Trump administration officials about why things went wrong, have revived questions about whether the F. A. A. is equipped to carry out its plan for modernization without creating more risks for the nation’s air traffic control system.

The crisis has also heightened concerns about durability and the lack of backups in the nation’s critical air traffic infrastructure, if a failure at one small facility is enough to bring the functionality of the entire network down.

During an interview Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Mr. Duffy said he could not guarantee that a meltdown like Friday’s would not happen again.

“First we have to figure out what happened,” he said, adding, “We’re going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the F. A. A.”

He also deflected when asked if he was ultimately responsible for the meltdown and owed air passengers an apology.

“I can’t apologize for what was passed on to us,” he said, accusing prior administrations of having failed to tackle known infrastructure problems.

“I don’t apologize for shutting down the airspace and keeping people safe,” he added.

Skepticism surrounding how the F. A. A. has been carrying out its air traffic modernization plan is not new.

In September, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan watchdog agency, issued a report raising concerns that the F. A. A. was in danger of “prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions” as it pursued its modernization plan. The report also criticized the agency for not having coordinated the schedules of 11,389 upgrade projects and not having conducted life-cycle cost estimates of existing technology, noting that “without them, the agency could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.”

But such questions are especially pertinent since Mr. Duffy chose to seize on Friday’s meltdown by demanding that Congress give him $50 billion in new funding for air traffic control upgrades by the end of the year. That is a drastically larger sum than he has asked for before — and one that many lawmakers say he has not shown he would responsibly spend.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat running to become majority leader, said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.”

On Saturday, the White House put its weight behind Mr. Duffy’s ballooning demand for funding, and on Sunday, President Trump weighed in on social media to claim that his administration could build the “BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the world,” urging Congress “to give the money, FAST!”

But Mr. Trump dedicated more of his attention to blasting the Biden administration for the F. A. A.’s air traffic infrastructure problems than detailing what $50 billion more would pay for.

Mr. Duffy also has yet to itemize his $50 billion request. For several weeks, he has been calling for a $30 billion influx in F. A. A. funding, but only about $10 billion of that request was specifically for air traffic modernization. Another $10 billion of the funds was envisioned for airport beautification, and the last $10 billion for improvement projects at towers, terminals and airports.

Last year, Congress appropriated $12.5 billion for air traffic modernization, nearly two-thirds of which lawmakers dedicated for telecoms upgrades and radar replacements.

On Saturday, Bryan Bedford, the F. A. A. administrator, told reporters that his agency would need “about $10.1 billion to finish modernization,” on top of the $12.5 billion Congress already appropriated.

On Sunday, Mr. Duffy said that while the money his department has requested will go to pay for needed radio and radar upgrades, it will not cover all the costs of upgrading a telecom system reliant in some places on 1980s wiring and routers from 2001 that have long been obsolete.

“What I don’t have money for is the new telecoms system; I don’t have money for new software,” Mr. Duffy said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.” “Those are critical pieces to the new infrastructure and it’s been historically underinvested in.”

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

The Flaw at the Heart of Anthropic’s I. P. O.

The New York Times November 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Video

By Natasha Sarin

Video by Havovi Cooper and Mehron Abdi

Anthropic is about to go public at a target valuation up to $1.4 trillion.

To prepare, the economist and Opinion contributor Natasha Sarin spent many nights examining the A. I. company’s 300-plus-page prospectus — and she found significant risks. Some of those risks are existential, including the possibility of human extinction, while others are merely financial in nature. In this video, she discusses what worries her most about one of the largest I. P. O.’s of the year.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Natasha Sarin: What I’ve got here is Anthropic’s 300-plus-page prospectus that the company filed before going public. A lot of this document, nearly 100 pages, is outlining very real risks that Anthropic sees — not just business risks to Anthropic, but risks that its technology has the potential to cause for all of humanity. And those risks are existential, and I mean really existential — like, potentially wiping out humanity.

Archival clip of Dario Amodei: I won’t lie to you, there are real dangers.

But Anthropic thinks that it has a solution for this. Instead of organizing itself like a traditional corporation, where it’s acting in the interests of its shareholders ——

Archival clip of “What Makes Us Tick”: Directors represent the stockholders and are responsible for the way the business is run.

—— Anthropic is organizing itself as a public benefit corporation, acting in the interests of humanity writ large. That’s what the co-founders wanted when they left OpenAI to start Anthropic. But what worries me is that the company is asking us to place a lot of faith in them to be able to manage these very real, very scary risks. And I’m just not sure that it’s capable of doing it by itself.

So let’s look at the company structure first. It’s pretty novel. The real power within Anthropic lies with two distinct groups: Its seven co-founders have a majority stake in the company, collectively, of 50.1 percent. That includes Dario Amodei, the C. E. O. of Anthropic, his sister, Daniela, who’s the company’s president, as well as five other members of the founding team, who all have roughly equal shares in the company and have control of it, and also the capacity to direct its day-to-day operations.

The second locus of control within Anthropic is this Long-Term Benefit Trust. This includes five trustees — four currently; one of the spots is open. And you should think about it almost as a group of wise elders that touch a lot of industries that Anthropic is related to. Things like public health or physics.

What sticks out to me, as an economist, is that this group includes Ben Bernanke, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, who guided this country through a financial crisis and has a deep array of research expertise in moments of crisis.

Archival clip of Ben Bernanke: I spent a great deal of my academic career studying not just the Great Depression, but the whole general issue of how financial crises and financial distress affect the overall economy.

Public benefit corporations are rare, but not unheard of. Companies like Warby Parker are structured similarly to act, at least in part, in the interests of the general public. What’s unique about what Anthropic has done is that they’ve given some teeth to this idea of acting in the public interest through the Long-Term Benefit Trust.

This group doesn’t day-to-day-manage Anthropic or its operations. Instead, what it does is elect a majority of the company’s board of directors with the goal of making sure that Anthropic is keeping humanity’s greater good in mind.

Right now, the trust has appointed three of those directors. One seat is open. The other three seats are held by Dario Amodei and his sister, Daniela, as well as the venture capitalist Yasmin Razavi. They are elected by shareholders. But even this structure — while unique, novel and important — just isn’t enough to meet the moment.

The Long-Term Benefit Trust moves inherently slowly. And in the world of AI, what we’ve learned already is that things move fast and the capacity for misaligned agents or cybersecurity threats is very real.

I spent many nights with this prospectus, and let me tell you, it is thick. This document from Anthropic contains information like the state of U. S.-China tensions and the race for artificial intelligence. Also, how much the company is spending annually on security for its C. E. O., Dario Amodei — that’s $3 million a year. It’s quite a lot. And also, who Anthropic views as its real competition: Google and OpenAI. Sorry to Elon; he did not make the cut.

But Anthropic devotes nearly 100 pages of this document to risk factors that it thinks its investors should know about before they invest in the company. They break these risk factors up into basically three categories: First, business risks. These are the kind of things that are generally highlighted by companies in documents like this one. A. I. is an intensely competitive industry, and Anthropic is telling us explicitly what it needs to stay at the frontier of artificial intelligence development, and how that’s not a foregone conclusion.

This prospectus also outlines policy or regulatory risks. For example, it talks through the potential consequences of some of the data center moratoriums that will impact its capacity to develop compute and then effectively train its models.

It also talks about the company’s altercation with the government over its stance that its technology shouldn’t be used in the development of mass surveillance technologies. It’s kind of weird, actually, that this prospectus, which is meant to be about educating investors about potential risks that the company faces, spends so much time talking about the risks that the technology presents to humanity.

In fact, it’s explicit: “Our A. I. models might behave in unintended, misaligned or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed.” That’s wild.

Archival clip of Dario Amodei: The nightmare scenario for six to 12 months would be that you have a swarm of these agents that form some kind of botnet collective, and, you know, could take down large segments of the internet.

But when you talk about what that could mean to the financial system — what that could mean to our water systems or our critical infrastructure — things start to get really scary. I agree with the Anthropic prospectus that those types of risks pose real concerns for the company — for its reputational harms, and potentially for its investors who stand to lose money.

That’s why Anthropic’s leaders have been calling — really begging — for more regulation and more involvement by the government to pace the frontier and the development of this technology, in which misaligned agents could easily reap significant economic harm, not just for investors, but for all of us.

Anthropic is going to go public in the next few days. It's a giant moment — for the company, for the A. I. industry, and, for all of us, too. I think it's commendable that Anthropic has set up a unique structure to help the company navigate the risks that transformative A. I. will present. But I'm concerned that one company can't possibly manage the immense challenges alone.

This video was produced by Havovi Cooper. It was edited by Mehron Abdi. The associate producer was Rebecca Shaid. Fact-checking by Mary Marge Locker. Cinematography by Marina King and Kyle I. Kelley. The Surf’s Way, Way Up as Huge Waves Pound the California Coast

The New York Times November 15, 2026

West Coast Weather

Advertisement

Supported by

Officials warned onlookers to stay off the beaches as waves of more than 50 feet in spots posed hazards. The intense conditions were too dangerous for even seasoned surfers at some beaches.

By Amy Graff and Jesse Klein

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

The largest waves in nearly two years pounded the California coast on Saturday, with the intense surf crashing onto beaches and raising the threat of flooding to coastal roads and communities.

High surf and coastal flood warnings and advisories were in effect along the coast as the National Weather Service advised people to stay out of the water and not even get near it.

“No selfie of the crashing waves is worth losing your life,” said Roger Gass, a meteorologist at the Weather Service office in Monterey, Calif.

The tumultuous surf arrived with a powerful swell that was generated by intense winds thousands of miles off the coast and traveled across the Pacific, building energy along the way.

The waves at the coast grew in size Friday night, as a rainstorm swept the state. They grew even larger Saturday morning, smashing into coastal piers and sending water farther up beaches than usual.

The biggest waves were expected in Northern California, with heights of more than 40 feet at fully exposed beaches and reaching more than 50 feet at Mavericks, the big-wave surf spot 20 miles south of San Francisco.

While the waves at Ocean Beach in San Francisco thundered onto the sand early Saturday, the beach itself was quiet.

“It’s really rough out there,” said Spencer Schenking, 30, of Maryland, who was visiting a friend and surfs a little bit back East.

The tide was out, but the beach was saturated with water. Many large standing pools drained back to the ocean.

Cece Louie, who comes to Ocean Beach every morning, said, “I’ve never seen the beach this wet.”

In Santa Cruz, about 90 minutes south of San Francisco, city beaches were closed through Sunday.

Around 270 homes in Santa Cruz County were under evacuation warnings. These are the biggest waves the region has seen since December 2024, when the surf tore apart the municipal wharf. On Saturday, the wharf was closed.

Jason Hoppin, a spokesman for the county, said that as of noon local time, there were a few road closures and no evacuation orders had been issued, though the threat of flooding remained.

“We’re seeing some minor flooding, but our infrastructure is holding up so far,” Mr. Hoppin said.

Santa Cruz has some of the most popular surf spots in the world, but the waves at most locations were too chaotic and intense on Saturday for surfers.

“I walked some of the shore this morning and did not see a single surfer at the Hook, which is unusual,” Mr. Hoppin said of the break that is often packed with surfers. “It’s like seeing an empty downtown in a big city.”

While the intense swell brought conditions too dangerous for even seasoned surfers at most beaches, it generated the huge walls of water that big-wave surfers crave at Mavericks, the famous break a half mile offshore from Half Moon Bay.

Mark Sponsler, who runs the website Stormsurf, estimated that waves at the site were more than 50 feet, potentially nearing 60 feet, on Saturday morning.

The big-wave surfer Bianca Valenti, 41, of San Francisco, was at Mavericks and said the waves were huge but that winds at the coast made them “very precarious and bouncy.”

Ms. Valenti said she saw both “great rides” and “some crazy wipeouts” on Saturday morning, and hoped conditions would improve.

Surfers also got into the water in San Francisco at Fort Point, where the Pacific Ocean becomes the bay.

Keith Hatcher, 43, a big-wave surfer, was getting ready to paddle out. He chose this location because his normal big-wave spots were too choppy and he was nursing an injury.

He also wanted to avoid the crowds at Mavericks. But this spot, a few miles west of the Golden Gate Bridge, was still a dangerous wave.

“It’s an adventurous beach,” he said. “To get out is a long paddle; there’s currents. And with the storm yesterday, there might be trees and logs in the lineup.”

Amy Graff is a Times reporter covering weather, wildfires and earthquakes.

Iran Attacks Bahrain for the Second Time in Days

The New York Times November 15, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The resumption of attacks after a two-month lull comes as peace talks between the U. S. and Iran appear to have stalled.

By Vivian Nereim and Aaron Boxerman

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Aaron Boxerman from Jerusalem.

Iran launched a drone attack on the Gulf Arab country of Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in days, as peace talks between the United States and Iran have faltered.

The Bahraini Defense Ministry said the country’s armed forces had intercepted several “Iranian aerial threats” before they struck their targets. Bahrain’s Interior Ministry also issued two alerts to residents on Sunday morning advising them to seek shelter.

There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed that Iranian forces had targeted a radar system at a Bahraini air base.

Bahrain hosts a major U. S. military base. The American military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday’s attack, which came two days after U. S. Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said it had shot down two drones fired by Iran toward Bahrain, without causing any injuries or damage.

The Revolutionary Guards said that Friday’s attack — which appeared to be the first time that Iran had targeted Bahrain since September — was retaliation for a previous American strike on a telecommunications tower in Iran.

After the U. S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran launched thousands of retaliatory missile and drone attacks at Gulf Arab countries that host American military installations. Those attacks had largely petered out as the two sides entered a stalemate.

The conflict has been deadlocked for months with few signs of progress toward a durable peace agreement between the United States and Iran. In the meantime, American and Israeli military officials have drawn up plans for renewed strikes that would likely target energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy according to U. S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

And in recent weeks, both sides have again exchanged fire around the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway in the Persian Gulf. The attacks have included sporadic U. S. bombing along Iran’s southern coast.

On Sunday, a spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, Esmaeil Baghaei, said that Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the United States or others.

Asked in a news conference in Tehran whether the Iranian attack in Bahrain signified a change to the country’s approach, and whether Iran was still awaiting an official American response in the negotiations, Mr. Baghaei said that Iran was “not waiting for anyone" and was focused on safeguarding its security.

President Trump has zigzagged over whether or not he might order a return to full-blown war. The initial campaign failed to compel Iran to abandon its nuclear program but did ensnarl global energy markets, which contributed to a resounding defeat for the Republican Party in the recent midterm elections.

It is far from clear whether a new U. S. or Israeli attack on Iran could force Tehran to make new concessions. The country has said it has rebuilt its military capabilities during the truce, and U. S. and Israeli officials will also have to consider whether they are willing or able to contend with Iranian missile and drone attacks across the Middle East, given their depleted stores of aerial interceptors.

Mediators from Qatar and Pakistan have shuttled to Tehran in recent weeks in an effort to avert a return to all-out war. Vice President JD Vance had backed the talks, as well as publicly blaming the war for Republican losses in the midterm elections.

Mr. Trump has now pulled Mr. Vance from the negotiations, writing on social media on Thursday that the United States does not need a deal with Iran.

“Those days,” he said, “have long since passed.”

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

The Big Questions About Jeffrey Epstein: What The Times Has Learned

The New York Times November 15, 2026

The Epstein Files

Advertisement

Supported by

By The New York Times

More than 60 Times journalists have delved into the life of the sexual predator whose secrets spurred an international reckoning over money, power and complicity. Leer en español

Few, if any, figures in recent history have caused as much legal, political, financial and reputational upheaval as Jeffrey Epstein. A convicted sex offender, Mr. Epstein was connected to many of the world’s richest and most influential people and institutions. He died in prison in 2019.

The public fascination with Mr. Epstein intensified after President Trump initially refused to release federal investigative records after pledging to do so. In late 2025 and early 2026, Congress and the Justice Department did release millions of pages of documents related to Mr. Epstein that have helped answer questions, though many mysteries remain.

The New York Times has been investigating Mr. Epstein’s finances, enablers and possible co-conspirators since his arrest on federal sex-trafficking charges in 2019. Based on our continuing reporting, here is what we know.

The most recent revelations about Mr. Epstein include:

One way Mr. Epstein kept finding new victims was by grooming young girls to bring other young girls, often their friends, to visit him. Very few of the women have talked publicly about doing so. Some had been labeled traffickers and conspirators. But that seemed wrong to Marina Lacerda, who was first brought by a friend to meet Mr. Epstein when she was 13 years old. Ms. Lacerdo talked openly with reporter Jen Percy about her experience, a story that she told over many hours of interviews this summer and that was corroborated by several other survivors and materials in the Epstein files.

Karyna Shuliak, 37, stands to inherit as much as $100 million from his estate, according to files released by federal authorities. A native of Belarus who met Mr. Epstein when she was 21, Ms. Shuliak has not been identified as one of his victims nor was she seen by federal authorities as a co-conspirator in his sex trafficking. He helped her in many ways, including her attaining U. S. citizenship and getting her into dental school.

Leon Botstein, who was forced to retire in June as the president of Bard College after revelations in Justice Department documents about his longstanding friendship with Mr. Epstein, resigned from all of his positions affiliated with the college on Oct. 7.

The resignation came as the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to Bard leaders saying that while Dr. Botstein was president, he “likely enabled and possibly even participated in” Mr. Epstein’s abuse. In a statement, Dr. Botstein called the allegations in the letter untrue and said he submitted his resignation “to protect Bard from any distraction.”

Links to all of our coverage can be found here.

Mr. Epstein has been accused by prosecutors and victims of raping, abusing and trafficking girls and young women. It was a vast, yearslong operation that involved:

In the mid-2000s, federal and state authorities identified more than a dozen such teenage girls in Florida. In many cases, Mr. Epstein’s longtime companion Ghislaine Maxwell recruited them under the pretense that they would be masseuses for a wealthy man at his mansion in Palm Beach.

Federal prosecutors later accused Mr. Epstein of abusing and trafficking dozens of girls at his townhouse in Manhattan, as well as in Palm Beach, from at least 2002 to 2005. He lured some by posing as a talent scout for Victoria’s Secret.

After he served time in a Florida jail for soliciting prostitution from a minor, Mr. Epstein appears to have shifted focus from underage victims to young women. He was often surrounded by aspiring models from Russia and Eastern Europe, some of whom later said they felt trapped under his control.

Some have accused several of those friends and associates of rape, though the men deny it.

They have accused him of raping or abusing them, including when they were girls — allegations that in some cases date to the early 1990s. At least one of those women, Virginia Giuffre, has died by suicide.

The federal government repeatedly missed opportunities to fully investigate or charge Mr. Epstein, until 2019. The missteps and lost opportunities included:

In 1996, Maria Farmer called the F. B. I. to tell the agency that Mr. Epstein had stolen nude photos of her underage sister. It ignored the tip for roughly a decade.

In 2005, the parents of a 14-year-old girl told the Palm Beach police that she had been paid to give a sexual massage to Mr. Epstein. That set off a state and federal investigation. While the authorities identified dozens of underage victims, the Justice Department — including the U. S. attorney for southern Florida at the time, Alexander Acosta — negotiated a deal: Mr. Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from just one minor.

The agreement also shielded any “potential co-conspirators,” including his female assistants, from prosecution. Though Mr. Epstein served his sentence in the county stockade, he was allowed to spend much of his jail time working from his office.

After being released early from his 18-month sentence, Mr. Epstein was welcomed back into elite society, attending parties, hosting dinners and continuing to do business with major financial institutions.

In the 2010s, a number of federal agencies, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, investigated Mr. Epstein, but he wasn’t charged.

In 2016, lawyers for some of Mr. Epstein’s victims urged federal prosecutors in New York to investigate him for sex trafficking. The prosecutors chose not to.

It wasn’t until 2018, after the newspaper wrote a series about the 2008 deal in Florida, that federal prosecutors in New York opened a criminal investigation. It culminated in Mr. Epstein’s being charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

Mr. Epstein did not grow up with wealth. He spent his formative years in an insular world, in Sea Gate, in Coney Island, which was then a mostly working- and middle-class Jewish refuge. But the picture of his boyhood we found contains the fuzzy outlines of his future self: From a young age, Epstein preferred the protective company of a tight group of brainy boys and fixated on girls.

As an adult, he amassed a nine-figure fortune through scams, fraud and the careful cultivation of billionaires and banks. His financial success involved:

Mr. Epstein’s first big break was landing a job at Bear Stearns in 1976. He eventually resigned after being caught improperly lending money to a client and violating rules around stock offerings, but he used the connections he forged there to jump-start his career as a financial trickster.

In the 1980s, Mr. Epstein, claiming to be a financial savant, engaged in a series of escalating scams.

In the late 1980s, a mutual acquaintance introduced him to Leslie Wexner, who ran the two retail companies. Mr. Wexner entrusted Mr. Epstein with full control over his finances before cutting ties with him around 2007. Mr. Wexner later said Mr. Epstein stole more than $100 million from him.

In 2012, Mr. Epstein began working for his longtime friend Leon Black, the co-founder of the private equity firm Apollo Global Management who said the money was for tax and estate planning work. Mr. Epstein also introduced Mr. Black to young women.

From the late 1990s through 2013, JPMorgan Chase, arguably the world’s most prestigious bank, serviced Mr. Epstein, despite employees’ concerns about his potential money laundering. In 2013, he switched to Deutsche Bank, which also ignored repeated red flags.

The combination of great wealth and a reputation for seeming to know everyone enabled Mr. Epstein to insinuate himself into the lives of important people in politics, business, the arts and academia. His strategy entailed:

As his fortune grew, Mr. Epstein made big donations to prestigious universities like Harvard and to individual scientists. The money led Nobel laureates and other leading intellectual figures to regularly socialize with and seek favor from him, and their presence helped grow his circle of influence.

Some of the doctors and others bent or broke the ethical rules of their profession, which allowed Mr. Epstein to offer perks to other acquaintances, like access to premier medical care, investment opportunities with hedge funds or a potential edge in school admissions.

Mr. Epstein’s vast Manhattan townhouse became the venue for regular dinner salons for an eclectic mix of artists, scientists, intellectuals, lawyers and businessmen. Visitors were greeted with photo arrays exhibiting Mr. Epstein’s ties to the ruling class.

One of his most valuable connections was to the former president. The relationship helped catapult Mr. Epstein into the public spotlight and secure his image as a whisperer to the rich and powerful.

Mr. Epstein also boasted extensive Wall Street connections to C. E. O. s (like James Cayne and Jes Staley); investment tycoons (like Glenn Dubin and Mr. Black); and powerful lawyers, like Brad Karp and Kathy Ruemmler. A secretive law firm would later try, and fail, to fix Ms. Ruemmler’s image. Ms Ruemmler told a House committee in July that Mr. Epstein “was a masterful liar.”

He had a long friendship with Stephen Hanson, a New York City restaurant mogul who performed an array of tasks for Mr. Epstein, including arranging jobs, visas and entertainment for women. And he collected high-profile friends and associates overseas, including Prince Andrew, the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak and top Norwegian politicians.

Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist, told a congressional committee in June that Mr. Epstein exploited information about his extramarital affairs “to pressure me to re-engage with him” after Mr. Gates had begun to sever ties with him.

Mr. Epstein was friends with Mr. Trump long before he became president, and he developed a relationship with Mr. Clinton during his time in the White House. Those relationships involved:

The two men became good friends in the late 1980s, hanging out together at casinos, Mr. Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate and other venues. A note and sexually suggestive drawing containing what appeared to be Mr. Trump’s signature was included in a 2003 book for Mr. Epstein’s birthday. Mr. Trump has denied writing the note.

Some of Mr. Epstein’s victims, including Ms. Giuffre, were recruited by Ms. Maxwell from Mr. Trump’s Florida club and residence, where Ms. Giuffre worked as a spa attendant. Mr. Trump said last year that he cut ties with Mr. Epstein in the early 2000s because he “stole” his female employees, although the relationship also deteriorated when the men fought over a piece of Florida real estate.

Shortly after Mr. Clinton was sworn in as president, Mr. Epstein made his first visit. Visitor logs show that he came back numerous times during Mr. Clinton’s first term, though it is unclear how often he met the president. In 1995, Mr. Clinton wrote a get-well-soon note to Mr. Epstein’s mother on a Post-it.

In 2002, after Mr. Clinton left the White House, Mr. Epstein flew him and others to several African countries. The trip was one of the first times that Mr. Epstein attracted significant media attention.

Mr. Epstein’s New York mansion showcased photos of him with each of them. When Mr. Trump became president, Mr. Epstein at times presented himself as someone who had inside knowledge about the administration, though it was most likely an act. Both Mr. Trump and Mr. Clinton have said they knew nothing about Mr. Epstein’s criminal activity.

Behind the scenes, the Epstein crisis was paralyzing the Trump administration to a far greater extent than the public knew. In their public statements, Trump’s advisers were full of bravado, dismissing the crisis. In reality, it was consuming the highest ranks of the administration.

Mr. Epstein’s inner circle and the financiers and banks that enabled him faced allegations of wrongdoing. But U. S. prosecutors charged only one person other than Mr. Epstein. The legal trail included:

She is the only person other than Mr. Epstein to face criminal charges in the United States. In 2021, she was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Some Republicans have expressed support for the idea that President Trump would pardon her.

In the months after Mr. Epstein’s death, federal authorities investigated a number of Mr. Epstein’s former personal assistants, who were accused by some victims of participating in his sex-trafficking operation. Prosecutors considered charging at least one, but they ultimately opted not to, perhaps because she said she was also one of Mr. Epstein’s victims.

Federal prosecutors apparently didn’t interview or subpoena Mr. Wexner, Mr. Black and Mr. Epstein’s longtime accountant Richard Kahn and lawyer Darren Indyke. A federal document described Mr. Wexner as a co-conspirator, though his spokesman denied that the government ever considered him one.

But the House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas to Mr. Black in June, and in September, held him in criminal contempt of Congress over not responding — a move that amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black.

Federal authorities interviewed women who accused Mr. Black and Mr. Staley, a former top JPMorgan executive, of sexual misconduct — allegations that both men deny. Prosecutors relayed those accusations to officials in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which did not bring charges.

As part of their investigations into Mr. Epstein, federal prosecutors subpoenaed the two banks that provided him with the greatest financial support, JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank. The prosecutors appeared to have quickly decided against charging either institution with wrongdoing.

Police departments and prosecutors in some other countries recently have taken a more aggressive approach. In Britain, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, and Peter Mandelson, a former top government official, have been arrested in connection with Epstein investigations. Neither has been charged.

We are tracking that fallout here.

Mr. Epstein spent 36 days at the now-shuttered Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City before he was found dead in his cell on Aug. 10, 2019. The medical examiner ruled his death a suicide.

For the most in-depth investigation yet into his death, we consulted tens of thousands of pages of newly released documents, obtained Mr. Epstein’s own notes handwritten in jail — never before made public — and interviewed dozens of people related to the case. We found abundant evidence that for weeks before his death, Mr. Epstein had written about and discussed the idea of suicide and attempted it at least once, and possibly three times.

The circumstances around his death include:

Mr. Epstein was found unresponsive with a cloth tied around his neck in his cell two and a half weeks before his death. He denied trying to take his own life, but he was psychologically evaluated and placed on suicide watch for barely a day.

The cellmate, Nicholas Tartaglione, said the note was written by Mr. Epstein. It was sealed by a federal court for years. The Times successfully petitioned the court to unseal the note in May 2026. It has not been authenticated but bears similarities to known writings by Mr. Epstein.

As one of the highest-profile federal inmates, Mr. Epstein was supposed to be under close supervision and to have a cellmate. But he was left alone in a cell on the evening of Aug. 9, 2019. Other inmates reported to jail authorities that he was despondent.

Guards were supposed to make regular rounds to check on prisoners. But on Mr. Epstein’s last night, the two guards on duty in his area stayed by their desks. The guards were criminally charged, but the charges were withdrawn as part of a deferred prosecution agreement.

Mr. Epstein was found unconscious early on the morning of Aug. 10 with a strip of orange bedding cinched around his neck. He was soon pronounced dead, in what was later ruled a suicide.

From virtually the moment his death was announced, there have been doubts and unfounded speculation about the circumstances. His brother, Mark Epstein, is among those who don’t believe he killed himself. The Department of Justice re-examined the death in 2023 and found no evidence of a conspiracy or criminality.

The phrase usually refers to the millions of Epstein investigation documents that Congress directed the Justice Department to release. But there have been more. Over the years, all three branches of the U. S. government have released records, and media outlets, including The Times, have obtained documents through leaks or public records requests. The materials include:

In August 2019, a federal appeals court unsealed one of the first main caches of Epstein-related files, part of a defamation lawsuit brought against Ms. Maxwell by Ms. Giuffre, one of Mr. Epstein’s most outspoken victims. The files included depositions, photos, flight logs and other materials that gave the public a powerful glimpse into Mr. Epstein’s crimes and network. The morning after the files were unsealed, he was found dead in his jail cell.

The trove of documents dribbled into public view in 2023 during a court fight between the U. S. Virgin Islands and the bank. Those files showed the chummy relationships between Mr. Epstein and senior bank executives.

In 2025, The Times obtained thousands of Mr. Epstein’s photos and documents, which showed the inside of his Upper East Side mansion — including surveillance cameras in his bedroom area — and some of his correspondence with men like Woody Allen and Mr. Black.

Bloomberg News published several articles based on thousands of emails from Mr. Epstein’s Yahoo account. Those emails and others were later posted for public perusal on a site called Jmail.

After taking office in 2025, Mr. Trump backtracked on his earlier pledges to release the government’s files on Mr. Epstein. That led to a political uproar. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which required the administration to release its files. In December and January, the Justice Department released millions of pages of records.

The Justice Department said it decided not to release many other records, because they would identify victims or could jeopardize ongoing federal investigations. Other documents appeared to simply be missing. That has stoked speculation about a possible coverup.

The Justice Department blacked out the names of some government lawyers or potential co-conspirators. It failed to protect victims’ names and included nude photos of potential victims. The Justice Department’s internal watchdog is now investigating whether the department’s disclosures followed the law.
