Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.

The New York Times November 15, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.

By Tripp MickleAna SwansonPaul MozurJonathan SwanJulian E. Barnes and Maggie Haberman

The reporters have been covering U. S. intelligence claims of China’s spying on Nvidia and America’s artificial intelligence industry.

Jensen Huang was agitated.

It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U. S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.

Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, set off a cascade of events that have reverberated from Silicon Valley to Washington to Beijing. Administration officials are now reconsidering A. I. export regulations, which could hurt some Silicon Valley businesses but tilt the A. I. race with China decidedly in America’s favor.

It has also brought into public view a feud among several senior administration officials and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that his department had been pushing Commerce for months to crack down on the flow of U. S. technology to China.

Now Nvidia, which was in many ways propping up the A. I. boom, which, in turn, was propping up the U. S. economy, is operating without a man many consider to be one of the most indispensable executives in the history of American business.

This is the story — based on a year of reporting, documents and discussions with more than 100 people, including current and former Nvidia executives and government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity — of how Mr. Huang’s secret slowly spilled into the open.

Last fall, business was booming for Nvidia. Its soaring stock price had it within a whisper of becoming the world’s first $5 trillion company.

Mr. Huang joined Mr. Trump in September for a formal state dinner at Windsor Castle hosted by King Charles III. Mr. Trump lavished praise on Mr. Huang at a gathering of business and tech leaders hosted by Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

“You’re taking over the world, Jensen,” Mr. Trump said.

But at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., some of Mr. Huang’s advisers were wrestling with The Times’s questions about Megaspeed. The company had purchased more than $2 billion of Nvidia technology in a year, making it one of the largest buyers of A. I. chips in Southeast Asia.

It was an example of the kind of middlemen popping up across the region. Companies like Megaspeed were legally buying American chips and building A. I. data centers that rented computing power to Chinese companies. But the U. S. government suspected that some, including Megaspeed, were breaking the law by funneling chips to China.

Nvidia’s sales from Singapore were swelling. By last summer, the island city-state accounted for 22 percent of the company’s quarterly total sales, or $10 billion, making it the second-largest chip buying region after the United States.

Over the previous two years, Mr. Huang had been seen twice with Ms. Huang in public at industry gatherings. She waited behind him patiently in a pink dress as he passed out noodles from a restaurant in Taipei to onlookers and spoke to the Taiwanese press. Then she climbed into the car with him to be shuttled away.

A senior Nvidia official told The Times that the dinner attended by Mr. Huang, Ms. Huang and several industry executives was a “business dinner.”

On another occasion, Ms. Huang was chatting at an industry party at a Taipei bar when she offered to ask Mr. Huang to join them. “She said, ‘I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,’ and then Jensen immediately showed up,” said Parker Schmitt, who is chief executive of NetThunder, a data software provider. Shortly after, Mr. Huang arrived and drank a whiskey shot with the group. He left the party, which he’d been invited to, shortly afterward with two other Nvidia executives who had joined him.

After the article about Megaspeed and Mr. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang appeared that October, Nvidia changed how it reported geographic sales. Singapore vanished from its financial disclosures as it started reporting sales based on “customers’ headquarters” rather than “billing location.” The company had previously said that large customers billed through Singapore, where taxes can be lower, but that products “are almost always shipped elsewhere.”

Late that month, Mr. Huang took a convention center stage in Washington in his signature leather jacket and black jeans. He trumpeted his company’s lead in A. I. chips and praised Mr. Trump for focusing on increasing the nation’s energy supplies. He thanked everyone for their work “making America great again.”

The next day, as Mr. Trump was flying to South Korea to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping, the president told reporters he was planning to speak to Mr. Xi about Nvidia’s most advanced A. I. chip, known as Blackwell.

Some people in government interpreted Mr. Trump’s comments as a signal that he might lift prohibitions on China’s access to America’s best technology — an outcome that could be a boon to Nvidia’s business, even as it flew in the face of longstanding policy goals to limit China’s access to American technology and protect America’s lead in artificial intelligence. (A White House spokesman declined to comment.)

The possibilities were huge for Mr. Huang. Though Mr. Trump had cleared the company to sell some of its lower-performing chips to China, Beijing had banned tech companies from buying them. The offer of Blackwell chips had the potential to break that impasse.

But after Cabinet officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U. S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, objected on national security grounds, Mr. Trump abandoned the idea.

Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about how American spy agencies had surveillance of Ms. Huang, the Megaspeed executive, whom they had determined was passing information to Chinese intelligence services. The surveillance revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Mr. Huang.

It was an alarming development for national security officials who long worried that Mr. Huang was too nonchalant about concerns that his chips could fall into the hands of the Chinese military or intelligence.

Though Mr. Trump chose not to do anything with the information, it raised questions inside the U. S. government about Mr. Huang’s judgment. It also raised the possibility that Ms. Huang may have gathered insight through Mr. Huang into Mr. Trump’s thinking on artificial intelligence, a vital issue of importance to Washington and Beijing.

For reasons that remain unknown, government officials didn’t tell Mr. Huang about the intelligence. Law enforcement officials sometimes warn Americans who are being targeted by a foreign government’s intelligence service — a practice known as a “defensive briefing.” In weighing whether to give such a warning, officials typically consider the risks of tipping off the target of their own surveillance, which in this case would have been Megaspeed’s Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang didn’t abandon his vision of selling chips to China. He continued to argue that that would make Chinese companies depend on American technology and create competition for China’s tech giant, Huawei. It would also be good for his business.

In December, he returned to Washington to press his case. He met with Mr. Trump at the White House and proposed selling a less powerful chip to China. Known as the H200, it was a generation older than the Blackwell, which was limited to the United States.

Mr. Trump was open to the idea, but he wanted something in return: a 25 percent cut for the U. S. government of any chips sold to China. Mr. Huang agreed.

By March, pre-purchase orders from Chinese customers were rolling in. At the company’s annual conference in San Jose, Calif., Mr. Huang told a hotel ballroom packed with more than 100 reporters and influencers, including a woman who refers to herself as the “A. I. princess,” that Nvidia was receiving purchase commitments from China and starting to manufacture chips to sell.

In Washington, Mr. Rubio started to put together an update about the surveillance of Ms. Huang. The classified memo, based on highly sensitive intelligence, outlined Ms. Huang’s close relationship with the Nvidia founder and her contacts with China’s civilian spy agency, the Ministry of State Security.

The memo was circulated to only a handful of Cabinet officials. It was sent as the administration made plans for the president to visit Beijing in May for a summit with Mr. Xi. When it came time to extend invitations to more than a dozen chief executives for the trip, Mr. Huang was left off the list.

But with little warning, Mr. Trump, who had seen news coverage of Mr. Huang’s exclusion, asked the Nvidia executive to meet up with Air Force One at a refueling stop in Alaska.

When Mr. Rubio learned of the invitation, while en route to Alaska, he briefed the president on the intelligence showing Mr. Huang had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset. Mr. Trump was not particularly moved by the information. Instead, he celebrated Mr. Huang with a social media post after the chief executive boarded the plane, saying it was an honor to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip to China.

On the ground in Beijing, Mr. Trump said he discussed sales of Nvidia chips to China with Mr. Xi. The Chinese government had been reluctant to give its approval to purchases of the less advanced H200 chips. But the conversation didn’t appear to persuade China to allow its companies to buy the Nvidia chips.

Some officials in Washington worried that Mr. Huang, to break the impasse, would push for approval to sell the more advanced Blackwells.

During Nvidia’s all-hands meeting in August, he was asked what he considered to be Nvidia’s greatest risk.

“It’s Washington, D. C.,” he said. “Policies that are made that are uninformed affect us, and they could affect us in a business way, and that could be irritating and frustrating.”

Midway through the meeting, his phone buzzed.

“There are only two people in the world that can call me,” he said. “One of them is President Trump.”

He picked up Mr. Trump’s call and stepped away.

Mr. Huang didn’t know it, but his secret was starting to spill.

Late last month, The Times reached out to Nvidia for comment on a report that would publicly reveal for the first time that Ms. Huang was being surveilled. U. S. intelligence had believed she was an asset for Chinese intelligence who was feeding information to Beijing and was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang. (Among U. S. intelligence and national security officials, the relationship was routinely described more pointedly as an affair. )

Even after The Times reported in October 2025 that Megaspeed was under investigation for smuggling chips into China, Nvidia had kept doing business with the company. And Mr. Huang had kept up his relationship with Ms. Huang, according to U. S. officials who reviewed the intelligence.

Megaspeed’s sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced A. I. equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology from June 2024 to February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius, a trade platform.

Mr. Huang told people around him that it was the first time he was learning that the U. S. government had been tracking his relationship with Ms. Huang.

Nvidia insisted that the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims that the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China.

(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Mr. Huang jumped to his own defense. In an interview with Bloomberg News, he said that his interactions with Ms. Huang had been “all completely normal and not unusual.”

Other outlets jumped on the story. Nvidia roped in Heller, the crisis communications firm that had been working for the Huang family since early 2025, to help once again. The company represents high-profile individuals, with past clients including Harvey Weinstein and Anthony Weiner, as well as the business side of The Times.

On Nov. 6, The Times reported on Mr. Rubio’s memo and said U. S. intelligence had identified her as working with the Chinese intelligence service.

Later that night, The Financial Times reported the U. S. government believed Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman was romantic. Nvidia declined to comment.

Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, who had been defending Mr. Huang, went to Mr. Huang’s house in Woodside, Calif. Mr. Huang confessed, said people familiar with the events that night.

Madison, his daughter, was flying to South Korea at the time. She was scheduled to participate in an A. I. event and meet local dignitaries. But the moment she landed, she was told the news and encouraged to fly back home.

Mr. Huang’s betrayal caused deep pain inside Nvidia. His family — including Madison; his son, Spencer; and son-in-law Nico Caprez — worked in prominent roles at the company. He had been married to Lori Huang for more than 40 years.

After Mr. Huang’s confession, Mr. Teter urged Nvidia’s board to act. The board and Mr. Huang separately drafted public statements. The board said it “had full confidence in Jensen,” even as it planned to hire an outside law firm to investigate the matter.

Mr. Huang apologized in a message to the company. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

He promised that he would earn back the confidence of employees and the board. Privately, he assured people around him, including Mr. Teter, who spoke with the board, that there were no other infidelities.

Bloomberg News earlier reported on Mr. Teter’s visit. The Information, a technology news site, earlier reported on the board’s deliberations.

Over the next few days, Mr. Huang received texts and calls of encouragement from friends, such as Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and the financier Larry Fink. President Trump also called him on Tuesday with a word of advice: Fight.

Some allies began to make plans to turn the tide. Mr. Huang told many of them that the woman wasn’t a spy. She was just a business customer.

But four days later, The Times contacted the company and Mr. Huang about another affair. This one was with a woman who directly reported to him, Kimberly Powell, a 48-year-old who led Nvidia’s health division. The two had been caught on camera in an affectionate moment during Nvidia’s annual conference in San Jose.

The company declined to comment. Mr. Huang, who was reached by phone, said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” Then, he hung up.

After the news broke, the 10-member board called an emergency meeting. Members called in from remote locations and deliberated over a decision none of them ever thought they would have to make.

The revelation of another infidelity showed that Mr. Huang, who had extolled the company’s code of conduct rules over the years, had been violating them. First, there was the relationship with a customer. Then, there was the relationship with an employee.

But in the world of corporate governance, the worst thing a chief executive can do is lie, especially in a crisis. It is a reason they get fired.

On Thursday morning, the company said Mr. Huang had resigned. The board had named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive officer.

Mr. Huang would have to surrender his life’s work.

In a series of extensive interviews last month with Emily Chang of Bloomberg TV, Mr. Huang acknowledged it was a high pressure role that required sacrifice.

“It should not be an easy job,” he said. “It shouldn’t be a job you take for granted.”

He added that he hoped to be with the company for another 20 years.

Ryan Mac, Georgia Gee and Kalley Huang contributed reporting.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Defeating MAGA Is Only Half Done

The New York Times November 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

David French

By David French

Opinion Columnist

The Republican Party has not learned its lesson.

Consider what’s happened since Nov. 3, when it faced the largest midterm electoral rebuke that any party has received since at least 1974.

President Trump elevated Stephen Miller to chief of staff, the man who is more responsible than any other person aside from Trump for the brutal immigration crackdown that may have alienated Hispanic voters for a generation.

House Republicans made Jim Jordan of Ohio the new minority leader. Jordan, for those who don’t follow these things closely, is one of the most pugilistic MAGA hatchet men in Congress, a “backroom brawler,” in the words of an Ohio Republican operative named Bob Kish. As The Columbus Dispatch observed, “In nearly 20 years in Congress, Jordan has not been the lead sponsor of a bill that became law.”

He is, however, a fixture on Fox News.

The White House and the Department of Justice have threatened Democrats with legal consequences if they investigate the rampant corruption endemic to the Trump administration. The very idea is preposterous. As the Supreme Court explained almost 100 years ago, “the power of inquiry — with process to enforce it — is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function.”

House Republicans wrapped both arms around Pete Hegseth, protecting him from impeachment (for now), even though he has violated the Constitution, violated the laws of armed conflict and helped plan and execute a blatantly unconstitutional war against Iran.

But perhaps nothing sums up the state of the Republican Party better than the report that Trump tried to stop Jensen Huang from stepping down as the chief executive of Nvidia, even as reports of multiple deeply troublesome affairs emerged, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

A call from one serial adulterer to another. Game recognizes game, I suppose.

For critics of MAGA, there are two ways of looking at these events. In the flush of victory, it might be tempting to smile or to even feel a small sense of glee. A Republican Party that’s learned nothing is a party that’s likely to keep losing — and to keep losing for the same reasons.

Hold on to the Trump roller coaster for two more years, minimize the damage as best you can and reap even greater electoral rewards in 2028.

That certainly might happen. In fact, it’s probably going to happen. What the Trump administration lacks in venality, it makes up for in incompetence, and it’s hard to see it substantially improving its fortunes before 2028.

But I have a different view: namely, that we shouldn’t delight in these failures so much as pray for the G. O. P. to come to its senses. No matter what happened on Nov. 3 (or what happens in 2028), American politics will be deeply unstable until there is an ideological and moral renaissance in the Republican Party.

In the absence of that renaissance, populist kleptocrats and brutal bigots will be the only alternative for voters who may become disappointed with Democrats. Our military alliances will always be one election away from peril, and the integrity of the Department of Justice will hang on the outcome of every election.

If you spend any time watching right-wing media or following right-wing accounts online, you’ll know that MAGA has settled on one message to explain the midterm wipeout: It’s the neocons’ fault. The establishment holdovers from the dreaded George W. Bush years coaxed or coerced the president into the ruinous Iran war, and without the Iran war, everything would have been just fine.

So what’s the solution? Double down on MAGA and “America first” until the last molecules of the old Republican Party have been swept away.

This is the reasoning that gives us Miller as the White House chief of staff.

This narrative isn’t just wrong; it’s idiotic. Trump’s approval rating was trending downward well before the Iran war, and the collapse in support from Hispanic voters was almost certainly a result, in large part, of the administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, perhaps the signature issue of the MAGA movement.

In reality, the time has perhaps never been riper for a conservative comeback.

But first, we have to define our terms. Trump is not a conservative. It might even pay him too much of a compliment to call him a populist; that would imply that he has anything that approaches a coherent ideology. In reality, Trumpism is nothing more than the attitude and impulses of one man, whatever they may be.

Certainly there are those who’ve tried to construct an ideology around Trump — JD Vance among them — and those people explicitly reject the ideology of the old G. O. P. They call it the dead consensus and have essentially sawed off every single leg of the old Republican stool.

The party is now less socially conservative. The G. O. P. watered down its commitment to the pro-life cause while countless Republicans celebrated (and even emulated) the conduct of perhaps the most cruel and hedonistic man ever to occupy the Oval Office.

Republicans are now weak in the face of our most dangerous enemies. I could never have imagined the day when a Republican president would side with the Russian aggressor over a nation that’s defending itself against impossible odds.

Republicans are now embracing central planning and a command economy. The Trump administration scorns free trade, unilaterally imposes illegal tariffs and takes ownership stakes in dozens of companies.

If Trumpism isn’t conservatism, then what is conservatism? George Will, the dean of conservative columnists, defined it well: The object of conservatism is to preserve the founding principles and institutions of the United States, including its ethos and its Constitution.

I can think of few better paths back to popularity for Republicans than to adopt Will’s formulation. In fact, constitutional conservatism can be among the most effective ways to combat the least popular aspects of Trumpism.

A constitutional conservative would propose legislative reform to take back the tariff authority from the president and put it back where it belongs: with Congress. This reform would help restore the balance of power between Congress and the president while also providing immediate relief to American families affected by tariffs.

A constitutional conservative would combat our nation’s terrible tendency to be too ready to resort to military force by restoring and enforcing Congress’s sole authority to declare war (and impeaching a secretary of defense who violated the Constitution).

A constitutional conservative would defend civil liberties from a Trumpist onslaught that has caused immense human suffering across the land. Due process has taken a beating in Trump’s immigration crackdown. Freedom of speech is under threat as he targets those he sees as his political enemies.

A constitutional conservative would also recognize the central role of the United States in preserving the global order that has prevented a third world war and would help an embattled friend and partner keep the Russian bear at bay.

And a constitutional conservative would defend the ethos of the founding — which recognizes the inherent dignity of all people — by remembering the fundamentally inclusive nature of the American experiment.

As James Madison said in his “Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments,” he opposed a bill establishing a tax to support Christian teaching, in part because it was “a departure from that generous policy, which, offering an asylum to the persecuted and oppressed of every nation and religion, promised a luster to our country, and an accession to the number of its citizens.”

There, in the words of the man who was indispensable to the creation of our very system of government, is a decisive rebuke to the nativism and bigotry of the MAGA right.

Conservatives don’t have to change themselves to oppose Trump and reach the millions of Americans who’ve rejected the Republican Party. They simply have to, at long last, be themselves again.

Therein lies the rub. Ten years of Trump have so divorced the Republican Party from any sense of ethics — or any coherent ideology — that for many people, the conservatism of even the recent past feels liberal. It feels woke.

Appeals to human dignity? A reverence for basic human rights? Preservation of liberal democracy abroad? It all sounds so squishy. And besides, if we go down that path, won’t millions of (ugh) Democrats agree?

In fact, I daresay that a majority of the readers of this column — liberal and conservative alike — agree with most (and perhaps even all) of the constitutional-conservative policy ideas I articulated above.

But that’s precisely the point. There is nothing wrong with consensus when that consensus is just. In fact — and this sounds so painfully obvious that it almost hurts me to type — doing popular things that are consistent with its principles is one way that a party attains (and keeps) power. It’s one way that it can climb out of the hole that it’s dug for itself.

But to act in a way that’s consistent with its principles, a party has to have principles. And that means that Republicans who want to revive the party without confronting or defying Trump are fooling themselves. There is no path back to decency — or to constitutional governance — without defeating MAGA.

And as much as Democrats might recognize that Republican dysfunction is their electoral opportunity, don’t forget the past 10 years. Trump has been Trump for a very long time, and he still won the presidency twice — including after he inspired a violent attack on the U. S. Capitol. Do not presume that MAGA won’t win again.

The stage has been set for a Republican civil war, and every American should be rooting for the revival of a decent, conservative Republican Party.

Our nation’s future may depend on it.

David French is an Opinion columnist, writing about law, culture, religion and armed conflict. He is a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom and a former constitutional litigator. His most recent book is “Divided We Fall: America’s Secession Threat and How to Restore Our Nation.” You can follow him on Threads (@davidfrenchjag).

Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap With His Family Business

The New York Times November 15, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm.

By Ana SwansonAaron Krolik and Paul Mozur

Ana Swanson reported from Washington, Aaron Krolik from New York and Paul Mozur from Taiwan.

In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U. S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A. I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A. I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A. I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U. S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U. S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

Cantor Fitzgerald has had business dealings with several data center companies in Southeast Asia that cater to Chinese clients, and could be affected by the regulations Mr. Lutnick is drafting, a review by The New York Times has found.

Cantor Fitzgerald served as a designated sales agent for an equity offering of up to $1 billion this year by Bitdeer, the Singaporean firm that will operate data center A201, in addition to having other financial ties to various global data center businesses. The relationship between the two companies began as early as 2024, when Cantor Fitzgerald helped Bitdeer arrange a stock offering of up to $250 million.

Mr. Lutnick steered Cantor Fitzgerald for decades, before recusing himself when he joined the Trump administration last year. The Commerce Department says Mr. Lutnick has complied with all ethics agreements, and his former business is now run by his sons.

These dealings are just a tiny portion of Cantor’s business, which stretches from investment banking and trading to real estate. Other investment banks have similar partnerships, and there is no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced Mr. Lutnick’s deliberations.

But the overlapping relationships are the latest indication of the potential conflicts that exist given Mr. Lutnick’s role in shaping rules around U. S. technology exports. And they demonstrate how the U. S. ban on selling chips directly to China has led to an explosion of data centers in Southeast Asia aimed at Chinese customers. It is now up to Mr. Lutnick to decide whether to tighten the rules in ways that would cut off this avenue.

In the administration, Mr. Lutnick has been seen as one of Nvidia’s strongest champions.

His department has been increasingly criticized in recent months for giving Nvidia unusual access to rule-making and investigations, and standing in the way of sanctions on Nvidia’s customers.

The issue has been thrust into the spotlight in recent weeks with the scandal over the Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman the U. S. government deemed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The woman, Alice Huang, had led Megaspeed, a firm that set up data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese companies. The U. S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling chips into China.

The United States in late 2022 started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.

But while Chinese firms cannot buy Nvidia’s most advanced chips outright, nothing stops them from renting those chips in data centers in Malaysia, Indonesia or Thailand.

The arrangement is viewed by many in Washington as a harmful loophole. While some argue that the sales help U. S. leadership in technology, many in the administration have argued for clamping down, and Congress is considering a bipartisan bill to do so.

In its final weeks, the Biden administration issued global rules to restrict the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access U. S. chips. But President Trump revoked those rules when he came into office, arguing that they stifled American business and innovation.

Trump officials said they would introduce a new rule to replace the Biden ones. But they have struggled to reconcile competing views in the administration about how aggressive the rules should be.

Mr. Lutnick has been described as delaying or deferring these technology controls at several points in the past year, arguing that they could affect companies like Nvidia, or U. S. trade relations with China and other countries.

People familiar with the discussions say the Commerce Department has pushed for a more scaled-back version of the rule. The department has proposed applying regulations to a handful of countries — Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa and Norway. Others in the administration have wanted global coverage.

The proposal was first reported by The Information.

The Commerce Department proposal would also apply only to future shipments of advanced chips, exempting data centers already filled with American technology. Companies would need to notify the government if Chinese customers use their data centers to train A. I. models. But they would not automatically need to obtain a license.

The Commerce Department had also argued for the rules to kick in when companies are using a larger amount of computing power, meaning fewer activities by Chinese companies would be regulated.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official, predicted that Chinese companies would find ways to sidestep the more narrow controls the Commerce Department is proposing.

“If you’re only restricting remote access to data centers in certain countries, then China will just rent from the data centers outside those countries,” he said.

Nvidia had been one of Cantor’s largest stock positions early last year, but last fall, the firm began steadily selling off shares. Cantor holds those shares on behalf of clients, not as part of its proprietary investment portfolio.

Still, Cantor Fitzgerald continued to help arrange billions of dollars of financing for industries ranging from data centers to cryptocurrency that depend on a steady supply of computing from Nvidia.

That includes Bitdeer, which is building out the Malaysian data center it expects to generate $1.7 billion in revenue over five years, according to a company statement.

That data center will likely serve Tencent, a Chinese internet giant that would be able to gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced A. I. servers, according to a person with knowledge of the arrangement. Bitdeer is part of Nvidia’s partner network, a program for companies that work closely with the chipmaker.

Bitdeer hosts a Chinese language website that lets customers rent A. I. chips and gain access to Chinese open source A. I. models through data centers in Malaysia, Canada and elsewhere. The Johor facility is one of five data centers the company plans to open in Malaysia in the coming years, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Cantor holds a stake in Bitdeer through its investment in Tether, the crypto company. It is far from the only American financial heavyweight investing in overseas data centers. Bain Capital, Citadel and Blackstone have all poured money into A. I. computing clusters across the region.

Cantor also previously provided financial services to Gorilla Technology, which is building data centers in Thailand and Indonesia, and has a contract to provide A. I. computing to Freyr AI, a Singaporean data center firm that corporate filings and job ads indicate has ties to China.

Cantor has worked with other Nvidia partners globally, including IREN, an Australian cloud computing company, and Lancium, a Texas data center developer.

A Commerce Department spokeswoman said that Mr. Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, nor do they discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him, she added.

Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment. Bitdeer did not reply to a request for comment.

Mr. Lutnick, as of October 2025, transferred his remaining ownership stake in Cantor to his family. Before that, he had been given what the White House had called a “limited waiver” that allowed him to participate in certain decisions that could have “a direct and predictable effect on Cantor Fitzgerald,” exempting him from a federal criminal law that would otherwise have required him to entirely recuse himself from these discussions.

Even after Mr. Lutnick finished transferring his ownership stake to his sons late last year, he still had to abide by an ethics rule prohibiting federal employees from using their public office for their private gain or the gain of friends and relatives.

The Times reported last year that Mr. Lutnick was promoting data center projects that worked with his family firms. Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, and two dozen other Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation.

Maggie Haberman and Eric Lipton contributed reporting.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

I’ve Tested Dozens of Planners. These Are the Best Ones

Wired November 15, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

There’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

The world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.

Roterunner

Shop (B5)

Amazon (B5)

Amazon (A5)

Shop (A5)

If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

Hobonichi

Amazon (Techo, January 2027 Start)

Amazon (Cousin, January 2027 Start)

If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

Cloth & Paper

Shop (Single Notebook, A5 Slim)

Shop (Clear Vinyl Cover, A5 Slim)

Shop (Travel Notebook Set, A5 Alim)

I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

Erin Condren

Amazon (2027 LifePlanner)

Erin Condren (Academic Planner)

I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”

Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

Kokuyo

Shop (A5 First Kit 2027)

Kokuyo (A5 First Kit 2027)

The Kokuyo Jibun Techo is another Japanese planner, but this one is a travel-notebook-style design, making it more customizable with a cover and multiple books that fit inside it. The First Kit comes with three books that fit into the included cover: Diary (labeled simply with the year), Life, and Idea. The 2026 versions are sold out, but you can buy the 2027 versions right now.

Big A## Planner

Shop (2027 Planner)

Looking for more of a monthly planner? The Big A## Planner is a massive planner with a nice monthly spread you can literally spread across your desk, with plenty of writing space for each day. Best for working from home, though; you don't want to have to fit this into your work bag.

Day Designer

Shop

Amazon

If you're looking for a great daily planner, the Day Designer is a popular option for a reason. It's bulky since it has pages for every single day, but it leaves room for both your schedule and a long to-do list.

Plum Paper

Plum Paper (A5 Vertical Priorities)

Plum Paper is my favorite classic-style planner, and you can easily customize it to start at any time of year and design the pages to fit your needs. I especially like the weekly A5 Vertical Priorities layout, and you can add all kinds of customizations into the daily columns, the habit tracker, and more to make it exactly what you want. But I've also left the habit tracker blank so I can adjust my habits as needed all year long.

Lemome

Amazon

I bought this no-frills hardback during Prime Day last year, figuring I couldn’t go wrong for less than 20 bucks, and I was right. It’s a handy A5 size with a monthly view calendar at the beginning of each month, and then a 5-by-2.5-inch square for each day. That’s it. There are some plain lined pages in the back if you need more space for notes, but if your planning consists only of to-do lists and tracking deadlines, you will love this.—Kat Merck

Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

Ban. do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban. do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

Laurel Denise

Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

Leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

Papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson

Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Midori

Amazon

Amazon

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

Up&Up

Target (100-Pack)

One of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

Why Choose a Paper Planner?

Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

What Sizes Do Planners Come In?

Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.

AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove

Wired November 15, 2026

I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.

YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.

More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to users and adding more controls over the commentary.

These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.

After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:

“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”

What a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.

In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.

Curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding new voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.

Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.

Spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.

Although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the company’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.

Review: Evercade Nexus

Wired November 15, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming. With a stable of reliable hardware, from the original Evercade handheld to the Evercade Alpha bartop arcade cabinet, it offers numerous ways to play, all built around an ever-expanding library of physical cartridges. Each brings a curated selection of classic titles and lost curiosities to modern players.

The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup. While it retains compatibility with every previously released Evercade cartridge, it’s also the biggest leap forward the line has taken so far, both in hardware and in what it might offer with games going forward. It’s a real level up—and it’s rather brilliant.

The most obvious change is the sheer size. Where Blaze’s previous handhelds were about on par with the original Game Boy Advance, aimed at pocketable play, the Evercade Nexus is closer in scale to a Nintendo Switch Lite. It measures 215 x 111 x 34 millimeters and weighs 410 grams—still easily portable, but more in the “buy a protective hard case and throw it in your bag” kind of way.

The size increase works in its favor, though. The larger design feels more substantial, with more real estate for your hands for better comfort. The control layout remains broadly the same as the Evercade EXP—a D-pad, ABXY face buttons, shoulder buttons, and triggers all return, with a few beneficial tweaks. Notably, the triggers are now chunkier and curved to meet your fingers, while all four shoulder inputs and the rear of the device are now nicely textured for better grip.

Evercade Nexus

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The big change is the addition of twin symmetrical thumbsticks. This has implications for Evercade going forward—more on that later—but it also improves Tate Mode (pronounced tah-tay, meaning vertical in Japanese), a returning feature from the Evercade EXP. As on that model, tapping the dedicated mode-shift button rotates the screen 90 degrees, letting you play vertically scrolling arcade games in the intended orientation, rather than crammed into a tiny pillar-boxed view on the widescreen display.

On the EXP, you’d hold the console on the left to use the D-pad for movement, which required duplicate A+B buttons on that side and cluttered the inputs. On the Nexus, Tate Mode rotates in the opposite direction, letting you use the right-hand thumbstick and the default ABXY buttons. It feels much better—again aided by the increased overall size—and keeps the device's design looking much tidier.

Whichever orientation you play in, the screen is bigger—a 5.89-inch IPS panel with an 840 × 512-pixel resolution for a 167 pixels-per-inch density, versus the original's 4.3-inch LCD—and brighter, now boasting 500-plus nits. It’s clear and colorful, and games look fantastic on it.

The only minor build-quality demerits are the D-pad, which feels a little too raised and prone to rocking—a slightly more flush fit would have been better—and the glossy finish under the face buttons and around the front trim. These accents are aesthetically pleasing, standing out from the matte plastic of the rest of the unit, but they attract micro-scratches far too easily. Those small gripes aside, the Nexus is a huge improvement on its predecessors, feeling less like a quirky gadget and more like a serious, modern gaming handheld.

The Nexus doesn’t actually see any boosts in processor power or memory. It still uses the 1.5-GHz quad-core chip in the EXP with 512 MB of RAM. That may not sound like much in 2026, but it’s significantly more powerful than the original hardware it emulates, and it ensures Evercade’s universal cross-device compatibility for every cartridge.

The downside is that the Nexus still feels slow at the system level. Booting it up takes about 35 to 40 seconds on average, and it can take about the same to load up a cartridge. Games don't have any performance issues, but getting there is sluggish. Disappointingly, there’s also no quick-suspend feature, forcing you to power off fully and back on between play sessions.

Evercade Nexus

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

There are some upgrades to the underlying tech, though. One material improvement is the battery, which jumped to a 5,000-mAh cell from the EXP's 3,000 mAh. Even with that bigger, brighter screen sucking up juice, the Nexus offers around five hours of play between charges, roughly an hour longer. On the audio front, the integrated front-facing stereo speakers are solid, offering louder, clearer output. Even better, the Nexus now supports Bluetooth, finally allowing you to connect wireless headphones, while still offering a 3.5-mm jack for wired headsets.

Bluetooth isn’t the only connectivity upgrade. The Nexus now supports the Wi-Fi 6 standard and can connect to 5-GHz networks (previous models could only use slower 2.4-GHz ones). That’s useful for downloading console updates and Evercade’s free Game of the Month. It also enables the new EverSync feature, unique to the Nexus, which allows multiple units to communicate wirelessly. Much like Nintendo’s GameShare, it’s set to allow multiplayer across devices even with only one cartridge, although I haven't been able to test this feature yet.

The underlying OS also gets a refresh. Hop into the settings menu and you'll find new customization tools. These let you adjust the color palette for the menu background and the glowing LED Nexus logo, select onscreen borders for non-widescreen games, and even tweak aspect ratios and virtual scan lines—all nice ways to personalize your device.

The glaring omission is any form of TV connectivity. Previous handheld Evercades featured a mini-HDMI out port, but that’s removed entirely here. It was always a nice-to-have rather than a major selling point, but it’s disappointing to lose a feature. Evercade players wanting TV play will have to opt for the Evercade VS-R set-top console.

While the Nexus hardware is a significant improvement, more exciting is where the games themselves may be heading. Almost every game on Evercade to date has been from the 8-bit or 16-bit era, if not earlier, a period that near-universally consisted of 2D titles. Adding thumbsticks opens the door to an entirely new generation of 3D games. Blaze says the Nexus works with 32- and 64-bit games, which dramatically expands possibilities for future releases.

More impressively, the first two cartridges to benefit from this generational leap also see Evercade step beyond emulation for the first time. Both the Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie double-pack and the DOOM and DOOM II collection are natively ported. That means improved performance, intentional widescreen aspect ratios to match the display, higher resolutions up to 60 frames per second, and on-cartridge save slots rather than virtual quick saves.

Evercade Nexus

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Banjo duology is the real standout so far, with the colorful worlds of Rare’s classic 3D platformers shining on the Nexus’ superior screen while taking full advantage of the dual thumbsticks (something the N64 controller lacked) to offer smoother camera controls alongside free movement. These are authentic and accessible versions of 64-bit gaming greatness, without compromise. This might be the best way to play this pair of games, period, and all the better for being able to do so portably. (For anyone who’s looked up the price of a Banjo-Tooie cart on the secondary market, a bargain, too.) The DOOM collection also holds up well, with classic boomer shooters and a stack of bonus missions and map packs, but as some of the oldest examples of first-person shooters, they show their age more.

The ports are to Evercade as an ecosystem, meaning the cartridges will still play on existing hardware—even Blaze’s budget Super Pocket devices—with camera controls mapped to shoulder buttons, albeit with a slower rotational view. It also partly explains the lack of power upgrades for the Nexus, as cross-device compatibility is a signature of the collection. Still, as Blaze works its way through gaming history, it feels as though a future Evercade will inevitably have to make a break to offer more power and support more recent games.

For now, though, the Nexus is hands-down the best way to play both Evercade’s vast library of games and this new pseudo-generation of native releases. With its better screen, bigger form, and added controls for 3D games, it’s a delight to play on. If Blaze can keep up the momentum with more dedicated ports, this will be a bright new age for the best old games.
